->**Hermetic Philosophy**<-

In the center of this page is a pasted circular emblem, a symbolic bookplate representing the core tenets of the hidden arts. 

The outer ring of the emblem bears the title **Hermetic Philosophy**, referring to the ancient tradition of knowledge attributed to Hermes Trismegistus. Within this ring sits a blue oval bordered in green, containing several layers of symbolic meaning:

At the very top, a **golden sun** radiates light downward, representing the divine source of life and the "Gold" of the perfected spirit. 

In the center, a **white pelican** is depicted in an act of "piety." <term>Pelican in its Piety: A traditional symbol where the mother bird pierces her own breast to feed her young with her blood; in alchemy, this represents the "Red Work" or the stage of projection and multiplication, where the philosopher's stone is used to transform other substances.</term> The pelican sits within a nest shaped like a crescent moon, suggesting the influence of the celestial bodies on earthly transformation.

At the base of the image lies a square block divided into four quadrants. Each quadrant contains a **red rose**, a clear reference to **Rosicrucianism** <note>The "Rose Cross" symbolism generally signifies the blooming of the soul through the physical hardships of the material world, often represented by the four-sided cross or square</note>.

# PREFACE

*...bringing them to light: so that men, eager for this most excellent and most useful **art**<note>original: "ars." In this period, "art" referred to a practical skill or craft based on specific rules, as opposed to pure theory.</note>, may be able to use and enjoy them. But someone will say that I, through these editions of mine, bring more harm than benefit to the **commonwealth**<note>original: "reipub." (reipublicae). In the 16th century, this often referred to the "Republic of Letters"—the international community of scholars—as much as the general public.</note>, since the art is vain and is no **science**<note>original: "scientia." Here meaning a systematic body of knowledge based on certain, demonstrable principles.</note> at all: because it deals not with things that are entirely certain, but with things that are uncertain and rarely happen—indeed, most rarely, or perhaps never—according to the opinions of many. For they claim that no one, in our own or the preceding century, has actually performed those things which the **writers** of this art so magnificently and in so many ways promise. Since it therefore lacks its intended **goal**<note>original: "fine." In the Aristotelian sense, the "finis" or "end" is the purpose for which a thing exists or the result it is meant to achieve.</note>, and since all things are done for the sake of a goal, it follows that there is neither art nor science here, and that those who engage in these things are ridiculous and foolish, or else believe in shiftless impostors. To these critics, enough and more has already been responded by excellent and most learned **philosophers** through certain demonstrations, and the **truth** of this art has been proven (especially...*

*...[the] ignorant and unskilled judge. For to the inexperienced* <note>original: "Inexperto." <meta>This page follows the end of the preface. The previous page ended with an exhortation to the reader to enjoy the works with a grateful heart and a "Farewell." This page begins a new section titled "Propositions or Maxims of the Chemical Art."</meta>

# PROPOSITIONS OR
## THE GREATEST MAXIMS OF THE
### *Chemical Art.* <note>original: "Ars Chemica." While "Chemica" eventually became modern chemistry, here it refers to the "Art" of alchemy.</note>

---

### PROPOSITION I.

Every pure and clean extract taken from its ore <term>minera: the raw mineral or ore from which metals are extracted</term>, from stones, or from foreign matter, which—without some preparation—does not melt like wax, is unsuitable for this work. From this, it is concluded that all metals are excluded, as are all species of Marcasite <term>Marchasitæ: a term used then for various mineral sulfides that look like metallic ores but are brittle</term>, glass, crystal, coral, and all pearls which do not liquefy in fire.

### *Proposition II.*

Every sublimable substance <term>sublimabile: a substance capable of "sublimation," turning directly from a solid into a vapor when heated</term> which adheres to the sides of the vessel, preventing the sight of foreign matter within the vessel, is remote from and unsuitable for this undertaking <note>original: "negocio," referring to the "Great Work" of alchemy</note>. For this reason, all four principal spirits <term>spiritus principales: in alchemy, "spirits" are volatile substances that vaporize easily</term> are especially excluded: namely, quicksilver <note>original: "argentum vivum," or mercury</note>, arsenic, sulfur, and every kind of tutty <term>tutiæ: zinc oxide collected from the flues of smelting furnaces</term> and magnesia <term>magnesiæ: a term used historically for various minerals, often manganese or magnetic iron ore</term>.

<summary>This page introduces the foundational rules of the alchemical "Chemical Art," defining which substances are unsuitable for the work. It specifically excludes non-melting minerals, metals, and volatile "spirits" like mercury and sulfur from this particular process.</summary>

<keywords>Propositions, Alchemy, Marcasite, Sublimation, Four Spirits, Mercury, Arsenic, Sulfur, Tutty, Magnesia</keywords>

--- Page 17 ---
<meta>This page continues the "Propositions or Maxims of the Chemical Art" from the previous page. While the previous section excluded common metals and volatile "spirits" like mercury and sulfur, this page further defines the boundaries of the alchemical materials by excluding animal and vegetable matter.</meta>

### PROPOSITION III.

Every mineral that does not possess the nature of earth is foreign and hostile to this work. From this, all things that come from animals are excluded, such as hair, blood, flesh, dung, eggs, and the like; and also all animals themselves, such as turtles, beetles <note>original: "caragdi," likely referring to beetles or other hard-shelled organisms often mentioned in catalogs of natural history</note>, moles, frogs, bees, and similar creatures.

### PROPOSITION IV.

Any thing that is animate, or that proceeds from inanimate things <note>The text here says "inanimatis" (inanimate), though the examples provided—wine and vegetables—are organic. The author is likely distinguishing between the "living" mineral used in alchemy and ordinary organic or inert matter.</note>, is unsuitable for this greater art. From this proposition, all animal superfluities <term>superfluitates: bodily secretions or waste products</term> are especially excluded, as well as all vegetables and everything that comes from them—such as wine, "burning water" <term>aqua ardens: distilled alcohol or spirits</term>, oil, honey, urine, semen, and similar things.

### PROPOSITION V.

Anything which cannot be blackened, whitened, and reddened <note>These three colors represent the core stages of the alchemical process: Nigredo (black), Albedo (white), and Rubedo (red)</note> by fire within one hour of a natural day, does not enter into the composition of this work as the principle of masculinity <note>original: "masculineitatis," referring to the active or "male" agent in the alchemical "marriage" or reaction</note>.

<meta>catchword: Propo-</meta>

<summary>These propositions define the "Chemical Art" by excluding all animal and vegetable substances, as well as any mineral that cannot undergo the three essential color changes (black, white, and red) under the influence of fire.</summary>
<keywords>alchemy, animal substances, vegetable substances, aqua ardens, masculine principle, Nigredo, Albedo, Rubedo, alchemical maxims</keywords>

--- Page 18 ---
<meta>This page continues the "Propositions or Maxims of the Chemical Art." Having previously excluded organic matter and defined the "masculine" principle, the text now defines the "feminine" principle and the necessity of duality and simplicity in the alchemical process.</meta>

### *Proposition VI.*

Everything that lacks red smoke <note>original: "fumo rubeo"; in alchemical practice, the appearance of colored vapors often signaled the presence of specific spirits or the success of a sublimation</note>, when enclosed in a small vessel over a proper fire, does not enter into the composition of this work in the role of the feminine principle <note>original: "foemineitatis"; the passive or receptive partner in the "chemical marriage"</note>. From the two aforementioned maxims, alums and salts are excluded, as well as every kind of borax <term>baurachiorum: alkaline salts or boraxes used as fluxes</term> and vitriols <term>gignarum: likely referring to metallic salts or vitriolic "seeds"</term>, and all liquids derived from them.

### *Proposition VII.*

No single thing <note>original: "vnius numeri," literally "of one number"</note> can complete a work of a higher order. ### Proposition XI.

Every medicine <term>medicine: in alchemy, this refers to the refined substance or Elixir that heals "diseased" base metals into pure gold</term> that cannot multiply itself infinitely is not part of the intention of the work of the higher order <note>original: "operis maioris ordinis"; this refers to the "Great Work" (Magnum Opus), the highest level of alchemical achievement</note>. ### Proposition XII.

Whatever exceeds the value of one ounce of pure gold is not of the intention of the higher order. And from this it is chiefly gathered that those things which compose the physical stone <term>physical stone: another name for the Philosopher's Stone</term>, if they exceed one ounce of pure gold in cost, they are not of the intention of the higher order. And from this it chiefly follows that 15 grains of ferment <term>ferment: the "yeast" or starter substance added to the alchemical matter to trigger transformation</term> are suitable for the work of the higher order, because they are purchased at a cheap price <note>original: "vili precio"; a common alchemical trope is that the "First Matter" of the Stone is something common and inexpensive, overlooked by the ignorant</note>.

### PHILOSOPHY

a 2

...thins the air. <note>The word fragment "-ti" from the previous page completes "extenuati," referring to the thinning or refining of the air.</note> Know, O **Assembly**, that the density <term>density: original "spissitudo," referring to the physical thickness, weight, or "grossness" of matter</term> of the four beginnings <note>original: "quatuor initiorum," the four elements: fire, air, water, and earth</note> rests in the earth alone. This is because the dense part of fire falls into the air; the dense part of air, along with that which is gathered from the dense part of fire, falls into the water. The dense part of water, and that which is joined together from the dense part of fire and air, rests in the earth. Thus the density of these four rests in the earth, and they are joined together within it. Therefore, the earth itself is denser than all the other elements, as is clearly apparent and can be seen. Fire, however, is rarer <term>rarer: original "rarior," meaning more subtle, thin, or less physically substantial</term> than the others; and just as the earth, being denser, is lower, so fire is higher and more noble. Air is indeed less rare than fire, and water in turn is less rare than air. For everything cold and moist is of less rarity than that which is hot and moist. And earth is of less rarity than water, because it is cold and dry; and everything cold and dry is less rare than that which is cold and moist.

When He was alone, He created four "simples" in number, which are the four elements <note>The four elements: Earth, Water, Air, and Fire</note>. Once they were created, He then created all things from them, both of the sublime and the inferior realms. This was because it was necessary for all creatures to be drawn from a specific root, from which they might multiply to inhabit the world. Therefore, before all things, God created the four elements, and afterward, He created whatever He willed from them—namely, various natures, some of which He created from only one element.

And **THE ASSEMBLY asks**: What things were created from two?

The Sun, however, and the Moon and stars, were created from a composite of fire and air.

->a 4<-

...created things come forth, which are also most precious. However, of those elements that come together, two are seen and touched, while two are neither seen nor touched. For if only those which are seen and touched are joined, without doubt the remaining ones are also mixed in, being present within the first two. But if you mix **our copper** <term>our copper: original "æs nostrum," referring to the specific alchemical starting material rather than common metal</term>, which is Earth, with Water, you will accomplish a great thing. 

**For** when our very copper is placed with **sea water** <note>original: "aqua maris"; in alchemy, this often refers to a salted solvent or "mercurial water" rather than literal ocean water</note> and cooked, it reveals Earth, drinking in the water and embracing the other two elements within itself. This is signified by the process of the work—namely, by the grinding and the coagulation <note>the thickening or solidifying of a liquid</note> of the **Stone** <term>Stone: the "Lapis," the goal of the alchemical process</term>—and immediately from these, **coins** <note>original: "nummos"; these represent the successful units or "tokens" of transformed matter</note> are made. But I shall hear what each of you is prepared to treat and say regarding this matter. Meanwhile, you may begin your exposition in such a way that it is not recognized by the foolish, yet not ignored by the sons of doctrine <note>a traditional term for students of alchemy</note>. And you, Aristenes, speak first.

**Aristenes** said: The key to this work is the **art of coins**. Take, therefore, the body which has been shown to you and fit it into thin plates. Next, place them in the water of our sea, which, while it is being governed, is called **Permanent Water** <term>Permanent Water: original "Aqua permanens," a solvent that dissolves metals into their primary state without evaporating</term>. Afterward, place it over a light fire until the plates are broken down and become water. Join this to the **Ethelia** <term>Ethelia: a term likely derived from the Greek "aithale," meaning a vapor, smoke, or a volatile spirit that rises during heating</term>, and roast them together over a slow fire until a **thick broth** <note>original: "brodium faginatum," literally a "fatted broth," describing the dense, oily consistency of the chemical mixture</note> is made. Then turn it into its own Ethelia until it is coagulated and becomes a varied coin...

# THE ASSEMBLY

...which we call the **flower of the sun** <note>original: "solis florem"; a poetic name for alchemical gold or the vital essence extracted from it</note>. Grind this with patience, and do not let it weary you to saturate it with the water that came out of it—which is the **permanent water** <note>original: "aqua permanens"; a stable, philosophical solvent that does not evaporate when heated</note>—until it becomes red. <meta>This page continues the "Turba Philosophorum" (The Assembly of the Philosophers), a foundational alchemical text presented as a transcript of a great meeting of sages. The previous page concluded the instructions of Pandulphus regarding the "permanent water" and the "white world," which signifies the albedo (whitening) stage of the Work. Here, the philosopher Ardarius takes the floor to provide specific technical instructions on the timing and substances required for the stone’s transformation.</meta>

# THE ASSEMBLY

**Ardarius** said: I will describe to you the **management of the stone** <note>original: "Regimen lapidis"; the specific set of rules, temperatures, and stages required to successfully create the Philosopher's Stone</note> and its composition. Take the hidden and honorable secret, which is **white magnesia** <note>original: "magnefies alba"; in alchemy, this is not modern magnesium but a cryptic name for a primary material, often associated with the "white" stage of purification</note>, which is mixed with the **living spirit** <note>original: "vivo"; likely referring to *argentum vivum* or quicksilver/mercury</note>. But you must not take it unless it is pure and clean; place it in its own vessel, and pray to God that He might grant you to see this greatest stone. 

Then cook it slowly. When you have drawn it out, see if it has become black; and if it is so, you have managed it excellently. But if it is not, manage it with the **white secret**, which is the greatest mystery, until the **blackness** <term>nigredo</term> <note>The first major stage of the alchemical "Great Work," symbolizing the death or decomposition of the old form before rebirth</note> appears—and indeed, a pure blackness, which lasts for exactly forty days. 

Afterward, grind it with its preparations, which are the **flower of copper** <note>original: "flos aeris"; typically refers to the green film or "verdigris" that forms on copper, used as a reagent</note> and **Indian gold** <note>original: "aurum Indicum"; a poetic or technical term for a specific yellow-colored precipitate or refined substance</note>, whose root is made of **saffron ointment** <note>original: "unguento croceo"</note> and **fixed alum**. Therefore, cook this diligently for forty days; when this is completed, God will show you the beginning of the stone. 

Cook it again, and soak it with the remaining **gum** <note>original: "gumi"; alchemical shorthand for a viscous, binding liquid or the "mercurial glue" that holds the matter together</note>, knowing that as many times as you soak the ash, it must be dried just as many times, and moistened again, until its color turns into that which you seek. 

Beyond these things, know that the perfection of this precious stone lies in managing it with a third part of the medicine, while keeping two parts back to moisten it in turns, cooking it until the proper color is reached. Let the fire be more intense than the first, until the matter flows like wax—which, when it is dried, holds itself together. Cook it, therefore, until it drinks the **glue of gold** <note>original: "colla auri"; likely referring to *chrysocolla*, a material used in soldering gold, but here used metaphorically for the final bonding of the stone's elements</note>, and when it is dried...

# THE ASSEMBLY

### OF THE PHILOSOPHERS

...Look, children of doctrine, how painters cannot paint with their colors until they turn them into ashes and pulverize them. Similarly, philosophers often cannot compose medicines for their sick unless the ingredients are broken and pulverized. Because if you manage that ash subtly, many things will proceed from it, for the reason that **copper** <term>copper: original Latin "aes"; in alchemy, this rarely refers to common copper but rather to the "Philosophical Copper" or the base metallic body chosen for the work.</term>, like a man, has a body and a spirit. Man’s breathing is from the air; similarly, copper, having breathed in moisture, receives life and is multiplied and increased like all other things. 

And for this reason, the philosophers said that when copper is burned, it becomes better than it was before. Furthermore, this copper of ours, when it is first cooked, becomes water; then, the more it is cooked, the more it is thickened, until it becomes a stone surpassing every metal. Afterward, it is broken, soaked, and roasted with a more intense fire until it is colored and becomes like *burnt blood* <note>original: "combusto sanguini similis"; a stage in the alchemical process where the matter takes on a deep red hue, often called the "Rubedo" or Reddening.</note>; then place the coins <note>original: "nummos"; likely referring to the small pieces of metal or the specific weights of the material being transformed.</note> into it, and it dyes them into gold. 

For just as sperm is not made from blood unless it is diligently cooked in the liver <note>original: "epate"; refers to the medieval physiological belief that the liver was the site of "concoction" or the refining of bodily fluids.</note>, so our work is by no means a **tincture** <term>tincture: a substance capable of "staining" or transforming the inner nature and color of a base metal into a noble one.</term> unless it is diligently cooked until it becomes powder, and thus through **putrefaction** the sperm itself is made spiritual in its effect. For then the color which you have sought will be found, and not otherwise.

**NICARUS** <note>Another speaker in this philosophical assembly; his name, like many in the Turba, may be a corrupted version of a Greek or Arabic name.</note> says: I command those who come after us to take the gold which they wish to multiply and reno- <meta>catchword: uare (to renew)</meta>

Therefore, putrefy it diligently until it becomes a spiritual powder in the color of dried blood, which color the power of the fire introduces, until it is clothed in an invariable color.

**ZEUMON** says: The sayings of the Egyptians lead us into error. ### THE PHILOSOPHERS

That which is precious is not made without that which is vile, nor that which is vile without that which is precious. Therefore, it behooves you to follow the sayings of the elders, who said: Nothing else is of use to you except to sublime the water and the vapor. For when you see those two purified natures become water, and the entire body of **Magnesia** <term>Magnesia: In medieval alchemy, this does not refer to the modern element magnesium, but to a mysterious "mother-substance" or raw mineral mass believed to contain the seed of gold.</term> melted into water, then certainly all things are vapor; by right, then the vapor contains its companion—that is, water [contains] water.

Wherefore the philosophers named both "vapor," because they are united together in **putrefaction** <term>putrefactio: the stage of the "Great Work" where the material decomposes and turns black, signifying the death of its old form before a new one can be born.</term> and **decoction** <term>decoctio: the process of prolonged heating or "boiling" the substance to refine it.</term>, and one contains the other so that it does not flee <note>In alchemical texts, a substance that "flees" is volatile and evaporates; the goal is to "fix" it so it remains stable under heat.</note>. Therefore, they become permanent. For the hidden nature is congealed in the body, and its color is changed, and it casts off its own nature, and is bound so that it does not flee. 

If **blackness** <term>nigredo: the black stage, considered the most difficult and essential part of the transformation.</term> appears, it is out of sickness, and it dies in putrefaction, and becomes **rust** <note>original: "rubigo"; here referring to a reddish or orange oxidation that signals the transition from the black stage toward the final red stage.</note>, and then by the law of nature it does not flee, because it has dismissed the servitude of flight, and the nature has been made free, following its spouse, adorning him with its color and beauty—not as it had done before, but having taken up the **gold coin** <note>original: "nummo aureo"; a metaphor for the "solar" or golden principle that provides the final perfection and life to the substance.</note>, it gives him life. 

And the philosophers have called this nature the **spirit** and the **soul**. Furthermore, they said that the moist spirit is black, yet lacking in defilement. And just as in man there is humidity and dryness, so in our work there is nothing else than vapor and water. For this reason, the ancients said o-

...Therefore he shall be patient of spirit <note>original: "longanimis"; implying the steadfast and enduring temperament required for the years of labor in alchemical practice.</note>, and will freely enjoy the fruits of patience; such a man shall walk in the just path of **this art** <term>this art: Alchemy, specifically the "Great Work" (Ars Magna) of transmuting matter and soul.</term>. Therefore, fear God, O **seekers**! For that which you seek is by no means of small value. You seek the greatest treasure and the most excellent gift of God.

...the philosophers have composed in all things, truth is always in their writings. **HYARGVS** says: The **bronze** <note>original: "Æs"; philosophers used the names of common metals like bronze, lead, or tin to refer to "philosophical" substances rather than the base metals found in a marketplace.</note> of which the Philosophers spoke before is not that of the common people, nor is it common tin; rather, it is our "body," which must be mixed with the body of **Magnesia** <term>Magnesia: Not the modern element magnesium, but a "mother" substance or prime matter used to draw the spirit into the physical body of the work.</term>, so that it may be cooked and ground without weariness until it becomes a stone. **MUNDUS** says: Enough has been said about rust; therefore, I shall speak about the poison <note>original: "veneno"; here, "poison" does not mean a toxin, but rather a "penetrating medicine" or the transformative elixir that "attacks" and changes the nature of base metals</note>. The poison is not a physical body, because the subtle spirits have made it a thin spirit itself; they have tinted the body and turned it into poison. The philosophers assert that this poison tints every body: and for this reason, they believe that whoever turns gold into poison has already reached his goal; but he who has not, has achieved nothing. But I say that unless you thin these things with fire, until those things rise like spirits, you have as yet perfected nothing.

You investigators of this art must also be informed that this sulfur could not whiten the copper until it was itself whitened in the prior work; for the habit of this sulfur is to **flee** <term>flee|To volatilize or evaporate when exposed to heat; a major challenge for early chemists was keeping "spirits" from escaping the vessel.</term>. Therefore, when its thick bodies flee and the vapor is **sublimated** <term>sublimated|The process where a substance is heated until it becomes a gas and then cools back into a solid on the upper part of the vessel, effectively purifying it.</term>, then you must contain it with another **quicksilver** <note>original: "argento vivo"; mercury.</note> of its own kind so that it does not flee. This happens as soon as the quicksilver and the copper itself are joined. For then they often mutually dissolve and conceive, and do not allow [the spirit] to flee, but both become quicksilver. And so, this which at first was neither copper nor quicksilver, was nevertheless made [into one] by the mixture of quicksilver: which, being added to the quicksilver, contains the former quicksilver that used to flee. Wherefore the philosophers said:

> **Sulfurs are contained by sulfurs.** <note>original: "Sulphura sulphuribus continentur." This is a famous alchemical axiom suggesting that like-substances must be used to stabilize or "fix" one another.</note>

Know further that sulfurs dye, and then undoubtedly flee, unless they are joined to quicksilver of their own kind. Therefore, do not think that this thing which dyes and then flees is the **coin** <note>original: "nummus"; a metaphor used for the alchemical stone or its base material.</note> of the common people; rather, the philosophers' intention is the "coin" which, unless it is mixed with the white or the red (which is quicksilver of its own kind), will undoubtedly flee. I command you, therefore, to mix quicksilver with quicksilver, until they become one and the same clean water, composed of the two. This, therefore, is the greatest **secret** <note>original: "arcanum".</note>,

**EXIMENUS** said: The philosophers have named our philosophy and our work by many and almost all the names of metals; but however they may call it, they always signify the **water** itself. Now the water receives them into its vessel and repels the flame of the fire from them. Quicksilver <note>original: "vivum"; short for *argentum vivum*</note> appears white to the sight, but when smoke <note>vapor or fumes from the fire</note> reaches it, it turns into red and becomes **Cambar**, which is to say, poison. **BODillus** <note>One of the legendary sages in the Turba Philosophorum, a text composed of a fictional debate between pre-Socratic philosophers.</note> said: All you disciples should know that nothing useful is made from the elements without the mixing of the male and the female, and the governance of heat: because the seed <term>seed|sperma; in alchemy, the vital essence or the combination of "Sulfur" and "Mercury" that begins the Great Work.</term> is generated from blood and desire. Thus, therefore, you must act in this art. And although it has many names, it is nonetheless named by one name, in which there is no difficulty: that which is most common of all things, by that name it is especially signified. <note>This refers to the alchemical trope that the "First Matter" is something cheap and common that people often overlook or discard.</note> But whoever names it more properly and aptly, renders it obscure and less to be understood. And in truth, it has but one name, and where it is of no use, there it is named magnificently and significantly: where it is useful, it is greatly concealed. It is a stone and not a stone, it is also spirit, soul, and body: it is white, black, and red, brassy, <term>Tyrian|tyrius; a prestigious deep purple or crimson dye</term>, and displayed in all the colors of the world. It is heavy, solid, unmoved by fire, unmoved by water, unmoved by wind: but also very light, hollow, spongy, moved by fire, moved by water, moved by wind: it is salty, it is...

# THE PRINTER
## To the Reader.

*It has pleased us, kind Reader, so that we might look out for your benefit, to also include another copy of the **Assembly** <note>original: "Turbæ exemplar"; referring to the "Turba Philosophorum" (The Assembly of the Philosophers), one of the oldest and most influential Latin alchemical texts, written as a transcript of a meeting between ancient sages</note> which we had in our possession, not so much because of a different order of contents, but rather for the variety of opinions and the names of the philosophers.* *For it happens that in the other volume, the same idea may be expressed with a different meaning, in different words, and attributed to another author; this is done so that in a matter of such great importance you may not go astray, but instead may follow in your **operations** <note>alchemical laboratory processes or experiments</note> whichever version appeals to you more.* *Farewell; and if you derive any benefit from this, you shall attribute it to that most distinguished and excellent Physician, Master William Rascalon of Worms <note>William Rascalon (Guilielmus Rascalonus) was a 16th-century physician from Worms, Germany, who provided the manuscripts for this edition</note>, through whose generosity we obtained these copies.*

Air, however, since it is hot and moist, shares a harmony with the moisture of water and the heat of fire; and for this reason, a generative friendship <note>original: "amicitia generans"; the alchemical concept where a middle element reconciles two opposites to allow for the creation of something new</note> is formed. Behold all the fruits which are made from thin aerial vapor, because life is shown to come from the air through the heat of the sun; and this is by God’s decree.

## DOCTRINE II.

**Ysindrus** <note>Likely a corruption of a Greek name, possibly Hesiod or Anaximenes, as this text often distorts classical names</note>. I praise the aerial things, for the work itself is refined by air. When it is thickened, it becomes thin; when it is heated, it becomes cold. Its thickness <term>thickness: (Latin: *spissitudo*) in this context refers to density or the materialization of a substance from a spirit-like state</term> occurs when it is dispersed in the heavens because of the sun’s distance. But its thinness occurs when, the sun being high, the air melts and becomes clear. It happens similarly in the temperament of Spring, in the distinction of a season that is neither hot nor cold. For according to the change of the established arrangement, to change the divisions of the year, winter is changed: therefore the air is thickened then, when the sun is moved far away from it. But when the air becomes thin, the sun is near; and when it is near, its heat reaches humanity.

## STATEMENT X

EXIMENUS <note>original: *Eximenus*; likely a corruption of the name Anaximenes, the Pre-Socratic philosopher</note>. All things were created from the four elements: namely the heaven, the thrones, the angels, the sun, the moon, the stars, fire, air, the sea, and all waters, the earth, and things diverse and similar. Listen, my dearest ones, for I have not related these descriptions of the elements to you in vain. For in them lies a hidden secret: namely, that of those elements, two are visible, and their power and work are known; while the other two are truly not seen nor touched, nor is their power or work seen, except within the first two elements. And unless those four elements are joined together, they accomplish nothing. Do not, therefore, consume your souls and your money in vain, nor bring sadness to your hearts. For you will accomplish nothing unless you turn the aforementioned copper into white, and make **coins** <note>original: *numos*; literally "coins" or "tokens," often used in this text to refer to the processed alchemical material in a specific, fixed form</note> through experience; thereafter, you must make that white thing red, until the tincture is completed. Therefore, break that copper, burn it, and deprive it of its blackness <note>the *nigredo* or blackening stage, associated with putrefaction</note> by cooking, moistening, and washing it until it becomes white; then bind it by the art.

### THE TWELFTH OPINION

**PARMENIDES** <note>A famous pre-Socratic Greek philosopher, here cast as one of the authoritative masters in the alchemical assembly</note>: Know that the **envious ones** <term>the envious: a common alchemical term for previous authors who intentionally used confusing metaphors to hide secrets from the "unworthy" or uninitiated</term> have written in many ways concerning waters, broths, bodies, and metals, in order to deceive those seeking this knowledge. [Perfec]t <note>Continuing from the previous page: "perfect the burnt copper"</note> it, knowing that unless you direct the natures of truth and their **combinations** <note>original: *complexiones*; referring to the balance of the four qualities—hot, cold, moist, and dry—within a substance</note>, and join blood-like things with blood-like things, you achieve nothing. Indeed, natures meet their own natures, and follow them, and rejoice in them, and when they rot, they are born. For Nature is governed, and in the same way she fell, she is raised up; and while she is destroyed, she is turned into dust and reduced to nothing: then she is reborn and renewed.

Strive, therefore, to know what it is that makes her rot and what renews her, and what its flavor is, and what its distance and proximity are, and how friendship arises after enmity, and how corruption and generation occur, and how those natures embrace each other, and how they become harmonious in a gentle fire.

Having noted and perceived these things, apply your hands to the work. But if you are ignorant of these stated qualities, do not approach the work; for it is entirely harmful, bringing misfortune and sorrow. Now, understand the words of the Sages, and keep this short saying in mind, namely: **Nature rejoices in nature, Nature contains nature, and Nature overcomes and conquers nature** <note>original: "Natura natura laetatur, & Natura naturam continet, & Natura naturam vincit & superat." In this single word the **whole work** <note>original: *totum opus*; the Great Work or the creation of the Philosopher's Stone</note> is contained.

### OPINION XIII.

LUCAS said: I shall speak on this matter, following in the footsteps of those who came before. ### FIFTEENTH OPINION

**ASSUBERES:** I say that sulphurs are contained by sulphurs, and moisture by moisture. ## PROPOSITION XVI

**Frictes** <note>Frictes is the sixteenth speaker in the Assembly. His name, like many in the Turba, may be a corruption of a Greek name, possibly related to "Anaxagoras" or "Democritus" in the textual tradition.</note> said: Know, seekers of wisdom: that the foundation of this art—for the sake of which many have perished—is indeed one thing that is stronger and more sublime than all natures among the philosophers; yet among beginners, it is the cheapest of all things. But we venerate this; and if kings recognized this, none of us would ever attain this matter. ## STATEMENT XVIII

**ZENON**. You have already taught the doctrine of how to create the white; what now of the red? I say that you cannot make the red unless you first strive to **whiten** <note>referring to *albedo*, the stage of purification where the matter becomes white, which must precede the final red stage, or *rubedo*.</note>: because the two natures are nothing other than the white and the red. Whiten the red, therefore, and turn the white into red, knowing that the year is divided into four seasons. The first season is of a cold nature: and it is **winter**. The second is of an airy nature: and it is **spring**. The third season is of a fiery nature: and it is **summer**. The fourth is **autumn**, in which the fruits are ripened.

# THE TURBA

...to those who come after, that there is an affinity between **Boritis** <term>Boritis: a cryptic alchemical substance, sometimes identified with a type of borax or a purifying flux used to cleanse metals.</term> and **copper** <note>original: *æs*; while this can mean bronze or brass, in the context of the *Turba*, it typically refers to the "philosopher's copper" or the base metallic soul.</note>, because the Boritis of the wise liquefies the copper and makes it as flowable as water. Therefore, divide the **poison** <term>venenum: in alchemy, "poison" often refers to a highly reactive or corrosive substance, such as a strong acid or a transformative mercury, which "kills" the base metal to prepare it for rebirth.</term> into two equal parts: in one part liquefy the copper; in the other part, grind, pound, and moisten the copper until it is drawn out into thin sheets. 

And cook it again with the first part of the poison until it drinks up two parts, and do this seven times; afterward, cook it for forty-two days. Then open the vessel, and you shall find the copper turned into **quicksilver** <note>original: *argentum vivum*; mercury.</note>. Wash this by cooking it until it is deprived of its blackness, and the copper will become "shadowless" <note>original: *umbra carens*; a state of purity where the "dark" or terrestrial impurities of the metal have been removed.</note>. 

Again, cook it continuously until it is congealed. Once it is congealed, it becomes the greatest **secret** <note>original: *arcanum*.</note>, which the philosophers have named **Boritis**. Cook that coagulated stone until it becomes like sea-brine; then soak it with the **permanent water** <term>aqua permanens: a central concept in alchemy representing a solvent that does not evaporate and has the power to dissolve and cook the "stone."</term> which I commanded you to keep, and cook it many times until its colors appear. 

This is the greatest **putrefaction** <term>putrefactio: the stage of the alchemical work symbolized by the color black, where the substance "dies" and decomposes before being purified and resurrected.</term>, which contains within itself the greatest secret. However, it is necessary for you to know that there is an affinity between the **Magnet** and **iron**, just as there is between copper and the permanent water. If, therefore, you govern the copper and the permanent water as I have commanded, the greatest secret will be made from it. 

Therefore, do it in this way: take quicksilver mixed with the **male** <note>original: *masculo*; likely referring to sulfur or a "fixed" metal that acts as the active, masculine principle to mercury's passive, feminine principle.</note>, and grind it strongly—but not with your hands—until it becomes a thin water. Divide this into two parts: in one part, cook it for forty days until it becomes a white flower, like the flower of salt...

### STATEMENT XXX

CUSTOS <note>The name means "Guardian." In the *Turba*, the speakers are often given names of historical or legendary figures.</note> says: I marvel, O Assembly of the Wise, at the great power of this water, which when it enters the body, turns it into earth, and then into powder. And you should know that if you take anything other than **our copper** <term>aes nostrum: not common metal, but the "philosophical" or prepared substance that serves as the base for the Great Work.</term>, and manage it with **our water** <term>aqua nostra: the secret alchemical solvent, often called "mercurial water."</term>, you will achieve nothing. Of these two, therefore, the nature is one, and a closeness is mixed between them; if this were not so, they would not combine so quickly, nor would they contain one another, nor become one.

**NICARUS**: I command those who follow us to take gold, and to multiply and renew it as they wish. Then, divide the water into two parts: with one, it is necessary to burn our copper. If you govern it well, it will become water which will be congealed by cooking, and then redness will appear. Therefore, soak this redness seven times with water, or until it drinks all its water; finally, cook it until it is dried out and turned into dry earth. Then, place it in a lit fire for forty days, and it will putrefy <note>original: *putrescet*; the alchemical stage of 'Putrefaction' or 'Nigredo,' where the matter rots and turns black to allow for new life and color to emerge.</note>, and its colors will appear.

### STATEMENT XXXVI.

**BARSENITES.** It is necessary to repeat what was said above. ### STATEMENT XXXVII.

**ZEUNON.** The sayings of the Egyptians lead us into error. That which we seek is sold publicly at a very low price, and if it were known, the merchants would not sell even the slightest bit of it. The Philosophers, however, have honored this vile and discarded thing, and have called it by every name: they said that it is a **stone and yet not a stone** <note>A famous alchemical paradox signifying that the "Philosopher's Stone" is a substance found everywhere but recognized by few.</note>, and that it is the **gum of Scotland** <note>original: *guma Scotiæ*; likely a corruption of *gummi Scythiae* (gum of Scythia) or a symbolic term for a sticky, resinous state of the matter during transformation.</note>. For this reason, the philosophers hid the power of this poison, because within it is the spirit you seek, which performs the tinting.

### PROPOSITION XLII.

**EFISTES** <note>This name likely refers to a participant in the assembly, possibly a corruption of a Greek name like Epistemon.</note> Pay attention, sons of doctrine, to what Hermes, the head of the Philosophers, said when he taught how to mix the natures. I command, however, that you do not pour the water all at once, lest the **Ysir** <term>Ysir: A variant of Yxir (Elixir), the transformative powder or catalyst.</term> be submerged: but pour it in little by little, grind, dry, and do this quite often, until they become water. And the philosophers said: Once the water is assimilated <note>original: "simitata". The method of managing heat and time.</note> bodies become spirits, and hot spirits are made that can tint <note>original: "tingunt". To 'tint' or 'dye' in alchemy means to successfully project the elixir onto a base metal to transform its color and nature into gold or silver.</note>.

### PROPOSITION LXIII.

**ADMION** <note>A speaker in the Assembly, likely a Latinized version of a Greek or Arabic name.</note> says: Wise men, you cannot reach the benefit of the art without a prolonged and continuous regimen <term>regimen: The controlled process of heating, timing, and chemical treatment required to transform the material.</term>. Therefore, he who is patient in the regimen will enter the art; but he who is not, let him not read our propositions, because they will cause him harm once read. And so the Master said: He who labors in reading our books, and devotes himself to them, not entangled in various thoughts, and prays to God, shall reign in a kingdom until he dies. For what is sought is not of little value, but is a gift of God; for this reason, there is need for patience and labor. For we see that he who grafts trees hopes for fruit in time; he who sows, reaps after months.

Watch therefore and learn to mix, to cook, to simulate <note>original: "simulare". In alchemical context, this often refers to "imitating" the natural process or achieving a specific appearance.</note>, to roast, to heat, to whiten <note>original: "dealbare". The stage of Albedo, or purification.</note>, to grind, to level the **Ethelia** <term>Ethelia: A term derived from the Greek word for "vapor" or "spirit," referring to the volatile substance that rises during sublimation.</term>, and to make the rust <note>original: "rubiginem". A reference to the reddening or "Rubedo" stage, the final part of the process.</note>, and finally to dye. These are many names, yet the regimen is one: but the decoction <term>decoction: The process of boiling or heating a substance in liquid to extract its essence or transform it.</term> is continuous, for which reason they have repeated it often, so that the compound may be ground and the cooking may be done perpetually; do not let the labor weary you. The goal, however, is that you adjust the temperaments <note>original: "complexiones". The balance of the four qualities: hot, cold, moist, and dry.</note>; then cook them in many ways, saturate the decoctions, and cook until the spirits become impalpable <note>original: "impalpabiles". So finely ground or refined that they cannot be felt by touch.</note>. And you shall see **Ysir** <term>Ysir: A variant of Yxir (Elixir), the transformative catalyst or "Stone."</term> clothed in a royal garment, and turned into a Tyrian color <note>Tyrian color: A deep purple or crimson dye, symbolizing the successful completion of the Great Work.</note>; then you will understand the sayings of the Philosophers.

### PROPOSITION XLIV.

**LARGUS** <note>A speaker in the Assembly; the name translates to "Bountiful" or "Abundant."</note> says: The Copper <note>original: "Æs." In alchemy, this rarely refers to the common metal, but rather a "philosophical" copper or the base material of the Great Work.</note> of which the first masters spoke is not copper, nor the tin of the common people; but rather it is our "body," which must be mixed with the body of **Magnesia** <term>Magnesia: In alchemical terms, this is not the modern chemical magnesium, but a "magnetic" or "attractive" primal matter, often described as a white or black earth that "draws" the spirit.</term>, so that it may be cooked and ground without weariness until it becomes a stone. Then, that stone is ground in a vessel with nitre water <note>original: "aqua nitri." A solution of saltpeter or a similar salty, acidic solvent.</note>, and it is liquefied until it is broken down. It is necessary, however, for you to have a water which, the more it is cooked, the more it thickens, until it acquires a rust <note>original: "rubiginem." This refers to the reddening or "Rubedo" stage, which signifies the nearing completion of the process.</note>, which is the very foundation of the work. Cook this, and grind it with Egyptian vinegar <term>Egyptian vinegar: An alchemical term for a highly potent, distilled solvent or acid capable of "mortifying" metals.</term>.

### PROPOSITION XLV.

**CADMON**. I signal to those who come after us that the round thing <note>original: "rotundum." The method of extraction is this: take one part of copper and three parts of permanent water <term>permanent water: Often referring to "mercury of the philosophers," a liquid that does not wet the hands and acts as a universal solvent.</term>; then let them be mixed and cooked until they thicken and become a single stone, of which the philosophers have said: Take one part of the sincere body and three parts of the copper of **Magnesia**; then mix them with "straight masculine vinegar" <note>original: "aceto recto masculino." A symbolic name for a strong, "active" acid.</note> mixed with earth, cover the vessel, and observe what is inside, and cook it continually until they become earth.

### PROPOSITION XLVI.

**ASCANIUS**. When we read in the books...

## SENTENCE XLVIII.

**Mosius** <note>original: *Mosius*. Likely a corruption of "Moses" or a specific sage named in the *Turba Philosophorum* tradition.</note> said: This one thing that has been mentioned so often, the philosophers have called by many names: sometimes by two names, and occasionally even by three. Now I shall tell you what it is: the first is that **fiery** thing; the second is the **composite** within it; and the third is the **water of sulfur**, by which the "one" is washed, ground down, and governed until it is completed. And this is what the philosopher hinted at when he said: The **quicksilver** <term>Quicksilver: Latin *argentum vivum*, or mercury.</term> that tinges gold is the quicksilver of **Cambar** <term>Cambar: A specialized alchemical term, here identified with Magnesia, but often associated with red lead or a specific state of the "living" metal.</term>.

The quicksilver of the late stage, however, is the orpiment or the **sulfur** that ascends from the mixed composite. 

Therefore, you must mix that thick substance with the **fiery poison** <note>original: *veneno igneo*. And again they said: "When all things become one, corporeal things are made incorporeal, and vice versa." 

Moreover, they said that every body is dissolved with the same spirit with which it is mixed; and that every spirit is altered and colored by the body in which the **dyeing color** <term>Dyeing color: Latin *color tingens*. Also known as a 'tincture,' this is the transformative power that allows the alchemist to change the color and nature of a substance.</term> resides. Blessed, therefore, be the name of Him who taught His chosen ones to turn the body into spirit; that spirit which possesses incorruptible heat, so that what had been a **fleeing sulfur** <note>original: *sulphur fugiens*. 'Fleeing' refers to volatility—the tendency of a substance to evaporate when heated.</note> is made into an **incombustible sulfur** <term>Incombustible sulfur: A stable, 'fixed' substance that can endure the fire without being consumed or evaporated.</term>.

Know further, sons of the doctrine, that he who can make the fleeing spirit red by means of the body joined to it, and then from that body and spirit can extract—with subtle skill—the thin nature hidden in its belly, has found the work. And note that by the length of cooking he dyes the body; this the philosophers expressed by saying: "When things are strongly ground and diligently cooked by fire, **fixed tinctures** <note>original: *tincturæ fixæ*. These are transformations that are permanent and can no longer be changed or undone by heat.</note> are created." And whatever they have narrated secretly in their books, they intended to signify **quicksilver**, which is sometimes called sulfur water, sometimes lead, and sometimes even a **coin** <note>original: *nummus*. Alchemical authors often used everyday names like 'coin' or 'money' as deck-names (*decknamen*) to hide the identity of their secret materials.</note>.

## PROPOSITION LVI.

**YS Imidrus** <note>Likely a corruption of a Greek or Arabic name, common in alchemical texts to lend authority to the discourse.</note>. Enough and more has been treated regarding the governance of the air and the moist spirit; I shall now complete what was omitted. In alchemy, it refers to a sublimated substance or a spiritualized vapor.</term>, of which mention was made above; when this water is whitened, it whitens and dyes. This the philosophers have called **Ethelia**, and **Orpiment** <term>Orpiment: Latin *Auri pigmentum*. From this, the **tincture** and the pure spirit ascend by a slow fire, and from this, the flower is sublimated. 

This entire secret is nothing other than quicksilver extracted by men—that is, through the agency of men. Furthermore, it must be known that to whiten the **secret copper** <note>original: *arcanum æs*. The hidden or inner essence of the base metal being worked upon.</note> does not...

### PROPOSITION 59

**Anaxagoras**. Take the burnt fugitive <note>original: *combustum fugiens*. This refers to a volatile spirit that has been subjected to fire.</note>, which lacks a body, and give it a body. **Constans**. What have we to do with the envious and their treatises? ## PROPOSITION LXXVII.

**Philotis**. The first composition, namely the **body of Magnesia** <note>Magnesia is a common alchemical term for the primary matter of the Stone, not necessarily the modern chemical magnesium.</note>, is made from many things: although they are made into one single thing, it is called one thing by the ancients, namely, **Albar of copper** <note>original: *Albar aeris*. ### PROPOSITION LXXVIII.

**AGMON**. As a corollary I say, that he who does not **liquefy and coagulate** <term>liquefy and coagulate <note>original: *liquefacit & coagulat*. This refers to the fundamental alchemical principle of *Solve et Coagula*: dissolving a substance to its base components and then recombining them into a higher form.</note></term>, errs in many ways. Therefore, **blacken** <note>This refers to the *Nigredo* stage, the first step in the Great Work, symbolizing death and the breakdown of matter.</note> the earth, and separate its soul and water, and afterwards **whiten** it <note>This refers to the *Albedo* stage, the second step of the process, representing purification and the "washing" of the matter.</note>, and you will find what you seek. I also tell you, that he who blackens the earth and dissolves the white with fire, until it becomes like a **naked sword** <note>original: *gladius denudatus*. Likely referring to the brilliant, sharp, or silver-like metallic luster of the purified substance.</note>, and who introduces the soul to that which was previously completely whitened, and **fixes** <term>fixes <note>original: *figit*. In alchemy, "fixing" means making a volatile substance stable so it no longer evaporates or changes when exposed to heat.</note></term> the whole with a **consuming fire** <note>original: *tabido igne*. Often implies a slow, melting heat that transforms the substance.</note> after it has been liquefied—that man deserves to be called happy and to be exalted above the circles of the world.

We do not doubt that this is enough for the **sons of doctrine** <note>A traditional term for students and practitioners initiated into the secrets of the alchemical art.</note> regarding the revelation of our **stone** <term>stone <note>original: *lapidis*. The Philosopher's Stone, the goal of the work, which is not a literal rock but a perfected substance.</note></term>, whose powers cannot be corrupted. If it is placed in fire, its power is increased; if you wish to **dissolve** it, it will be dissolved; if to **coagulate**, it will be coagulated. No one can be without it, and everyone needs it. And though it has many names, it is nonetheless known by a single name, and where the father is, there it is **hidden** <note>original: *cælatur*. This can mean 'hidden', 'carved', or 'sealed'.</note>. It is also a **stone and not a stone** <note>A classic alchemical paradox indicating that the material has physical form but divine or spiritual properties.</note>, spirit and soul and body. It is white, volatile, hollow, and **lacking hair** <note>original: *pilis carens*. A cryptic description used in the *Turba* to describe a smooth, refined state of matter or perhaps the appearance of mercury.</note>, which no one can touch with their tongue when cooled without injury. If you make it fly, it flies; and if you say it is water, you speak the truth; and if you say it is not water, you speak a falsehood. Not so—

# ALLEGORIES UPON THE book of the Turba.

The allegories upon the book of the **Turba** <note>original: *Turba Philosophorum*. This is one of the oldest and most influential Latin alchemical texts, presented as a gathering of philosophers discussing the secrets of nature.</note> begin. And first, concerning **man**.

Take a man, shave him, and draw <note>original: *trahe*. In this context, it implies a process of grinding, rubbing, or dragging the substance across a surface to break it down.</note> him over a stone or a metal plate until his body dies and its **density** <note>original: *spissitudo*. In alchemy, this refers to the solid, coarse, material state of a substance before it is purified or vaporized.</note> vanishes. Know for certain that once it has lost its density, it will become **spiritual**; afterward, return its soul to it. Next, place it in a bath for forty days so that, just as a seed dies in the womb—which is truly the beginning of nature's **regeneration**—a new creation may rise and the goal may be achieved.

Take a **bull** with its flesh and blood, its horns and its hooves, and turn it into water. Mix it with its blood and process the whole; afterward, roast it until it turns red. Afterward, turn the **copper** <note>original: *æs*. While this literally means copper or bronze, in alchemy it often refers to the "base" metal or the "body" of the material being transformed.</note> into divine tinctures.

Take a **Cock**, crowned with a red crest, and while it is alive, strip it of its feathers. Then, place its head in a glass vessel and keep it there for an hour. Afterward, store the cock again and process it until it is softened and purified, and spread it upon marble. Then, with the feathers having been removed from it, process and shear it very strongly. Then, leave it in **horse dung** <note>original: *equorum fimo*. Decaying horse dung was a standard laboratory tool for alchemists, used to provide a gentle, steady, and natural heat for fermentation or digestion.</note> until it grows feathers again. And when you hear that cock crowing like a living cock, know that you have walked the right path.

# ON THE TURBA <note>original: *Super Turbam*. This refers to the *Turba Philosophorum*, or "Assembly of the Philosophers," a foundational text in the Latin alchemical tradition.</note>

Take a **viper**, which is called *de rexa* <note>original: *de rexa*. Likely a technical or regional name for a specific type of snake, used here as an alchemical symbol for a volatile substance.</note>, and deprive it of its head and tail; in these two places its venom liquefies, from which the **spirit** <note>original: *spiritus*. In alchemy, the "spirit" is the volatile, vaporous essence of a substance that can be released through heat.</note> proceeds. Therefore, divide the head and the tail, and store each by itself in a glass vessel. Take the remaining body and cook it over a slow fire until the flesh is separated from the bones. And afterward, place the flesh upon a metal plate, and process it until the body is turned into **spirit**, and its **flexibility** <note>original: *flexibilitas*. This refers to the physical "toughness" or "oiliness" of the matter; the alchemist seeks to remove this to reach a dry, crystalline, or "spiritual" state.</note> is taken away from it. 

For that which is flexible cannot be refined. Then, join it to its head and grind it together until the body [is fully processed], so long as any flexibility remains within it. Dry a body of this kind in the sun or by the fire, so that you may see what you seek. Once this is completed, know that you have a **body penetrating bodies**, and a **nature containing nature**, and a **nature rejoicing in nature** <note>This triad—nature containing nature, nature overcoming nature, and nature rejoicing in nature—is one of the oldest and most famous axioms in alchemy, traditionally attributed to Bolos of Mendes.</note>, which is called the **perfection of the philosophers’ theriac** <term>theriac: originally a medicinal "universal antidote" against poison, used here to describe the alchemical Elixir that "cures" base metals into gold.</term>.

There is in the sea a **round fish**, lacking bones and skin, and it possesses within itself a fatness—a wonderful virtue—which, if it be cooked over a slow fire until its fatness and moisture completely depart, and afterwards is ground very strongly and soaked with seawater until it shines; then let it be buried for a week, and afterward let it be whitened by roasting. And when it has been well whitened, and its water restored to it: afterward let it be soaked in its own moisture; then, after the soaking in moisture, let it be roasted until it appears **yellow** <note>original: *citrinus*. The "citrinitas" or yellowing was a specific stage in the alchemical process, indicating the approach of the final "Red" work.</note>. It thus becomes the **philosophers’ eye-salve** <term>eye-salve: Latin *colirium*. An allegorical substance that allows the "eyes" of the practitioner to see the hidden truth of nature or completes the final tincture.</term>: with which, the eyes being anointed...

...the ancient secrets of the philosophers could easily be perceived. In the **moon of the sea** <note>original: *maris luna*. Men have **olives** from which they extract oil, and that oil is combustible. However, the **oil of the philosophers** is not extracted in this way. Nevertheless, its nature is combustible, and it always remains immobile. The method for making it is as follows: 

We take the olives, which we have kept clean and whole, and we grind them with their own water. Afterward, we boil them. We also cause the dregs to descend to the bottom, the water to stand in the middle, and the oil to flow out on top. Afterward, we separate the water. # FROM THE VISION OF ARISLEUS THE PHILOSOPHER, AND THE ALLEGORIES OF THE SAGES.

## *RIDDLE I.*

When some of the more diligent disciples of the philosophers had gathered once again, along with Pythagoras—the most senior of whom was Arisleus, son of Abladius, followed by Paris, son of Belchiotus, Armenius, son of Archias, Meditatalus, Phaliseus, Echamisius, Parmenides, and Eximesias, son of Admirus—Auerca <note>Likely a speaker within the dialogue or a variation of a name found in the *Turba* manuscripts.</note> asked Arisleus <note>Arisleus is a central figure in alchemical lore, often interpreted as a latinization of a Greek or Arabic name; he serves as the primary narrator of the "Vision."</note> whether he could explain, by means of an example or a parable, how those seeking the **art** <note>original: *artis*. In this context, "the art" is Alchemy, the sacred process of material and spiritual transformation.</note> might be allowed to gather fruit from that **immortal tree** <note>A symbolic representation of the Philosopher's Stone or the completed Alchemical Work, which grants "fruit" in the form of wisdom and health.</note> which the aforementioned disciples and the others in the **Assembly** <note>original: *Turba*. This refers to the *Turba Philosophorum* (The Assembly of the Philosophers), one of the oldest Latin alchemical texts, written as a debate between ancient sages.</note> had described. 

And he replied, "I will certainly speak as best I can, though perhaps I may not satisfy your specific wish." 

And Pythagoras spoke again: "Speak, then, as aptly as you are able." 

And Arisleus said: "I saw myself and certain others from the Assembly riding toward the shores of the sea, and behold, I saw the inhabitants of the sea lying together with one another, yet nothing was born to them; and they were planting trees, yet they bore no fruit; and they were sowing seeds, yet nothing grew. And I said to them: 'What is the matter with you? Even though there are so many of you, is there no philo- <note>The text cuts off here at "philo-", clearly intending to continue with "philosopher" on the following page.</note>

<summary>This page introduces an alchemical allegory where the philosopher Arisleus is asked to explain the secrets of the "immortal tree" through a parable. He describes a vision of a sterile seaside kingdom where the inhabitants mate and plant, but nothing grows, symbolizing a failed alchemical union.</summary>

"...[philoso]pher <note>The text begins mid-word: *[philoso]phus*.</note> is he who might teach you?" And they said to him: "What is a philosopher?" He replied: "One who knows the nature of things." And they asked: "What use is his knowledge?" And I <note>Arisleus, the narrator.</note> answered: "If a philosopher were among you, your children would be multiplied, and trees would be born for you that would not die, and their fruits would never fail; and you would be kings, overcoming all your enemies."

Leaving there, they reported these things to their lord, the **King of the Sea** <note>original: *Regi marino*. In alchemical allegory, the King of the Sea often represents the *prima materia* (prime matter) or the spirit hidden within the depths of substance.</note>. And when we had been summoned by him, and he demanded gifts from us, we replied that we carried **hidden gifts**, namely the **art of generating** <note>original: *generandi artem*. This refers to the alchemical power to "grow" or "multiply" metals and spiritual wisdom.</note>, and the art of planting trees and sowing seeds, from which trees and fruits whoever might eat would never hunger again.

And the King said: "That would be the greatest gift of all, if your master truly sent this. Tell me then, what do you have?"

And I said: "Lord, although you are a king, you rule and govern poorly: for you have joined males to males, knowing well that males do not produce offspring. For generation comes from the joining of the male and the female; and true generation occurs only if nature is joined to nature—the male to the female—like to like and fit to fit, and they are mixed together."

And he replied: "I do indeed have a son and a daughter, and for that reason I am king over my subjects, because they possess nothing of these things; yet I have carried this son and daughter within my own **brain** <note>A symbolic reference to the idea that the dual principles (male and female) originate from a single source or "Idea" before they are manifested.</note>."

And I said: "Lead your son **Thabritius** <note>original: *Thabritium*. In alchemical literature, Thabritius (or Gabricus) represents the solar/sulfuric principle—the active, masculine seed of the Work.</note> to us." Having heard this, I also demanded that his sister **Beya** <note>original: *Beyam*. Beya represents the lunar/mercurial principle—the receptive, feminine soul or "white woman" of the Work. The union of Thabritius and Beya is a central motif for the chemical marriage.</note> be brought to us.

<summary>Arisleus challenges the King of the Sea's rule, arguing that alchemical "generation" requires the union of male and female principles, leading to the introduction of the symbolic figures Thabritius and Beya.</summary>

# PHILOSOPHER.

The King said: "Why do you want **Beya** <note>original: *Beyam*. In alchemical allegory, Beya represents the feminine principle, the "white" substance often associated with the Soul or Mercury.</note>?" And I: "Because generation does not happen without her, and although she is the sister of her brother and a woman, she nevertheless improves him, because she is from him." But when Beya was brought forth, behold, she was a girl white, tender, and sweet. While we were joining **Thabritis** <note>original: *Thabritim* (also known as Gabricus). He represents the masculine principle, the "red" substance associated with Spirit or Sulfur.</note> and Beya, "Look," said the King, "has the man not taken his wife?" And I: "So our father Adam commanded his sons, and if you agree to this, O King, you will be blessed, and they will beget for you many kings and queens, grandsons and granddaughters; and your son Thabritis and his sister Beya will bring you profit, and if they should die, they shall live again."

But when the King agreed and the brother lay with the sister, behold, Thabritis died immediately. Therefore the king, cursing me and you, imprisoned us in a **glass house** <note>original: *domo vitrea*. This is a famous alchemical metaphor for the sealed glass flask or "philosopher's egg" where the chemical reaction—the 'marriage' and 'death'—must occur in isolation.</note>, above which house he built another, and above that yet another, and we were trapped in these three houses. Then I said to the King: "For what reason, in your haste, have you brought this punishment upon us? At least give us your daughter again; perhaps she will restore life to your son Thabritis." And he said: "Do you wish to kill my daughter as well?" And I: "Do not be hasty, King, to bring tortures upon us; wait a little while and give us your daughter, and shortly after you will have both son and daughter living again."

When she was given to us, she remained with us in the prison for eighty days, and we remained in the darkness of the waves, and in the intense heat of summer, and [the heat] of the sea...

## RIDDLE II.
### Concerning the Stone.

In our sea, there is a **little round fish** <note>original: *pisciculus rotundus*. A common alchemical metaphor for a specific substance—often interpreted as the "Salt of the Wise" or the hidden spark of life—found within the chaotic "sea" of the initial matter.</note>, lacking both bones and skin, which contains within itself a fatness and a wonderful virtue. When it is cooked over a silent fire until its moisture and fatness are entirely gnawed away and consumed, it must afterward be ground very forcefully and soaked in the water of the sea until it softens. Then it should be buried for a week; then roasted until it glows with heat. When it glows and has become sufficiently white, and its water is returned to it, it is afterward soaked in its own proper moisture. Finally, after this soaking of moisture until it appears yellow and is roasted, it becomes the **philosophers' eye-salve** <note>original: *collyrium philosophorum*. Historically, a *collyrium* was a medicinal eye-wash. Here, it is used metaphorically: the "Stone" grants the alchemist a new way of seeing and understanding the hidden laws of nature.</note>. When the eyes are anointed with its liquid, the secrets of the philosophers can easily be seen and understood.

->*Mercury speaks of himself.*<-

## DEFINITION OF THE STONE, AND
## of what principles it consists.

### *EXERCISE I.*

As we are about to treat of the **Stone of the Philosophers** <term>Lapis Philosophorum</term> <note>The legendary substance sought by alchemists, believed to be capable of transmuting base metals into gold and silver, and acting as a universal medicine.</note>, we must first see from what beginnings, or from what elements, the Stone of the philosophers consists. According to the consideration of all philosophers, **Mercury** <term>Mercurius</term> <note>In alchemy, Mercury is not just the liquid metal (quicksilver) but the feminine, fluid, and "mother" principle of all metals.</note> is the father of all metals. The philosophical Stone, moreover, is a metallic matter, converting the substances and forms of imperfect metals <note>Imperfect metals refers to "base" metals like lead, tin, or iron, which lack the stability and color of gold.</note>. That this conversion does not happen except through its own like <note>A reference to the alchemical axiom *similia similibus*, meaning that to change a metal, one must use a substance that shares its fundamental metallic nature.</note> has long since been proclaimed by all philosophers. It is necessary, therefore, for the Stone of the philosophers to be birthed from metallic matter. From which metallic species it may be generated, all the philosophers resound—especially in this little book <note>original: "libello"; refers to the *Turba Philosophorum*, one of the oldest and most influential Latin alchemical texts, written as a transcript of a debate among ancient sages.</note>—saying: that in Mercury is all that which

PHILOSOPHY.

It is sought by the wise. For by whatever reason its substance or form is joined to bodies, it receives such substance and form; and just as it is tinted by bodies, so it also tints <note>In alchemy, "tinting" or "coloring" refers to the process of transmutation, where the Stone imparts its golden quality to a base metal.</note>. And just as flesh is generated from coagulated blood, so also **Gold** <term>Sol</term> <note>original: "Sol" (the Sun). In alchemical texts, the Sun always represents Gold.</note> is generated from coagulated **Mercury** <term>Mercurius</term> <note>Mercury was seen as the "First Matter" of all metals; here it refers to a purified philosophical state rather than common quicksilver.</note>; and as blood is the origin of flesh, so is Mercury the origin of Gold. And as blood is in the flesh, so also Mercury is in the stone of the Sun: because Mercury itself is congealed into the stone of the Sun, and thus Mercury is Gold, and its Gold is Mercury. And all metallic bodies are Mercury, whether pure or impure, because they are generated from it. And as Mercury is the beginning of all metals, so Gold is the end and the ultimate of metals; and all metals, clean and unclean, contain within them Gold, **Silver** <term>Luna</term> <note>original: "Luna" (the Moon). The alchemical symbol for Silver.</note>, and Mercury. But there is only one true Gold, which is drawn out from them, about which there is much in this book.

These two principles—namely the active masculine and the passive feminine—do not come together in their entire substance. Instead, a **seminal matter** <note>original: *materia seminalis*</note>, which is the sperm, is drawn out from their substances. For just as a husband procreates offspring with his wife, it is not necessary for the husband's entire body to be converted into sperm so that they may later be mixed; rather, the masculine sperm is drawn from the husband’s body, and the feminine sperm is drawn from the wife’s body. These two sperms are mixed during the union of intercourse and are cast into the **field of nature** <note>original: *agrum naturæ*; an alchemical metaphor for the womb or the reaction vessel</note>, which is to say, into the woman’s womb.

Thus, by the internal power of the two sperms—which is called the **formative force** <note>original: *vis formatina*, likely a variation of *vis formativa*; the hidden power that gives shape to life</note>—and by the heat of the container (namely the womb), the human body is formed, being nourished by the menstrual blood.

In a similar way, it happens in the artificial generation of metals: from a masculine mercury and a feminine mercury mixed together and cast into the field of nature, and then vitalized by the **menstrual mercury** <note>original: *mercurium menstrualem*; alchemists used this term for a specific solvent or "solvent-water" that nourishes the "embryo" of the metal within the glass vessel</note>, an offspring is generated that is similar to its parents.

It is not the case, however, that the entire metallic body is converted by some artifice into masculine and feminine mercury and then joined and fermented to procreate a **solar or lunar body** <note>These terms refer to Gold and Silver, respectively</note>. ...[sul]phur being left behind; but it must be considered that the earth is composed from the raw states of either the **Moon** <term>Luna/Silver</term> or the **Sun** <term>Sol/Gold</term>, or indeed from the Sun alone. Yet the opinion of **Arnold** <note>Referring to Arnold of Villanova, a 13th-century physician and alchemist</note> is not to be blamed, for it is supported by this reasoning: that every **tincture** <note>original: *tinctura*; a substance capable of transforming or "coloring" a base metal into a noble one</note> must contain an ingredient stone, and must consist of the very thing it intends to transform. If, therefore, you wish to transform **Venus** <term>Copper</term> with your stone, it will be necessary to have also obtained the earth from Venus. This earth is created through **calcination** <note>original: *calcinationem*; the process of heating a substance to high temperatures to reduce it to a powder or ash</note>, and is converted into ash; then the ash, through **sublimation** <note>original: *sublimationem*; the purification of a substance by heating it into vapor and then condensing it back into a solid</note>, is converted into the **quintessence** <term>the "fifth essence" or purest form of a substance</term>, and the quintessence through solution is converted into water, and the water through **coagulation** <note>original: *coagulationem*; the process of turning a liquid into a solid or semi-solid state</note> is converted into the stone, which marks the beginning of the **Magistery** <term>the Mastery, or the completion of the alchemical Great Work</term>. From this stone, water and mineral earth are extracted once more; when this earth has been calcined and whitened, it receives its own vapor again, fixing it and uniting it in an inseparable union. This is achieved entirely through purification or sublimation, which is followed by fermentation and nourishment.
