# ON THE CONVERSION OF NA-
### *tures and their commixture.*

## EXERCISE VI.

### PARMENIDES.

The method of the art for converting things into one another is as follows. First, dissolve the **Stone** <note>The *Lapis*, or the central material of the alchemical work.</note> into its own **Mercury** <term>Mercurium</term>. Authors call the Stone "metallic"; wash it, reduce it, fix it, and wax it. That is to say: dissolve the coarse into the simple, wash the dark into the bright, reduce the moist into the dry, and fix the volatile into its own body. 

To **dissolve** is to divide and corrupt, and to create the **First Matter** <term>materia prima</term>. To **wash** is to bury <note>original: *inhumare*; the process of placing the vessel in a warm "earthy" environment like a dung-heap or sand-bath for steady heat.</note>, to distill, and to calcine <note>original: *calcinare*; reducing a substance to powder through heat.</note>. To **reduce** is to enrich, to wax <note>original: *incerare*; a process of adding moisture to a dry substance until it reaches a waxy consistency.</note>, and to refine. To **fix** <note>original: *figere*; making a substance stable so it no longer evaporates or "flies" when heated.</note> is to betroth <note>original: *desponsare*; a metaphorical term for the union of substances.</note>, to resolve, and to coagulate. 

Through the first, nature works inwardly; through the second, outwardly; through the third, above; through the fourth, below. But modern practitioners ruin the end of the work: for when they cease their labor, it is then that they ought to have just begun. But one dissolves by dissolving and coagulating, another by dissolving and fixing; one confuses the middle of the process, another the end. Thus they falter in the art like fools. In short, I say that they do not produce the **tincture** <note>The powerful essence used to transform base metals into gold.</note> of even a single pen- <note>The text cuts off mid-word; likely *nummi*, meaning a small coin or a penny.</note>

<summary>Parmenides defines the four core alchemical operations—dissolving, washing, reducing, and fixing—as the essential stages for preparing the Philosophers' Stone. He criticizes contemporary alchemists for failing to understand the sequence and timing of these internal and external natural processes.</summary>
<keywords>Parmenides, alchemical operations, dissolution, fixation, calcination, inceration, First Matter, tincture, Turba Philosophorum</keywords>

...unless all things have been properly digested in the conversion of natures, so that first the coarse is converted into the thin—that is, the body into water. Then, the water is converted back into a body or earth. Next, you must add—or rather, instill—the soul. This is achieved if you add the soul along with the water (that is, the spirit) to the body. Finally, you must nourish this animated body with its own milk <note>original: *lacte suo*; a metaphor for the specialized solvent or "mercurial water" that feeds the growing philosopher's stone.</note>—that is, with its own water, from which the work was co-created or begun from the very start. 

Regarding the mixing, we are taught that the proportion should be balanced so that there are three parts of water to one part of lead <note>original: *plumbi*; in alchemy, "lead" often refers to the "base" or raw starting material rather than common metallic lead.</note>. Or, better yet, two parts of copper to seven parts of "poison" <note>original: *veneni*; likely referring to a corrosive substance or "quick-silver" (mercury).</note>, as <term>Zeno</term> <note>Zeno of Citium, the founder of Stoicism, who appears as a speaker in the *Turba* dialogues.</note> says later. 

Some practitioners—such as those who dissolve in water that has been distilled and revived seven times—mix by dissolving two parts of water to one part of lead, guided by a <term>sesquialter</term> <note>A mathematical ratio of 3:2; a common harmonic and alchemical proportion.</note> proportion. Once these two have been skillfully and perfectly mixed and well-fitted together, ensure that the water becomes "metallic" <term>aqua metallica</term>. Then, place that same water into its glass vessel and cook it for forty days of **putrefaction** <note>original: *putrefactionis*; the stage of "blackening" or decay (*nigredo*) necessary for the rebirth of the matter.</note>. This is done at the **first grade of fire** <note>The lowest level of heat, often compared to the warmth of a brooding hen or a summer sun.</note>, until the lead itself liquefies and rots.

# ON THE MARRIAGE OF THE SUN & *Moon.*
<note>original: *DE CONIVGIO SOLIS & Lunæ*; "Sun" and "Moon" are the standard alchemical symbols for Gold and Silver.</note>

## EXERCISE VII.

### SIMON.
<note>original: *ZIMON*; Likely referring to Simon the Magician or a traditional persona within the *Turba Philosophorum* dialogues.</note>

This philosopher seems to agree that both perfect bodies <note>Gold and silver</note> should be taken for the composition of the Elixir, whether that Elixir is intended to be white or yellow <note>original: *citrinus*; the "citrine" or yellow stage often precedes the final red stage of the philosopher's stone.</note>. The reason is that neither flows easily without the other. Moreover, the goal of this entire alchemical secret is for the Elixir to flow immediately—specifically, before the "flight" of Mercury <note>original: *fugam Mercurij*; referring to the volatility of mercury, which tends to evaporate or escape when heated before it can be "fixed" by the solid metals.</note>.

However, I read no authors, or very few, who suggest this or specify when these two bodies—namely those of the Sun and Moon—should be applied: whether at the very beginning of the work (during the <term>solution</term> <note>The process of dissolving a solid into a liquid state.</note>) or at the end (during the <term>fermentation</term> <note>The stage where the "stone" is joined with a metal to determine its final transformative power.</note>). Therefore, let whoever wishes to try it see for themselves what should be done and chosen.

This method does not please me very much. For if it were done in this way, the resulting Elixir would necessarily be neither white nor yellow, but of a mixed color. Nevertheless, it is possible that this opinion should be interpreted as follows: namely, when the Elixir is intended to become red <note>original: *rubeum*; the final, most potent state of the Stone.</note>, one should first take the filings of the Moon <note>Silver filings</note> and dissolve them with Mercury; then, from those joined elements, one should collect the ear—

Although the philosopher Senior <note>Zadith ben Hamuel, a 10th-century Arabian alchemist whose work was highly influential in the Latin West.</note> believes that three "lights" must be wed in the mixing of the work (or of the "waters")—specifically the Sun, the Moon, and the Serpent—and that one is the brother and the other the sister of the serpent (who he says helps to harden and retain the serpent), he is, in my judgment, mistaken. For it is sufficient to sow the serpent in its own sister. The reason for this error is that the Sun is not "terrified" <note>original: *terrificatur*; in alchemy, this refers to the metal being shaken or altered from its fixed state. However, if it were purified in a similar way, then nothing would stand in the way: for it would be joined to both the Moon and the Serpent <note>The "Serpent" usually represents Mercury, known for being volatile and "slippery" until it is fixed by other metals.</note>.

# IN THE ASSEMBLY. <note>original: *In Turbam*; referring to the *Turba Philosophorum* or "Assembly of the Philosophers," one of the oldest Latin alchemical texts.</note>
<meta>catchword: Of so.</meta>

...[gum]ma <note>The text continues a list of synonyms from the previous page.</note>, **Vinegar**, **Urine**, **Sea Water**, the **Dragon**, the **Serpent**. 
According to the understanding of this philosopher, you should proceed toward perfection in this way: 
Grind the **stone** <note>original: *lapidem*</note> into a very fine powder (that is, grind it, namely, by fire, not with hands <note>Alchemical "grinding" often refers to the chemical breakdown caused by heat rather than literal physical crushing.</note>) and place it in the clearest **celestial vinegar** <note>original: *aceto cœlestino*; likely a reference to a highly purified acid or distilled spirit used as a solvent.</note>, and immediately it is dissolved into **philosophical water**, as if from a fountain. 

And if it has been totally dissolved in this way, then distill the matter, coagulate the distillation with tempered heat, and finally **calcine** <term>calcina</term> <note>to reduce a substance to powder through prolonged heating.</note> it—namely, after its coagulation in its own manner—and in the fourth solution it **tints** <note>original: *tingit*; the "tincture" or ability of the stone to transform base metals into gold.</note>. 

And this solution of ours is according to nature: but let this be kept forever in memory: **That no foreign thing is received by the Philosophical Stone, nor does anything foreign enter into the Philosophical Stone.** 

Therefore, let whoever wishes see to it, lest they be deceived here by the name of "vinegar." For one thing, of one kind and nature, admits nothing alien: and it is most true that it is one thing, and made from one thing. 

Because when **Mercury** is prepared into **Blessed Water** <note>original: *aquam Benedictam*</note>, then it has the power of dissolving the **perfect body** <note>Usually referring to Gold.</note> into Mercury through artifice, and thus the whole compound is Mercury—namely, the one thing from which the stone is made. And in that unique thing (namely Mercury, or the stone) there are four: the **body**, the **soul**, the **spirit**, and the **tincture**; also **earth**, **water**, **air**, **fire**, **ferment**, and **oil**.

### EXERCISE IX.

->ZENON.<- <note>Likely referring to Zeno of Elea or Zeno of Citium, who appear as speakers in the *Turba Philosophorum*.</note>

In the alchemical work, it is necessary first of all to completely **mortify** <term>mortify</term> <note>original: *mortificare*; in alchemy, this refers to "killing" the external, crude form of a substance to release its inner spirit or essence.</note> and exhaust the **stone**—that is, the body, soul, and spirit—since nothing produces fruit in this art unless it has first been mortified. Moreover, these dissolutions or separations occur by means of mercury: for it first dissolves the body and performs the separations, which are then joined again through the **ferment** <note>a substance, often compared to yeast, added to the alchemical matter to "ripen" it and catalyze the transformation into gold.</note> and mercury. But it must be carefully noted here that at the beginning of the work, Mercury is called **Water**; then, when the **blackness** <note>original: *nigredine*; the *nigredo* stage, symbolizing the death and putrefaction of the old form.</note> appears, it is called **Earth**; then, once it has been **sublimated** <term>sublimated</term> <note>the process where a solid turns into vapor and then back to solid, used here to symbolize the "Air" phase.</note>, it is called **Air**; then, when it has been reddened (moreover, the air must by itself...

## EXERCISE XI.
->PANDULPHUS.<-

If the previous teaching does not please you, the philosopher brings forward another here, which we shall suitably explain in this form. Let there be taken of the **water abstracted from the stone** <note>original: *aqua abstracta à lapide*</note> its own weight—that is, a weight equal to the stone—and let the stone itself and the water be well mixed together, and placed under the governance of their own fire, and let care be taken so that it does not flow out. Or let the whole matter be placed in a **Mary's bath** <term>Mary's bath</term> <note>original: *balneo mariæ*; a double boiler or water bath used to provide gentle, even heat.</note>, and the matter will be dissolved into a milky water, which water shall be called **Virgin’s Milk** <term>Virgin's Milk</term> <note>original: *Lac virginis*</note> and **Philosophers' Vinegar** <term>Philosophers' Vinegar</term> <note>original: *Acetum philosophorum*</note>. Then let it be allowed to be elevated into **heaven** <note>original: *cœlum*; the top of the glass vessel, representing the process of evaporation or sublimation.</note>: and then let it be commanded to descend into **earth** <note>original: *terram*; the bottom of the vessel, representing precipitation or condensation</note>, that is, reiterate all operations as is proper. For during the dissolving it will ascend into heaven, and during the coagulating it will descend, and the spirit is united with the earth, and then let it be **calcined** <term>calcined</term> <note>original: *calcinetur*; reduced to a fine powder through high heat.</note> again, and it will be a **fixed stone** <note>original: *lapis fixus*; a substance that has become stable and will no longer vaporize when heated.</note>.

...is and flowing. But let it be noted that the stone is to be dissolved four times, and one must proceed with it through all steps, as the philosopher suggests. And as many times as the stone is dissolved, so many times must that solution be guarded with the **Seal of Hermes** <term>Seal of Hermes</term> <note>original: *sigillo Hermetis*; an airtight seal, often made by melting the glass neck of a vessel to ensure no vapors escape.</note> until the Elixir itself is seen to be coagulated; then **calcined** <term>calcined</term> <note>original: *calcinatum*; reduced to a fine powder through dry heat.</note>, and once again reduced into a powder.

And in the fourth dissolution (the philosophers say), the greatest care must be taken lest the Elixir flows and becomes **glass** <note>original: *vitrum fiat*; if the heat is too high, the material may vitrify. In alchemy, turning to glass was often seen as a "death" of the matter because it became inert and could no longer be "multiplied" or used as a medicine.</note>, for if that were to happen, it would be of no use. For the Elixir must be calcined—that is, reduced to a powder—not vitrified. 

However, the flowing of the Elixir is avoided if the fire is governed with good reason—that is, very gently. And even if the philosopher says here that the fire should be more intense, let it nevertheless be held perpetually in memory that the fire, from the beginning of the work until the end, should be one and the same, in the **likeness of an infant in the mother’s womb** <note>This is a common alchemical metaphor for a constant, temperate, and nurturing heat that must never be allowed to go out or fluctuate wildly.</note>.

Next, let it be noted that the philosopher here calls the "clean white" <note>original: *album mundum*</note> the already fermented stone; then, when he says the body must be soaked seven times, he means those two-thirds are to be divided into seven parts and soaked seven times. ### *THEOPHILUS.*

Theophilus teaches here that the poison <note>original: *venenum*; in alchemy, "poison" often refers to the volatile, transformative agent or the "mercury" that "kills" the base metal so it can be reborn as gold.</note> must be divided into two equal parts. Let the parts of the Elixir be two to seven, or three to one, and let there be a fire of proper putrefaction <term>putrefaction</term> <note>original: *putrefactionis*; the stage of decomposition or "blackness" where the matter breaks down and rots, a necessary step before purification.</note>.

Indeed, it should be thought that the philosophers command the water to be divided into two parts for this reason: to signify that the Elixir, after fermentation <term>fermentation</term> <note>original: *fermentationem*; the process of "leavening" the alchemical stone with gold or silver to give it a specific direction and stability.</note>, requires as much water as it required during the fermentation itself (although some think otherwise and teach a third part by number). It must be saturated, and throughout seven cycles it must be moistened or nourished by the same portion with which the copper itself was dissolved. And when the already mentioned portion has been applied to the Elixir in this way through seven turns after nutrition, then the Elixir is mature for tinting <term>tinting</term> <note>original: *tingendum*; the final act of transmutation where the Elixir "dyes" or transforms the base metal into a precious one.</note>.

For we see in conception, up until birth, that its heat (unless it happens accidentally, that is, unnaturally) does not change in the mother's womb, but is always the same. But if the soul were not present, then the spirit and body would be separated from each other by the fire; but with the soul joined to the spirit and body, this whole does not care for fire, nor for any other thing of the world.

## EXERCISE XV.

### ZENON.

Between the three mentioned above, there exists such a desire <note>original: *libido*; here referring to chemical affinity or natural attraction.</note> or conformity: because just as the sperm of the man and the woman are released into the woman's womb <note>original: *matrice*</note> in the form of milk for seven days, and in the form of blood for nine days, and in the form of flesh for twenty days, and the limbs are brought forth over thirty days, and at the end of those days God pours in the blessing of the human seed—namely, the soul or life—in the same way it occurs in the seed of the active body, which is the Moon <note>original: *lunae*; representing the white or silver principle</note>, and of the passive body, which is Mercury, with the nourishment of the menstrual flow, which is the salt Alembrot <term>Salt Alembrot</term> <note>A specialized alchemical salt, often a mixture of corrosive sublimate and sal ammoniac, used as a powerful solvent or flux.</note>. ...it is necessary for the living stone to be nourished; and I believe that the condition of nourishment and of augmentation <note>original: *augmenti*; the alchemical process of increasing the quantity or the potency of the Stone</note> is the same, drawing my reasoning from the very meaning of the words.

For to nourish <note>original: *nutrire*</note> is to administer food tenderly and sparingly, just as tender and frugal food is provided to a boy or an infant. When, however, he begins to become somewhat mature, solid, and robust, then the food is also increased.

Instead, a weight of two parts can be given to the Elixir <term>Elixir</term> <note>The final, perfected state of the alchemical medicine, capable of transmuting metals or healing the body.</note> at once, so that the now-mature Elixir does not exceed the food of augmentation except by one part. This is because a third part of the Elixir ought to exceed the food, so that the food may be overcome <note>original: *conequi*, likely a typo for *concoqui*, meaning to be digested or transformed</note> by it. For the body is weightier than the food. 

But it is also necessary to observe this in the process of increase: that when augmentation is applied to the stone, that very augmentation must thereafter be continued through all species of decoction <note>original: *decoctionis*; the process of heating a substance in liquid to mature it</note> in a tempered fire.

### THE PRINTER to the Reader.
<sig>n 4</sig>

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'A' featuring a large capital letter surrounded by an ornate square border filled with scrolling foliage and floral motifs.</image-desc>

Friend reader, you should know that here, at the beginning of this book—truly titled the *Golden Hour* <note>original: *Aurea hora*; likely referring to a specific manuscript or section often associated with the *Aurora Consurgens* or similar medieval alchemical texts</note>—we have deliberately omitted an entire treatise of Parables, or allegories. By these allegories, in the ancient manner of the "shadow-dwellers" <note>original: *tenebrionum*; a derogatory term used by later Renaissance editors to describe those who lived in what they considered the "Dark Ages," or those who wrote in obscure, veiled language</note> (as the conditions of those times and ages dictated), the author has allegorically dragged almost the entirety of Holy Scripture—especially the works of Solomon and the writings of the Psalmist <note>original: *Psaltes*; referring to King David</note> himself, but most of all the Song of Songs—toward Alchemy, even against the text's own will. He did this to such an extent that all those [sacred] writings seem to have been written for no other reason (if we believe this man) than for the honor and praise of Alchemy. 

Indeed—and this is a wicked thing to say—he most profanely twisted the very most sacred mystery of the incarnation and death of Christ our Lord toward the mystery of the Stone <term>Stone</term> <note>The Philosopher's Stone, the goal of the "Great Work," believed to be a substance that could transmute metals and heal all diseases.</note>, along with many other principal monuments of our faith. I do not believe (at least in my opinion) that this was done by him with evil intent—for the author otherwise seems pious in other respects—but rather that it was a product of that age of darkness. For those people, since they were ignorant of the true meaning of the holy scriptures...

# THE RISING DAWN: Which is called the *Golden Hour, and regarding its second Treatise.* <note>original: *Aurora Consurgens*. This is a famous medieval alchemical text, often attributed to Thomas Aquinas, though that authorship is highly debated by scholars today.</note>

## PROLOGUE.

<image-desc>Ornamental woodcut initial 'I' within a square frame, decorated with dense foliage, depictions of birds (including one resembling a hawk or pelican), and a small mammal nestled in the vines.</image-desc> In the things already stated, it has been shown to the discerning person by the authorities of the Sacred Page <note>original: *Sacræ paginæ*; a common medieval term for the Bible or Holy Scripture</note> that this science is nothing else but a gift of God and a <term>Sacrament</term> <note>In an alchemical context, *sacramentum* refers to a "holy mystery" or a "hidden secret" rather than a church ritual</note> enwrapped in various symbolic discourses and parabolic speech, as well as in riddles and mystical veils. This was done so that the dull and the foolish—who are ignorant of nature even if they know how to read their A.B.C.Ds—might not seize and usurp it for themselves. For this reason, those who desire this knowledge must sharpen their intellect and wit with great subtlety; they must often and very often, inside and out, before and behind, turn and return <note>original: *volvere & revolvere*; an idiom for studying a book deeply or "revolving" the ideas in one's mind</note> the sayings of the <term>sages</term> <note>original: *sapientum*; referring to the "Philosophers" or legendary alchemical masters of antiquity</note>. For it is not the way of the wise to speak foolishly, even though the understanding of their words is mostly contrary to the sound of the letters <note>meaning that the literal, surface-level reading of alchemical texts is often the opposite of their intended chemical or spiritual meaning</note>. For whoever accepts the sound of the words but does not possess the inner understanding [shall achieve] nothing—

<summary>This page introduces the "Aurora Consurgens," framing alchemy as a divine gift from God that is intentionally hidden behind riddles and metaphors to prevent the "foolish" from abusing it. It emphasizes that the true meaning of alchemical writings is often the opposite of their literal surface meaning.</summary>

# GLOSS ON THE PROLOGUE of the treatise on Astronomy.

Aristotle, writing word for word to Alexander <note>original: *Aristoteles ad Alexandrum*; a reference to the *Secretum Secretorum*, a widely read medieval text falsely attributed to Aristotle that contains occult and medicinal wisdom.</note>, says: **Saturn** rules the earth, **Mercury** rules **Aquarius** <note>original: ♒; while usually the sign for the air-sign Aquarius, in this elemental context it likely refers to the sphere of Water or the qualities of that sign as a container for the "living water" of the philosophers.</note>, **Jupiter** rules the air, and the **Sun** rules fire. And a correspondence is not accepted here in the [temporary] action of the Planets, but in those operations which they hold always, continuously and perpetually, through the ultimate power which is above all the powers of these works. 

And this is not the place for demonstrating these difficult matters, but I have made mention of it for this reason: because it is necessary and extremely useful to you, on account of the frequent treatise in which [matters are discussed] more determinately concerning the particulars and individuals of certain **planetary plants** <note>original: *uegetabilium Planetarum*; the belief that every plant on earth is "governed" by a specific celestial body that grants it its medicinal or alchemical properties.</note>. 

Therefore, the knowledge of the properties of these things belongs to the **philosophers** <note>meaning natural philosophers or alchemists</note>; but the knowledge of natural things belongs to the **physicians**. I do not wish this to be hidden from your wisdom: that everything lacking light <note>referring to plants that grow in shade, underground, or have "dark" properties like leaden hues.</note> among the nature of plants is ruled by **Saturn**, and is attributed to him. And whatever of the plants is flowering and luminous is ruled by **Mercury**, and is attributed to him. And whatever of the plants is flowering but does not bear fruit is attributed to **Mars**, and is ruled by him. 

Then, compose and join these in different ways, and you may say: Every plant bearing fruit is created by **Venus** and **Mars** <note>The union of the "female" Venus and "male" Mars was a common alchemical metaphor for the generation of "fruit" or the Stone.</note>. Likewise, some plants grow by branches, some by seeds, and some are born without seed or planting <note>A reference to "spontaneous generation," a common belief in medieval biology.</note>. It is therefore clearer than light from the aforesaid that every species of plants...

### Chapter I.

IT MUST BE KNOWN first, that this divine science of **Astronomy** <note>In this period, "Astronomy" and "Astrology" were often used interchangeably to describe the study of how celestial bodies influence earthly events.</note> makes use of terms according to the course of the **Planets**, as well as their influences, and the number and power of the twelve signs of the **Zodiac** <term>Zodiac: the "circle of animals" or path of the sun, divided into twelve sections that determine the "disposition" of things on Earth</term>, just as **Aristotle** <note>This likely refers to the "Secretum Secretorum," a popular medieval text falsely attributed to Aristotle, written as a letter of advice to Alexander the Great.</note> testifies to **Alexander**, saying: That **Saturn** holds the earth, **Mercury** the water, **Jupiter** the air, and the **Sun** the fire. 

For everything lacking light among the number of vegetable things is ruled by **Saturn**, and is attributed to him. And whatever vegetable thing is flowering but not bearing fruit is attributed to **Mars**, and is ruled by him. And every flowering and fruitful vegetable thing is attributed to the **Sun**, and is ruled by him. 

And again he adds: Then compose and join these divisions and days; every vegetable thing bearing fruit but not flowering—such as the apple and the palm—is attributed to **Saturn** and the **Sun**. And every flowering thing not bearing fruit is ruled by **Mercury** and **Mars**. 

See how **Astronomy** has woven this gift of God together with the powers of the **Planets**. For Aristotle says that every vegetable lacking light is ruled by **Saturn**. He means the black and dreggy <term>feculenta: sediment-heavy or thick; refers to the "dregs" of the elements found in the earth</term> earth: and every

Whatever is flowering and luminous is ruled by **Mercury**; it requires the first **whitening** <term>Whitening: also known as "albedo," the second stage of the alchemical Great Work where the matter is purified</term> of the earth itself. In the second month, **Jupiter** works through his heat and moisture, digesting the matter into a certain fleshy mass which is called an **embryo**. 

In the third month, **Mars** works through his heat and dryness, digesting and separating that matter into limbs. 

In the fourth month, the **Sun** works by sending in the spirit of life. 

In the fifth month, **Mercury** works, forming the features and the breathing passages. 

In the sixth month, **Venus** works, arranging and ordering the eyebrows, the eyes, the testicles, and such things. 

In the seventh month, the **Moon** works to expel the fetus; and if it is born then, it can live; otherwise, it is weakened by the power of the signs <note>This refers to the astrological belief that an eighth-month birth was often fatal because it fell under a less favorable planetary influence</note>. 

The same author testifies, saying: When the **Sun** is in **Aries** and in his **exaltation** <term>Exaltation: a specific position in the Zodiac where a planet's power is greatly increased</term>, then the first degree is completed, which is weak by reason of its heat. And it is the order of water. 

When the **Sun** is in **Leo**, then is completed...

## Geometrical Sayings in a Parabolic Style.

### Chapter II.

Furthermore, note that Geometry and Arithmetic have, in part and in whole, obscured this most noble science with their various distinctions of numbers. For the boundary and the end of the entire Work is sealed within the divisions of numbers. Regarding this boundary, many "sons of doctrine" <note>A traditional term for students or initiates of the alchemical arts.</note> have gone astray and complained. For the philosophers, at the limit of this science, added to and subtracted from the sum of the root <note>Likely referring to the "root" or base material of the Philosopher's Stone.</note> by means of the parts that make up the whole—using the smallest, the middle, and the greatest number. They did this so that the foolish might not be able to understand.

For Aristotle <note>The text attributes this to Aristotle, though it refers to the *Book of the Seventy Precepts*, a pseudo-Aristotelian work of Arabic origin.</note> says in the *Book of the Seventy Precepts*, in the chapter on "Alternations": The alternations of the seventy precepts are manifold: ten. For first they agree, second they also agree, and thirdly they follow. For ten corresponds to ten; here finally the divisions must follow. 

But let our reader attend to the prior order. As the Author of the Three Words <note>Referring to the *Liber de Tribus Verbis* (Book of Three Words), an influential alchemical text.</note> says: "From three, two numbers are understood." For the length of seven days is completed. And the Elder <note>Referring to the 10th-century alchemist Zadith Senior.</note> says, "In seven days, perhaps the whiteness will appear." <term>Whiteness: Known as the "albedo," this is the second major stage of the alchemical work, signifying purification and the transition from the "blackness" to a silver-like state.</term> And indeed in the second [part] he reports that all things will be ten according to the number of equi—

### The Weights of the Wise.

And know that the juice of the **vine of the wise** is extracted in the fifth <note>likely referring to the fifth vessel or fifth stage of distillation.</note>; one part of it is also completed at the end of thirty. The **Assembly of the Philosophers** <note>original: "Turba philosophorum," one of the oldest and most famous Latin alchemical texts, written as a transcript of a meeting of ancient sages.</note> and **Alphidius** <note>An influential Arab alchemist often cited in medieval works.</note> say it occurs in the four parts of the year: namely, Winter, Spring, Summer, and Autumn. Curiously, the legendary British king appears in some alchemical traditions as a master of the Great Work.</note>; others say by the month; others by the week; others by the day. All of these are the same and one in the total, but they differ in the root. All of which it is necessary...

### Natural things spoken according to the process of nature. Chapter III.

Consequently, natural science—just as it is the concern of physicians and natural philosophers to consider—has surrounded this comforting, treasury-holding science <note>The "treasury-holding science" refers to alchemy, which was often called the "Treasury of Philosophy."</note> with its own processes. Indeed, the philosophers have placed this principle in many parts of their writings. For they say: things do not come to be except according to their own natures, just as a human comes from a human, and a lion from a lion. 

And **Aristotle** says: "The most natural of works is to generate something like itself, as a plant generates a plant, and a cow a cow." 

And **Hermes** <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary founder of the alchemical tradition.</note> says: "Nothing is suitable to a thing except that which is closest to it in its own nature, and a similar offspring is generated in that thing." That is to say: if you seek a medicine that heals metals, its origin must be from metals, since the species is tinted <note>original: "tingatur." In alchemy, "tincture" refers to the power of the elixir to transform or "dye" a base metal into gold.</note> by its own kind. 

And **Senior** <note>original: "Senior." This refers to Senior Zadith (Ibn Umail), a 10th-century Arabic alchemist whose works were highly influential in the Latin West.</note> says: "The seed of the man, cast into the womb of the woman, by its thinness and subtlety adheres to it for seven days, until it is **coagulated** <term>coagulatur: the process of a liquid becoming solid; in alchemy, this is the 'fixation' of a volatile substance.</term> in all the members of the woman, and it reaches the flesh and becomes flesh; and upon the bones and becomes bone; and upon the nerves and hairs and becomes like them. Furthermore, it is coagulated within ten days and becomes like cheese, and is turned red..."

## *Discourse in Riddles: Chapter V.*

After the parabolic style follows the problematic <note>original: "problematicus"; referring to a style of writing that poses "problems" or riddles for the reader to solve, common in alchemical literature.</note>, which Hermes pursues in this way, saying: I have considered a bird held in veneration by the wise, which flies while it is in Aries, Cancer, Libra, or Capricorn <note>These are the four cardinal signs of the zodiac, marking the beginning of the four seasons. In alchemy, they represent the complete cycle of the Work through the changing qualities of heat and moisture.</note>. And you shall acquire her for yourself as an everlasting thing from pure minerals and rocky mountains. Divide her principal parts, which will remain for you after the division; although it may be small and blackness may dominate it, nonetheless it is joined with the earth, and you will perceive many colors within it. The wise man calls it the **Earth of Wisdom**, **Bronze**, or **Lead**. You shall roast it, therefore, with a strong fire for a small number of four days; for a middle number of seven; and for a greater number of ten, and then it is called by the wise the **Silver Earth**. Its second part, which is flowing, is called the **Water of Wisdom**. The third part is the **White Earth**: you shall cause this to be distilled four times in small, middle, and maximum number for seven days, and then it is called **Manifest Gold**. The fourth part is that which possesses a great whiteness, and it is called the **Air of Wisdom**, or **Gnumi** <note>original: "Gnumi"; an alchemical term likely derived from the Arabic "khnum," often referring to a metallic spirit or a hidden essence.</note>.

## ON NATURAL THINGS

### *How the stone is likened to the Seed of man in the procreation of offspring, Chapter VII.*

Now, however, we must thirdly consider to which natural things this science should be compared. For it is likened to the human male seed for this reason: it is drawn from all the limbs of a man and possesses the power <note>original: "virtutem"; the inherent potency or essence</note> of all those limbs, and is poured into a natural vessel which is the womb <note>original: "matrix"</note>. There it dies and is nourished by a moisture of the same nature until a human being is formed in the required number of days, and no longer. 

In the same way, the seed of this science is drawn out from the metallic body, having all the power of the metals in potential. It is then placed in a natural vessel, which is the permanent water <term>aqua permanens: a fundamental alchemical solvent, often identified with purified mercury or a "living" water that does not wet the hands</term> and the vinegar of the philosophers <note>original: "acetum philosophorum"; a specialized acidic or corrosive substance used for breakdown</note>. In this vessel, it dies, putrefies, is enlivened, and that bronze <note>original: "æs"; here referring to the base material or "body" of the metal in the vessel</note> grows, along with other things receiving nourishment. This vessel, moreover, is one and the same throughout the whole work, completing the white and red tinc- <note>The text cuts off mid-word; likely "tincturam" or tincture, the final stage of the alchemical goal.</note>

**Plato** <note>In alchemical texts, "Plato" often refers to a pseudo-epigraphical author rather than the Greek philosopher himself</note> maintains that **alums** <term>Alums: A group of mineral salts, typically potassium aluminum sulfate, used as astringents and in dyeing</term> bring about brilliance, **salts** cause dissolution, and **vitriols** <term>Vitriols: Metallic sulfates (like copper or iron sulfate) known for their glassy appearance and corrosive properties</term> break apart or constrict. For **raw alum** <note>original: "alumen crudum"</note> is said to abound in moisture, but **calcined alum** <term>Calcined: A material heated to a high temperature to drive off volatile substances or moisture, reducing it to a powder</term> is said to be in a state of extreme dryness. The true property of salts is to dissolve, to corrode, to moisten, and to liquefy an acidic thing. For it is said that one should calcine bodies with salt, because salt corrodes their corrupting moisture. Furthermore, salts cause bodies to flow easily in the fire. It should be noted that some salts are **fixed** <term>Fixed: A substance that is stable in fire and does not evaporate or fly away</term> and some are **volatile** <term>Volatile: A substance that easily evaporates or sublimes when heated</term>.

For everything fixed is used as a "body" or as a "tether" <note>original: "retinaculo"; literally a halter or stay, meaning a substance that holds the spirit in the heat</note>, and such things are extracted from calcined matters; as it is said, "Extract the **Alkali Salt**." <term>Alkali Salt: Originally salt derived from the ashes of the saltwort plant; in alchemy, it refers to any basic salt used as a flux</term> For many extract it, yet they do not prosper in it, because they extract it from that in which the **Alkali Salt of the philosophers** is not present.

For just as Alkali Salt is extracted from **quicklime** <note>original: "calce viua"; calcium oxide</note>, or from **potash** <note>original: "cinere clauellato"; literally "clubbed ashes" or pearl ash</note>, or as **salt of tartar** <term>Salt of Tartar: Potassium carbonate, obtained by heating the sediment from wine casks</term> is extracted from the calcined tartar itself by means of a suitable moisture until no sharpness remains, so too our salt—which is the **tincture** <term>Tincture: The potent alchemical liquid or powder capable of "dyeing" or transforming base metals into gold</term>—is extracted from the "lime" of metals through **putrefaction** <term>Putrefaction: The stage of the alchemical work where the matter turns black and decomposes, often called the "Nigredo"</term>, until the entire compound puts off its own nature and puts on another. Of such a salt **Senior** <note>Senior: Refers to Senior Zadith (Ibn Umail), a 10th-century Arab alchemist</note> says: "First it becomes ash, then salt, and from that salt, through various operations, comes the **Mercury of the philosophers**." ## Concerning the many kinds of quicksilver
### Chapter XIII.

In the comparison of quicksilver, it must be noted that quicksilver is threefold: this is to extract the **philosophical fire**. This, according to the vital soul, is called fire, or the soul, or the **quintessence** <term>Quintessence: The "fifth essence" (quinta essentia); the purest, most spiritual part of a substance that remains after the four elements are stripped away</term>.

Of the first kind, the *Assembly of Philosophers* writes, saying: 
> Quicksilver is the fire that burns bodies.

And again: it is necessary, therefore, for the flame of fire to take hold of the body so that it may be broken down and made weak; for this fire must be extracted by a fire of the same nature <note>original: "igne connaturali"</note>, as the **Senior** <note>Senior Zadith: A common reference to the 10th-century alchemist Zadith ben Hamuel, whose work was highly influential in the Latin West</note> says: 
> Our fire is water; if you know how to give fire to fire, and mercury to mercury, it is enough for you.

The envious <note>In alchemical literature, "the envious" usually refers to earlier masters who deliberately hid their secrets from the uninitiated.</note> have said: It is a stone, and not a stone, but truly a **gum**, as is written in the *Assembly of the Philosophers* <note>original: "Turba philosophorum"; one of the most influential early Latin alchemical texts, framed as a transcript of a meeting of ancient sages.</note>. And for this reason, the philosophers, being cautious as they write lest their teachings perish, did not openly set down its arrangement in their books, lest just anyone should recognize it; for if the foolish knew it, they would not hold it in such low esteem <note>Alchemists often claimed their "First Matter" was a common, cheap substance that ignorant people would despise if they saw it in its raw form.</note>. ### *Of Arsenic and Orpiment.*
#### *Chapter XIV.*

It is also compared to **arsenic** and **orpiment** <note>Orpiment is a deep yellow arsenic sulfide mineral. And **Arsenic** is called the male, by reason of its color and dryness; while **Orpiment**, by reason of its heat and moisture, is called the female, as the *Assembly of the Philosophers* says: I have shown you the female in orpiment, and the male in lead. For many times it is used to represent sulfurous fire, and more often the spirit which departs from the body, which is the water by which all things are given life and increased.

### *On Marcasite, Magnesia, and Tutty. Chapter XV.*

It is also compared to **Marcasite**, **Magnesia**, and **Tutty** <note>Tutty, or *thutia*, is a crude zinc oxide usually collected from the flues of brass-making furnaces. In alchemy, it was valued for its medicinal and purifying properties.</note>. It is compared to **Marcasite** in color: for just as Marcasite has silver and golden sparks mixed within the earth, so in the philosophical work <term>The Philosophical Work: Also called the *Great Work* (Magnum Opus), this is the process of creating the Philosopher's Stone.</term> similar signs appear, as Morienes <note>Morienes was a legendary 7th-century hermit-alchemist said to have taught the secrets of the stone to the King Khalid ibn Yazid.</note> testifies, saying:
> Know that the stinking earth quickly receives the golden sparks, as mentioned above. <note>original: "Scito quod terra foetida cito recipit scintillas aureas, vt suprà."</note>

It is also said to be similar to **Magnesia** <note>In medieval alchemy, "Magnesia" often referred to a black mineral like manganese or a magnetized ore, rather than the modern element magnesium.</note>, by reason of its weight and its ability to break all metals.

It is also said to be similar to **Tutty**, by reason of its quenching. For just as it is commanded that Tutty be quenched <term>Quenching: The process of heating a substance and then rapidly cooling it in a liquid, often repeated many times to purify or "subtle" the material.</term> seven times, or nine, or ten, or twelve, so that its earthiness might be refined and its sulfurousness destroyed; so the philosophers command that their work be repeated, so that everything superfluous in the manifest <note>The "manifest" refers to the outward, visible physical properties of a substance.</note> may be cast away, and the things absent in the depths or in the hidden parts may be added.

Indeed, it must be noted that there is a double spirit: one in the body, and this must be removed—that is, extracted—and it is of a fiery nature, as the *Assembly* <note>original: "Turba," referring to the *Turba Philosophorum* or *Assembly of the Philosophers*, one of the oldest and most cited Latin alchemical texts.</note> testifies, saying: 
> Know that the body cannot dye <term>Dye: In alchemy, "dyeing" (tincturing) refers to the internal transformation of a metal's color and nature, not just a surface coating.</term> itself, unless the spirit is extracted, which is hidden in its belly, and it shall become water and a body without a spirit; which is of a spiritual nature, from which colors appear, because the thick earthy substance does not dye, but...

### *On the Individual Qualities of All Metals. Chapter XVI.*

From this point, it is compared to all metals in their qualities, in their natures, in their colors, and in their softness and hardness—both in their manifest <note>Outwardly visible or physical.</note> and their hidden <note>The internal, spiritual, or "occult" essence.</note> aspects. It is compared to gold and silver by reason of the perfection of their colors which persist in the fire, and by their weight, as well as their ductility <term>Ductility: The physical property of a metal that allows it to be hammered thin or drawn into wire without breaking.</term>. It is compared most especially to gold, since gold is nobler and more perfect than all other "three-bodied" things <note>This likely refers to the "tria corpora" or the three primary principles (often Salt, Sulfur, and Mercury) that alchemists believed composed all metallic bodies.</note>. Because of this eternal perfection, it is called **Philosophical Gold**, which is similar to it: as the Philosopher <note>Likely referring to Hermes Trismegistus or Aristotle, the "Philosopher" par excellence in medieval scholarship.</note> testifies, saying: 
> Those of the present and the past have made nothing, except gold from gold and silver from silver; yet that gold or silver was not of the common kind. <note>original: "Præsentes & præteriti non fecerunt aliquid, nisi ex auro aurum, & ex argento argentum: non tamen aurum illud vel argentum fuit vulgi."</note>

There is, moreover, a **Philosophical Gold** that is not bought for a great price, as Alfidius <note>Alfidius was an Arabic alchemical authority frequently cited in medieval Latin texts; his identity is often associated with the philosopher Al-Kindi or a legendary figure.</note> says:
> Know that this stone, which is the subject of this secret, was placed by God so that it need not be bought for a great price, since the way is found by the chosen, so that it might be possessed by the poor and the rich alike: namely, so that anyone might easily arrive at it through reason and knowledge. <note>original: "Scitote, quòd hic lapis, de quo hoc arcanum agitur, Deus non emendum magno pretio posuit, quoniam via electis inuenitur, ut à paupere & diuite haberi possit: ut scilicet ratione & scientia ad eam quisquis possit leuiter peruenire."</note>

And Morienes <note>Morienes was a 7th-century legendary hermit-alchemist said to have taught the secrets of the stone to the King Khalid ibn Yazid.</note> says: 
> Every thing which is bought for a great price is a lie: for... <note>original: "Omnis res quæ magno emitur pretio, mendax est: quoniam..."</note>

Wherefore it must first be seen what the **calcination** <term>calcination: the process of heating a substance to high temperatures to effect a change in its physical or chemical state, often to reduce it to a powder or "ash."</term> of the philosophers is. And it must be known that the calcination of the philosophers is threefold: two of the body, and the third of the spirit. The first is the beginning of our work, of which it is said: calcination is the deprivation of cold humidity by a removing combustion; or the reduction of dry earth to ashes.

And the philosophers have exemplified this using the example of wood, in which there are three humidities: the first is watery and cold, and this prevents the wood from burning; the second is unctuous, or oily, and it is this which causes the wood to burn. These two are vaporizable in fire and are capable of being consumed. But the third is left behind in the ash, and it is very small and subtle, fixed and perpetual, and not at all flammable. And it is this third moisture that is **vitrifying** <note>original: "vitrificans." Turning into glass.</note> and promises a glass-like transparency. 

In such a manner is the calcination of the philosophers commanded to be done, as was previously described regarding the wood; and it is truly achieved through the **philosophers' vinegar** <term>acetum philosophorum: not literal vinegar, but a powerful acidic solvent or "mercurial water" used to break down substances.</term>, or through the **permanent water** <term>aqua permanens: a symbolic term for the transformative liquid (often mercury or a specialized solvent) that does not evaporate when heated.</term>, and by no other thing. 

And note this: for such humidity, as was said, which is the principle of **liquefaction** <note>original: "liquefactionis." The process of a substance becoming liquid or melting.</note>, must be in the bodies; as **Hermes** <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary Hellenistic figure regarded as the founder of alchemy.</note> says: "The principle of all liquefiable things is water." The action of the **Fifth Essence** <term>Quintessence: The "Quinta Essentia," the purest and most refined core of matter, believed to be the celestial element from which the stars are made.</term>, whether it be called **sublimation**, **inceration**, or **imbibition** <term>imbibitio: The process of repeatedly "feeding" or soaking a solid substance with liquid until it is saturated.</term>, or the interpretation of all these aforementioned terms. This **calcination** <term>calcinatio: The process of reducing a substance to a fine powder through heat; here, the author emphasizes a "philosophical" calcination that preserves the life of the matter.</term> is performed so that the parts dried out by the fire and constricted may become spiritual, or be made subtle and rare through the "spirit," which is the dissolving water that moistens the scorched earthy matter itself. There is also an impressed heat which, together with the humidity, acts to break down the matter, transforming it into an aerial resolution through the process of digestion. Indeed, in the **first calcination**, two types of humidity are removed: namely, the cold, watery kind and the kind that causes burning. In this **second calcination**, however, the "earthiness" and "fieriness" are removed through the resolution of our water. For all things that this water dissolves, liquefies, and softens, it then disturbs; from this, through repeated decoctions <note>original: "decoctiones," long-term heating or boiling.</note>, aerial resolutions result by way of evaporation.

Hence, this is the **solution of the philosophers**, when the dry earthy parts become soft: in such a way that their dryness, which is a form of hardness, is turned into softness. This softness is called "water" which moistens, much like rainwater or any other form of humidity. For it is said that the more a thing is "dry," the more it is "soft," since in Alchemy, only this specific dryness "tinges" <note>original: "tingit," the ability of the alchemical medicine to "color" or transform the base nature of a metal into gold.</note> and no other; this is the refinement or "rarity" of the elements.

It is also called **inceration** <term>inceratio: Literally "waxing." An alchemical process of adding liquid to a dry powder until it reaches the consistency of wax, allowing it to melt and penetrate other substances.</term> for this reason: since the earth has been deprived of its own moisture, it is necessary to "wax" it. That is, one must drench it with moisture so that it may flow and have the power of "entry," and so that it may represent the metallic form, as the *Assembly of the Philosophers* <note>original: "Turba philosophorum," one of the oldest and most influential Latin alchemical texts, presented as a transcript of a meeting of ancient sages.</note>...

...losophers speaks figuratively: Just as a man lies in a tomb until he becomes dust, once his days are complete, God returns to him his soul and his spirit. When infirmity is removed, that matter is purged, and after the flash of light <note>original: "coruscationem," suggesting a sudden brilliance or gleaming during the chemical reaction</note>, it is improved—just as after the general resurrection, a man becomes stronger and younger than he had been before in this world.

And this is the **liquefaction** of bodies. 

The Philosopher, however, works through water, whereas the common person works through fire. Hence it is said: "Liquefy the bodies with a liquefaction that is not common, but our own, which is done with water." 

Therefore, incineration is the **imbibition** <note>the process of the solid "drinking" or absorbing a liquid</note>, or the making of a paste, or the liquefaction of a dry, hot thing until it is intoxicated <note>original: "inebrietur," meaning saturated to the point of being "drunk" with the solvent</note>. For everything that is thirsty desires to drink; as Aristotle says, "Thirst is the appetite for the cold and the moist." For this reason, it is also called "the thirsty earth."

This second part is also called **sublimation** <term>sublimatio: The process of heating a substance so it rises as vapor and then solidifies again; symbolically, it is the "elevation" of matter from a base state to a spiritual state.</term> for this reason: because that which is in the lower part of the vessel is elevated and exalted to the upper vessel, which is called an **alembic** <term>alembic: The lid or "helmet" of a distilling apparatus that collects vapors.</term> or a long **aludel** <term>aludel: A series of earthenware pots or a tall condenser used in the sublimation process.</term>. 

It is also called this so that the density of the elements may pass into their rarity through elevation—such as the dryness of **earth** into the moisture of **water**, the coldness of water into the heat of **air**, and the moisture of air into the dryness of **fire**. And these **transmutations** must occur through the degrees of fire, ascending even unto "heaven"—which is the alembic of the Philo[sophers].

The more something is washed, the clearer it will be: and if it has not been washed, it will not be clarified. And **Geber** <note>Jabir ibn Hayyan, an 8th-century polymath whose Latinized works, such as the *Sum of Perfection*, were foundational to medieval alchemy.</note> in the *Book of Perfection* says: that it is not fixed unless it is brightened, and the most radiant substance is drawn out from it, according to the manner of its own nature. For "washing" is said to be the removal of a defiled thing. Likewise it is said, "Go to the woman washing clothes, and you do likewise." <note>This is a common alchemical metaphor; just as a laundress uses water and soap to remove dirt from fabric, the alchemist uses "philosophical water" to remove impurities from the metal.</note> And **Hermes** <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary father of the "Hermetic" arts.</note> says, in the beginning it was red, and in the end white. For it is said: "Fire and **Azoth** <term>Azoth: the universal solvent or "mercury of the philosophers," believed to be the essential agent of transformation.</term> cleanse and wash the **laton** <term>laton: a term for the base, "dirty" metal (often compared to brass) that must be purified into gold or silver.</term>." And **Kaled the Younger** <note>Khalid ibn Yazid, a legendary Umayyad prince often cited in alchemical texts.</note> says: "He who knows how to take away the blackness from its surface, purifies and increases it by that washing."

It is also called "killing" or **mortification** <term>mortificatio: the process of "killing" the base nature of a substance, stripping it of its current form so it can be reborn as something more perfect.</term>, by reason of the vegetative and ordered life, and of the accident—that is, the heat impressed within it. For everything that has a heat moving and acting from itself through its transformation is said to live. And for this reason, **Alchemy** <note>original: "Alchimia"; here referring to the substance or "elixir" being prepared.</note> is said to live imperfectly; and the philosophers have studied how to kill this life, and to return an eternal and permanent life. ...that is, to burn: because death will reveal him. Therefore, let us do this many times, until it dies and is softened."

It is also called "vivification" <note>original: *vivificatio*; the stage of 'bringing back to life' or animating the matter after its symbolic death.</note>, on account of nourishment, or vivification itself, or on account of the metallic humor <term>humor: the essential moisture or 'fluid' within a metal that allows it to be transformed.</term>. For everything that is nourished is nourished because of its diminished state. And that which is brought to life is brought to life for two reasons. The Philosophers, however, wish to nourish their "grain" with its own connatural moisture until it grows and brings forth such fruit as it possesses within itself. And they wish to restore life to that which has died from its metallic form, until it achieves a perfect metallic fusion. Some of the philosophers call such vivification or nourishment the **Ingress** <term>Ingress: the 'entry' or penetration of a spiritual or liquid agent into a solid body to transform its nature.</term>.

And this is what **Geber** means when he says:

> "Either we grant entry to those things which, by their own density, are not permitted to enter, by means of the repeated dissolution of non-flammable spirits." 

Through these clever methods, it is necessary for every substance to have "entry," for its success depends upon this benefit, as does its ability to be altered by the discovered mixture.

This second part is also called **putrefaction** <note>original: *putrefactio*; the stage of decomposition where the "old" form of the matter breaks down to allow for a new birth.</note>, or **corruption**, by reason of what is manifest <note>original: *ratione manifesti*; referring to the outward, visible appearance of the substance.</note>. > When copper is refined and boiled in vinegar with medicinal substances until it dies, and when its whiteness penetrates to the exterior so that its internal part becomes external, similar to silver in its whiteness: when we have done this, we find its power of **tinting** <term>tinctura: the transformative power of an alchemical substance to change the color and nature of a base metal.</term> is enduring, and of greater staining and penetration; so much so that it does not differ from the color of pure silver in any way; indeed, it is filled with tint and is of a more perfect whiteness.

> Know that there is no generation without corruption; therefore, apply your study to putrefaction.

...[grinding] it among the philosophers, it is called the **stone with its runner** <note>original: *lapis cum cursore*; the "runner" is the upper stone or muller used to grind materials on a flat slab.</note>, and the **mortar with its pestle**.

# RISING <note>original: *CONSURGENS*; likely referring to the title *Aurora Consurgens*, or "Rising Dawn."</note>

The philosophers have established five distinctions through which their **tincture** <term>tincture: in alchemy, a substance capable of infused color and quality into a "lower" metal to transform it</term> or **Elixir** <term>Elixir: the "philosopher's stone" in liquid or powder form, used for transmutation or healing</term>—both the white and the red—is fully composed and completed; without these, no tincture can exist. The first is to empty out what is superfluous; the second is to change the medicine into a white or yellow color; the third is to provide the ability for metallic fusion; the fourth is to make such fusion permanent in the fire; the fifth is to provide the proper weight to every metal into which it is poured. And these five can be found within a threefold number, namely: **measure, number, and weight** <note>This is a reference to the Biblical Book of Wisdom 11:20, "but thou hast ordered all things in measure and number and weight," a foundational concept for medieval science and alchemy representing divine order.</note>, which are the perfection of all necessary things.

Then follows the third part of this work, which is described by **Hermes** <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary "thrice-great" founder of alchemy, often called the "Father of Philosophers."</note>, King of the Greeks and Father of Philosophers, in this way:
> **The wind carried it in its belly.** <note>original: *Portauit illud ventus in ventre suo*; a famous line from the *Emerald Tablet*, suggesting the volatile or spiritual nature of the alchemical substance being transported by air or "breath."</note>

The philosophers call this part **distillation** <term>distillation: the process of vaporizing and condensing a substance to purify it and separate the "spirit" from the "body"</term>, or clarification. Therefore, after the matter has been **calcined** <term>calcined: reduced to a powder through high heat</term> by a liquid-like moisture and stripped of its previous name <note>original: *denominatiuo priuata*; meaning the substance has lost its original identity (like "lead" or "mercury") to become the raw material for the Work</note>, and then released from its fiery earthiness, it is necessary to distill it—that is, to clarify it and to bring forth the transparency and clarity of the air. For distillation is said to be the clarification of a thing with transparency; and this distillation is the completion of the total serenity of the work through clarity. And it is performed three, or four, or five, or six, seven, eight, or nine times,

### *Concerning the effects of this medicine or Tincture. The Final Chapter.*

Fifth and finally, we must proceed to the power, nobility, and effect of this praiseworthy philosophical tincture <term>tincture: (Latin: *tincturæ philosophicæ*) in alchemy, a potent liquid or powder capable of transmuting metals and healing the body</term>; which is a tower of strength against the face of the enemy. <note>original: *à facie inimici*; a phrase often used in medieval texts to signify protection against disease, old age, or spiritual corruption.</note> And it should be known that the ancient sages found four principal effects or virtues in this glorious treasury of a science, which is a source of both comfort and aid. **I** entered the house of the elder Habielfaim <note>A Latinized Arabic name, likely referring to an ancient master or a variation of Hermes; the text belongs to the Arabic-Latin alchemical tradition.</note> one day for the purpose of visiting him, and I sat at his right hand. There is also another method derived from the preparations, and it is just as Joseph <note>likely referring to a pseudonymous alchemical authority, sometimes associated with the 'Sayings of Joseph' in the Arabic-Latin tradition</note> said: "Mix fire and water, and they will be two. Mix air with earth, and they will be four: then make the four into one, and you have reached that which you desire." Then, let the body become no body, and let that which is weak over the fire become not weak, and you have grasped wisdom.

Therefore, act according to what Joseph said regarding this; the preparer of these things from the beginning to the end is the **hot and fixed, honored water**. It is she who reveals the **tincture** <note>original: *tinctura*; the transformative essence or "color" that changes the nature of a substance</note> in the **projection** <note>original: *proiectione*; the final stage of the work where the Stone is cast onto base metal to effect transmutation</note>, and were it not for her, there would be no purpose for any wise man in any root of wisdom. And she herself is the **mediatrix** <note>a female mediator or middle-point</note> between opposites. She herself is the same: the first, the middle, and the last.

Understand this which I have shown you, and know the manner of the word, for she reveals the tincture. For such is the usual cunning <note>original: *improbitas*; literally 'wickedness,' referring here to the deliberate obfuscation and technical trickery used by alchemical authors</note> and **sophism** <note>a clever but misleading argument intended to hide the truth from the uninitiated</note> of the wise; perhaps they introduced a term in one sense, while beneath it lies another. And I hope that these things will become apparent through my words: because he hints to you much regarding their secrets and sophisms, and God will grant you prosperity. If, however, the method of any of the wise should one day be revealed from their writings, it will not be opened to a man unless he reads the book in our **verses** <note>original: *carmina*; poems or rhythmic incantations used to encode alchemical recipes</note>. For I have explained to you and to all my brothers whatever they obscured...

# TO EUTHICIA.

The philosophers, to the best of their ability, cried out on behalf of the fathers and sons <note>original: *pro patribus & filijs*; a reference to the lineage of alchemical knowledge passed down through "generations" of masters and students</note>. What could be understood in a few pages, they themselves weigh down across many pages, buried in **tropes** <note>original: *tropicis*; figurative language, metaphors, or allegories used to hide secrets from the uninitiated</note>, and they wrap the matter in even greater obscurities, which the intellect is never able to grasp. 

I, however, so that my memory might endure, sat in solitude with the ancients, considering the books of the old masters. I sought this <term>knowledge</term> <note>original: *scientia*; specifically the "Science" or Art of Alchemy</note> from any of those who sat with you and inquired after it. Yet when I spoke to them, they did not understand me; for they held in their hands books that describe to them **Alkabric and Alkakir** <note>original: *Alkabric Alkakir*; likely Latinized corruptions of the Arabic *al-kibrit* (sulfur) and *al-kar* (pitch/bitumen), used here to represent the messy, physical materials that distract "puffers" from the true philosophical work</note>, which are the species or vain things they know and by which they are occupied. These are the things that deter those who are so occupied, for they dwell on their own questions and stray from the truth, blinded by ignorance.

When I saw you and your face there among them—judging by what your expression hinted at—and when I explained things based on the secondary grasping of your intellect, I turned my face toward you. I have explained to you that which my knowledge had enclosed within my breast, so that you might know the **soul of knowledge** and the place of the secret. I have done this so that you might distinguish between me and the men who dwell on errors and vanities, based on what you have read in the books of others, and what they have spoken and brought forth from the words of the **Wise**—the ancients, the moderns, and those who are sought after. None of these others has dared to explain even a single letter from the sayings of the ancient philoso... <note>the text cuts off at *philoso*, implying *philosophorum* or "philosophers"</note>

# ROSINVS

In each of those falsified substances a **single body** has been incorporated; for this reason, they similarly spoke of "one body" and "bodies," and because of this, they said that this one is from those. The **spirit** and **soul** <note>original: *spiritus & anima*; the volatile and vital principles of the material</note>, through multiple operations, are the **stone and not a stone**. This is the stone which the Sages of the Art compare to the **Eagle-stone** <term>Eagle-stone: original *lapis Aquilae* or *Aetites*; a hollow geode containing a loose stone that rattles inside, historically believed to assist in childbirth and here used to symbolize the "matter within the matter"</term>. For the Eagle-stone is a known stone; and there is a stone in its belly—a stone that moves—by which they signified, among the ascending ones, the **ash extracted from ash** <note>original: *cinerem extractum à cinere*; a term for the ultimate purified residue of the work</note>. 

Similarly, it is a stone in whose belly is a stone that moves; in the same way, when they dissolve it, its **water** comes forth from it, which was congealed within it, and it moves by ascending and exalting itself into the air. By this, they signify the **spirit** and **soul** which is in its belly. And this is the stone in whose belly is a stone, while the **dregs** <note>original: *fex*; the solid residue or "dead" matter left behind</note> from which that ascending thing emerged remain immobile. 

Then, its soul appears from it afterward, and it is the **ash of ash**, which **Marian** <note>Marian: Refers to Maria the Prophetess (Maria Prophetissima), a foundational figure in alchemy credited with inventing the *balneum Mariae* or bain-marie</note> named the "congealed coagulator," their water in their earth; she greatly magnified this ash. And this is the **leaven** <term>leaven: original *fermentum*; a substance that "ripens" the work, much like yeast causes bread to rise</term>, and the leaven of the leaven of the gold of the common people, and of their leaves <note>original: *foliorum*; likely referring to thin plates or scales of metal</note>. And this is the leaven of those bodies to which they are reduced; and the ash is the leaven of the water, which is their gold. Therefore, they named this ash the **Leaven of leaven**, and through this, the more one considers it, the more their water is hidden. And as for what the *Rosarius* <note>original: *Rosar.*; likely referring to the *Rosarium Philosophorum* (The Rosary of the Philosophers), a famous alchemical florilegium</note> said: "if you melt the body"—he does not mean here a melting by fire, but...

It signifies its dissolution, so that it may become the **living silver of the wise** <note>original: *argentum vivum sapientum*; the "mercury of the philosophers," a purified, non-vulgar form of the metal</note>, and from it, its **flowers** <note>original: *flores*; refers to the volatile essences or sublimates that rise during heating</note> are extracted. By the **mountains**, however, he signified **cucurbits** <term>Cucurbit: original *cucurbita*; a gourd-shaped glass vessel used as the bottom part of a distillation apparatus</term>, and by the **peaks of the mountains**, he meant **alembics** <term>Alembic: original *alembica*; the cap or head of a still that cools vapors and directs them into a receiver</term>. To **return them to their roots**, however, is to place it back upon that from which it originated. 

He named the cucurbits "mountains" because **Sun and Moon** <note>original: *Sol & Luna*; the alchemical symbols for Gold and Silver, or the masculine and feminine principles</note> are found in the mountains. So also in these "mountains," which are the cucurbits, their Sun and Moon are generated, and in them the work is done; and these are the lesser of their leaves and their gold, and in them he reveals its preparation. 

All of this is spoken in **metaphor**, and it is a wonderful and beautiful metaphor. He does not mean literal mountains, nor does he mean the tops of human heads by "higher places." Nor is that which is "reaped" from them actually **hair**, as some commentators have said—those who labored over hair and consumed their money and their days in the pursuit of vanity. Instead, wisdom is said to be—

And indeed she <note>Euthicia</note> signifies: For **Hermes** said, "Put the **ff.** <note>The abbreviation *ff.* or *f.* is explained immediately below as representing both 'species' and 'spirit'</note> in a **thick piece** <note>original: *pecia spissa*; likely referring to a thick cloth or a specific type of vessel</note>, and set them to cook in the fire."

Therefore, the first **f.** signifies **species**, and the second **f.** signifies **spirits**.

For this reason, **Democritus** <note>Referring to Pseudo-Democritus, a foundational alchemical author</note> said: "Wash in moisture, and wash away the moisture until its **blackness** <note>original: *nigredo*; the first major stage of the alchemical Great Work, symbolizing decay and the stripping away of old forms</note> enters." 

[Euthicia asks:] To what end do the philosophers call that blackness "the **blackness of money**," <note>original: *pecuniae nigredinem*; this may be a metaphorical reference to the 'value' or 'capital' of the starting material, or a corruption of a term for pitch</note> yet none of you depicts it with the **face of a bird**? <note>original: *avis vultum*; a reference to the 'Crow’s Head,' the standard symbol for the *nigredo* stage</note>

She said: "The diversity of names causes me to wander into error."

He answers: Let not what you see force you into error; mix the **dry** thus with the **moist**, until the **soul** dries the **spirit**—that is, the **conception**—and puts it to flight in its own belly: because the soul went out from the spirit, and the soul lives by the spirit.

Therefore, **Euthicia**, if you wish to confirm these things I have told you, take **sea alum** <note>original: *alumen marinum*; a mineral salt used as a reagent</note>, that is, the **moist Spirit**: dry it—that is, **sublime** it into powder—and **putrefy** it, so that it may now be freed from its dregs. Once the moisture is washed away—namely, the excess watery part—it is **thin**, that is, **subtle**. From there you extract the **earth**—that is, **fix** <note>original: *fige*; the process of making a volatile substance stable and resistant to fire</note> it—and beware of fire during the **governance of water** <note>original: *regimine aquae*; the stage of the process controlled by liquid or heat levels</note>. For fire is an enemy until they become reconciled to one another, namely through **fixation**. And know that if you make fire and water to be in harmony—that is, the **volatile spirit**...

<meta>This page continues the dialogue between the alchemist Rosinus (the Arabic-Latin name for Zosimos of Panopolis) and his female student, Euthicia. ...in describing it, he answers: “It is a **stone** <note>original: *lapis*; here referring to the Philosopher's Stone</note> having glory and color within itself.” 

And she asks: “From where does its color come?” 
He answered: “From its most intense **bitterness** <note>original: *amaritudo*; in alchemical terms, this often refers to the caustic or purifying nature of the substance during its black stage, or *nigredo*.</note>.” 
And she: “From where comes its bitterness and intensity?” 
He answered: “From the **impurity of its metal**.” 
And she: “Does its red color ever rise above?” 
He answered: “Indeed.” 
And she: “Is it ever even hotter than fire?” 
He answered: “Fire in comparison to it is as water in comparison to fire.” 
And she: “Is it stronger than fire?” 
He answers: “No.” 
And she: “Why then do you assert that it is stronger than fire?” 
He answers: “Because when fires encounter one another, one consumes the other.” 
And she: “Is this force of its heat visible to men?” 
He answers: “No.” 
And she: “Why then did fire strengthen it?” 
He answered: “Because the **soul of fire** <note>original: *anima ignis*; the essential, spiritual heat or energy</note> is hidden within its own soul.” 
And she: “Is this stone therefore **spiritual**?” 
He answered: “Do you not know this, that the spiritual strengthens the spiritual, when it consumes its filth and its superfluities and separates them from it? Since it was said that fire strengthens it, therefore provide a comparison known to me.” 
He answered: “Gladly. Do you not see how **Petroleum** <note>original: *Petroleum*; literally 'rock oil.' It is used here as a metaphor for a substance that holds a latent, powerful fire that is only activated by contact with an external flame.</note>, if touched by the hands, does not burn; but if it is touched by fire, it touches nothing without itself being burned?” 
And she: “Therefore the stone which is seen does not burn except by fire?” 
He answered: “Indeed, just like Petroleum, it does not burn except by fire.”

And she asked: "Does this stone burn everything?"
