...support of the soul. And when it has remained for some time, that which is stronger will prevail in it, so that it converts the whole body into soul, and the soul into spirit.

The fourth step of our governance <note>original: *regimen*; the systematic series of chemical operations</note> is the **betrothal of the stone** into a bodily lime <note>original: *calx*; the powdery residue left after a substance has been roasted or calcined</note>, so that it may be fixed in that body from which it was taken from the beginning. And this is because when the spirit has dissolved the body and the soul so that they exist in their own form, it does not remain fixed unless you "occupy" it <note>original: *occupaueris*; in this context, to bind or tether the volatile spirit so it does not evaporate</note>. 

Truly, the occupation is that you join the spirit with the body from which you prepared it in the beginning, because in that body it is held back from its flight, leading to the lasting endurance of the body. And therefore **Plato** <note>Medieval alchemical texts frequently cited "Plato" or "Aristotle" to provide ancient authority to their chemical recipes</note> says: "When the spirit has dissolved the soul and the body together, it does not stand fixed. Join it, therefore, with the body, so that it may generate its own likeness. Nor should you join it with just anything so that it might stand by itself, but only with that from which it originated." If you do this, it becomes the **Elixir** <note>original: *Iccir*; a Latinization of the Arabic *al-iksīr*</note>. 

And know that for all workers, the purpose fails after the completion of the work if they omit this secret. Note these words, therefore, and mark these mysteries. Because when the spirit has dissolved the **white foliated earth**, none of them remain fixed unless you occupy the spirit with that body from which it was prepared in the beginning. 

The spirit is **Mercury**, and its first body is **white and red sulfur**. Therefore, when the spirit has dissolved the sulfurous body in all things as was prepared above, it is not fixed unless you occupy it with...

# SHORT TREATISE #

...with new sulfur, from which it was prepared in the beginning. For white and red sulfur, as **Aristotle** <note>original: *Aristot.*; medieval alchemists frequently cited pseudo-Aristotelian works to lend authority to the theory that sulfur and mercury are the parents of all metals</note> says, congeals quicksilver <note>mercury</note> into gold and silver. Join your work, therefore, with the body, so that it may generate its own likeness; if you do this, the **Elixir** <note>original: *Iccir*; a Latinized version of the Arabic *al-iksīr*</note> will be set above other bodies—that is, the body you join it with—otherwise, it will not be fixed: because nature is not contained except in its own nature.

And this is because, as **Plato** says: "Nature follows nature, and nature contains nature," and it teaches it to fight against the fire <note>referring to the substance's ability to remain stable and "fixed" rather than evaporating when heated</note>. Perform, therefore, the betrothal of the husband and wife, and you shall have the whole mastery <note>original: *magisterium*; the completed Work or the philosopher's stone</note>.

But their preparation, as **Avicenna** <note>Ibn Sina, the Persian polymath whose works on chemistry and medicine were foundational to Western alchemy</note> says, is this: That first you cleanse the husband on one side, and the wife on the other, so that once purified from filth they may be better joined; for if you do not prepare the bodies, they cannot be loved <note>an alchemical metaphor: substances must be purified before they can chemically react or "bond"</note>. Therefore, make peace between the elements, so that they may love each other in a fitting embrace.

For the sharp mastery of the philosophers places the soul into the limes <note>original: *calces*; the fine powder or ash resulting from calcination</note> of the bodies; then the vigor of the spirits crushes them into the smallest limes of the leads. Also, when you wish to put the ferment into the **Elixir**, first mix it with the spirits, because unless you do this, its nature would not be imprinted upon them. Mix the ferment well, therefore, with the elements, and you shall have the mastery.

# AVICENNA ON #
# CONGEALING AND #
## the binding of stones. ##
### Chapter I. ###

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'T' featuring a stylized vine and floral pattern within a square frame.</image-desc>

PURE EARTH does not become stone, because
it does not create a continuous mass, but
remains fragmented. For the prevailing
dryness within it does not permit it to be
bound together. Stones are formed, however, in
two ways: by binding <note>original: *conglutinando*; the process of "gluing" or cementing solid particles together</note> and by
congealing <note>original: *congelando*; the process of a liquid solidifying into a solid</note>. For in some stones, earth is the dominant element;
in others, however, water. Sometimes the initial
mud <note>original: *lutum*; a moist, malleable mixture of earth and water</note> is dried out, and a certain thing is created
which is midway between mud and stones,
and then it becomes stone. Viscous <note>sticky or thick</note> mud
is more suitable for this transformation, for this is
capable of binding. On the banks of the Geon <note>original: *Geon*; the Gihon, one of the four rivers of Paradise. Medieval scholars often identified it with the Nile or the Oxus river in Central Asia</note>
earth was seen which appeared to be converted into
stones in the space of 33 years. From water, however,
stones are formed in two ways. One is when
water falling drop by drop is congealed <note>referring to the formation of stalactites and stalagmites</note>.
The other is when something descends from
running water which settles on the surface of the
bottom of that water, and becomes stone.
For there are certain places where water, when
poured out, is converted into stones, which are of
various colors; and there are waters which, when taken up
from the source, do not congeal, but if they are
poured near their own bed, they congeal and
become stones.

<summary>This page marks the beginning of Avicenna's influential work on mineralogy, explaining that stones form either through the binding of dry earth or the solidification of mineral-rich water.</summary>
<keywords>Avicenna, mineralogy, petrification, geology, Geon River, congealing, binding, formation of stones</keywords>

# MINERALS. #

We know therefore that in the earth exists that mineral power <note>original: *vis illa mineralis*; a theoretical creative force in medieval natural philosophy believed to drive the growth and formation of minerals within the ground.</note> which congeals waters. Therefore, the origins of stones are formed either from a muddy substance, or a viscous one, or from a substance in which [water] prevails, which is congealed by a certain mineral power; or earth prevails within it, causing it to be coagulated. In the same way Sal ammoniac <note>original: *Sal armoniacum*; ammonium chloride, a volatile salt highly prized by alchemists for its ability to sublimate and react with metals.</note> is congealed, but the earthy power is not sufficient to transform it into salt; rather, heat assists it. For heat, arriving, coagulates it by a hidden power; and perhaps it is formed from cold, dry earth, and from water earth is made when the qualities of earth overcome it, and vice-versa. There is, however, a certain substance which some ingenious people use when they wish to coagulate a dry thing, which is composed of two waters and is called virgin's milk <note>original: *lac virginis*; in alchemy, this refers to a white, milky precipitate or solution, often created by mixing a lead-based solution with an acidic or salty one.</note>, which is its most certain effect. Therefore, stones are made from mud by the heat of the sun, or from water coagulated by a dry, earthy power, or from hot water that has been dried out. Likewise, certain plants and certain animals are converted into stones by a certain mineral, stone-making <note>original: *lapidificatiua*; the quality or "virtue" of turning something into stone.</note> power; and this happens in a stony place, or by a certain sudden, discordant power which comes out of the earth during an earthquake. This power converts [things] into stones, so that in that hour this transmutation of the bodies of animals and plants occurs, as well as that which is nearby, such as the transmutation of waters. It is, however, impossible that any complex thing <note>original: *complexionatum*; a substance made of a specific "complexion" or mixture of the four primary elements (Earth, Water, Air, Fire).</note> should be entirely converted into a single elem- <note>The text cuts off mid-word; likely "element."</note>

...power: because elements and elemental compounds, having been transmuted, pass into one another toward the dominant quality <note>original: *in dominans*; referring to the Aristotelian theory that in a mixture, the strongest element or quality—hot, cold, wet, or dry—converts the others into its own nature.</note>. Hence, that which falls into salt-pans becomes salt, and that which falls into fire becomes fire. Some things change more quickly and others more slowly, according to the power of the active qualities and the resistance of the passive ones.

There is also a place in Arabia which colors all bodies existing within it with its own color. When that mass fell, it bounced back from the earth several times like a ball, because it was composed of tiny pieces clinging to...

### On the Cause of Mountains.
### Chapter II.

Mountains also arise sometimes from an **essential cause** and sometimes from an **accidental cause**. From an **essential cause**, as when the earth is raised by a violent movement <note>referring to seismic activity or earthquakes</note> of the ground, and a mountain is formed. From an **accidental cause**, such as when a deep hollow is carved out by winds or the flow of water, occurring gradually until a vast depth is created; consequently, a great height rises up next to it, and this is the principal cause of mountains. There are also some earths that are soft and some that are hard. The soft ones are carried away by water-flows and winds, while the hard ones remain, and thus an elevation is formed.

Just as the generation of mountains occurs, so does the generation of stones, because the flow of water continuously brings oily clay to them, which over a long duration dries out and becomes stone. Furthermore, it is not far-fetched to suggest there is a <term>mineralizing power</term> <note>original: *vis mineralis*; a theoretical virtue or force in medieval science believed to transform elements and compounds into stone or metal</note> that converts waters into stones. And for this reason, in many stones, certain parts of aquatic animals <note>Avicenna is remarkably identifying fossils here, recognizing that these "stony animals" were once living creatures from the sea</note> and other things are found. Mountains have been formed, as it were, over many ages, as we have said, provided they are not in a state of decay. The substances...

<sig>Cc 2</sig>

<summary>In this passage, Avicenna explains the formation of mountains through seismic activity (essential causes) and erosion (accidental causes). He also discusses the petrification process, correctly identifying fossils as the remains of aquatic animals preserved in stone by a "mineralizing power."</summary>
<keywords>geology, mountain formation, erosion, fossils, mineralizing power, earthquakes, petrification, Avicenna</keywords>

--- Page 428 ---
<meta>This page continues Avicenna’s discussion of geological formations, specifically how sedimentary layers and mountains are formed through the action of water and the sea, before transitioning into a formal classification of minerals.</meta>

<page-num>404</page-num>
<header>AVICENNA</header>

Furthermore, the yellow clays <note>original: *luteæ*; referring to the yellowish, clay-like deposits often found in sedimentary layers</note> that are found on high peaks are not made of that same stony material. Instead, they consist of material worn away from mountains, or terrestrial matter, or other substances brought by water along with mud and vegetation. These are mixed with the mountain clay—or perhaps they are ancient sea-mud, which remains uniform in substance. In such cases, one part becomes stone while another does not, instead remaining soft or dissolving due to some prevailing quality. The sea has its ebb and flow <note>original: *recessus & accessus*; referring to tides and the historical transgression/regression of oceans</note>; it carves out certain places and elevates others, and at times has covered the entire earth. From this action, it scrapes away soft materials and leaves the hard ones behind, piling them up in certain locations. Once these soft materials were piled up and cut off from the water, they dried out and were converted into mountains.

### *On the four species of mineral bodies.*
### *Chapter III.*

Mineral bodies are divided into four species: namely, into **stones**, **fusible substances** <note>original: *liquefactiua*; these are metals which can be melted</note>, **sulfurs**, and **salts**. Some of these possess a rare <note>meaning porous or less dense</note> substance and a weak composition, while others have a strong substance; some are ductile <note>original: *ductibilia*; capable of being hammered or drawn out, like gold or copper</note>, and some are not. Among those of weak substance, some are **salts**, which dissolve easily in moisture, such as alum, vitriol <note>original: *calcamentum*; likely a corruption of *chalcanthum*, referring to metallic sulfates</note>, and sal ammoniac <note>original: *sal armoniacum*; ammonium chloride</note>. Others are oily and do not dissolve easily by moisture alone, such as sulfur and orpiment <note>original: *auripigmentū*; a yellow arsenic sulfide mineral used as a pigment</note>.

<meta>catchword: But</meta>

<summary>Avicenna explains how mountains and sedimentary layers are formed by ancient sea movements and the drying of mud, then introduces a four-fold classification of minerals: stones, metals, sulfurs, and salts.</summary>
<keywords>geology, sedimentation, sea levels, mineralogy, classification of minerals, salts, sulfur, vitriol, orpiment, Avicenna</keywords>

--- Page 429 ---
<meta>This page continues the classification of minerals from page 404, moving from a general definition of salts and fusible substances into a specific discussion of mercury (quicksilver) and the physical properties—such as ductility and "wateriness"—that define metals, stones, salts, and sulfurs.</meta>

<page-num>405</page-num>
<header>MINERALS.</header>

But **quicksilver** <note>original: *argentum viuum*; mercury</note> belongs to the second category <note>referring to the "fusible substances" or metals mentioned on the previous page</note>, although it is the fundamental element of ductile substances, or is similar to certain ductile things. Now, all ductile substances are capable of being melted; for the most part, things that are not ductile cannot be melted, or at least they cannot be softened except with great violence. The material of ductile substances is a **watery substance** mixed with an **earthy substance** in a strong mixture, such that one cannot be separated from the other. This watery substance is congealed by cold after heat has acted upon it, a process called **epthesis** <term>epthesis: a term derived from Greek meaning "boiling" or "maturation," referring to the internal "cooking" of minerals within the earth</term>. An example can be seen in wine, which does not freeze easily because of its oiliness <note>original: *vntuositatem*; literally "unctuosity," a quality medieval scientists believed prevented substances from becoming brittle or solidifying in a standard way</note>; for this reason, it is not ductile.

**Stones**, among mineral substances, are materially watery, but they do not solidify through water [cold] alone, but also through **dryness**, which transforms their "wateriness" into "earthiness." There is no excessively oily moisture in them, and therefore they cannot be drawn out <note>meaning they are not ductile or malleable</note>. Because their solidification comes from dryness, they are generally not easily dissolved, except through specific natural methods of dissolution.

**Alum** <note>original: *Alumen*</note> and **sal ammoniac** <note>original: *sal armoniacum*; ammonium chloride</note> belong to the genus of **salts**. In sal ammoniac, the portion of "fire" is greater than that of "earth." For this reason, the entire substance **sublimates** <note>original: *sublimatur*; transitions directly from a solid to a vapor when heated</note>; it is essentially water mixed with a hot, extremely subtle smoke of a highly fiery nature, which has been solidified by dryness.

The wateriness of **sulfurous substances** is mixed with earth in a powerful combination through the boiling of heat, until they become oily; afterward, they are congealed by cold.

<sig>Cc 3</sig>

<summary>This page explains the elemental composition of minerals, arguing that metals are a "watery" and "earthy" mix refined by heat, while stones and salts are formed through "dryness" and different levels of "fiery" smoke.</summary>

Indeed, **vitriols** <term>atramenta: literally "blackings," these are metallic sulfates such as copperas or green vitriol, used historically to make ink and dyes</term> are composed of salt, sulfur, and stones; there is within them the mineral power of certain fusible bodies that are formed from them, such as **vitriol-stone** <term>calcamentum: a term for vitriol used specifically in tanning or shoemaking</term>. And **alachar** <note>original: *alachar*; likely a Latinization of the Arabic *al-zaj*, referring to various types of vitriol</note> are generated from larger grains of vitriol, and its saltiness does not dissolve except with that which is in that sulfur; afterward it congeals, and it then receives its mineral power from certain bodies. Therefore, that which receives the power of **iron** will be red or saffron-colored, like **alathar** <note>likely another variant of vitriol, specifically "colcothar" or iron(III) oxide</note>. But that which has received the power of **copper** will be green. For this reason, it is possible for these two to be created artificially.

**Quicksilver** <note>original: *argentum viuum*; mercury</note> is like water that is mixed with an extremely fine earth in a powerful, sulfurous mixture, to the point that it cannot rest on a flat surface; this is due to the great dryness that exists within it, and for that reason it does not stick to what it touches. Its whiteness comes from the clarity of that water and from the whiteness of the fine earth within it. Its specific property is that it is congealed by the vapor of sulfur; perhaps in this way it is "frozen" by lead, or easily by the vapor of sulfur. It appears, moreover, that quicksilver and things similar to it are the **fundamental element** of all fusible substances <note>referring to the "Sulfur-Mercury theory," a cornerstone of medieval alchemy which claimed all metals were composed of these two principles in varying proportions and purity</note>. This is either because all fusible things, when they are melted, are converted back into it, or because they do not melt until they are heated, and when they have been melted, they appear red. But **lead**, without a doubt, when it is melted, is quicksilver; yet it does not melt unless it is heated, and when it [liquefies]... <note>original: *& cum li-*; the text breaks off here, continuing with the catchword "que" for *liquaturque* on the next page</note>

**Tin**, on the other hand, seems to contain good quicksilver but poor sulfur; furthermore, these components are not well-ground or blended, but are joined as if in small, distinct particles, and for that reason, it does not achieve the perfection of other metals.

...sulfur <note>original: *phur*; completing the word from the previous page</note> is bad, of an evil, foul-smelling, and weak vapor; for this reason, it does not congeal well. Indeed, let the practitioners of **Alchemy** know that the species <note>The essential nature or "blueprint" of a substance</note> of things cannot be transmuted; but they can make things similar to them, and dye a red metal with yellow so that it appears to be gold, and dye a white metal with whatever color they wish, until it is very similar to gold or **copper** <term>æs: a general term for copper or its alloys</term>. 

They can also wipe away the impurities of lead, yet it will always remain lead, even though it may look like silver. Furthermore, I do not believe it is possible for the **specific difference** <note>original: *differentia specifica*; in Aristotelian logic, the essential quality that distinguishes one species from another</note> to be removed by human ingenuity, and it is not possible for one **complexion** <note>original: *complexio*; the specific balance of primary qualities (hot, cold, moist, dry)</note> to be converted into another; for these perceptible traits are not the "differences" by which a species is changed, but are rather **accidents** <note>original: *accidentia*; external or non-essential properties like color, smell, or taste</note> and properties. 

Their true differences, however, are not known; and since the difference is unknown, how can it be known whether it has been removed or not, or how it might be removed? But the stripping away of accidents—such as vapor, color, and weight—or at least their reduction, is not impossible:

<meta>catchword: because (original: quia)</meta>

<summary>In this influential passage, Avicenna argues that while alchemists can skillfully mimic the appearance of gold and silver using dyes and salts, they cannot actually change the essential species of one metal into another. He applies Aristotelian logic to suggest that human art can only alter "accidents" (surface traits) rather than the "specific difference" (true essence) of a substance.</summary>

Therefore, if you read and understand my words, you shall reach your goal and give thanks to God. But if there is one whose composition is weak and whose understanding is too brief, and he does not reach his goal, let him not blame his ignorance on me, nor say that I have erred; rather, let him blame himself for failing to reach his purpose.

## CONCERNING THE PHILOSOPHER'S STONE
### *A little work metaphorically describing the secrets.*

# RACHAIDIBI, VERA-
# DIANI, RHODIANI, AND
### *Kanis, philosophers of the King of the Persians*
### *On the matter of the philosophical Stone,*
### *a fragment of a most sharp dialogue.*

RACHAIDIBI, son of Zetheibida, philosopher to the King of the Persians and the Prince of the Romans, said: The seed <term>seed: original "sperma," referring to the foundational substance or "starting material" of the alchemical process</term> of the stone is cold and moist in its manifest <note>original: "in manifesto" — meaning the outward, physical properties that can be observed</note> state, and in its hidden <note>original: "in occulto" — referring to the internal, essential nature or potential energy of the substance</note> state, it is hot and dry. Therefore, he says: make the cold and moist part hidden, and place the hot and dry part in the manifest state. In this way, your coldness and moisture will be hidden so that they might never be diminished; for if they were diminished, the stone itself would be diminished. 

When, therefore, the coldness and moisture are hidden, act by hiding them so that you may thus compose that heat and dryness—which was both in the hidden and the manifest—and so, from the spirit, let a body be made in two degrees, and it shall become a sphere, and blood, and flesh. <note>The author is describing the "Inversion of Qualities," a central alchemical theory where one must flip the internal and external properties of a substance to achieve stability.</note>

Rhodianus says: The seed is white and liquid. This liquid first forms a sphere in its proper place for five days; and it receives flesh and blood, limbs and form, and the imaginative power from God Most High; and it comes to its birth, and shines and rises in its own time. Which are two <note>The text cuts off here at the end of the page. The comparison of the Stone's creation to the gestation of a human fetus was a common way for alchemists to explain the "organic" growth of the Work.</note>

<vocab>Rachaidibi, Veradianus, Rhodianus, Kanis, Philosophical Stone, Persians, Romans, Seed of the stone</vocab>

<summary>This page introduces a dialogue between four Persian philosophers concerning the "seed" of the Philosopher's Stone, explaining how its internal and external elemental qualities must be balanced and inverted. The process is described using biological metaphors, likening the maturation of the alchemical stone to the development of a fetus.</summary>
<keywords>Rachaidibi, Rhodianus, four qualities, manifest and occult, alchemical embryology, seed of the stone, Persian alchemy</keywords>

*In the first chapter I will speak of Mercury and its nature, as well as the sulfur that it contains within itself.*

*In the third I will speak of the joining of body and spirit, and the dissolution of the stone into the first matter.*

*In the fourth I will speak of the extraction of water from the earth.*

### On the nature of perfect bodies, that is of the sun and the moon, and their sulfur.
### Chapter II.

**Gold** <note>original: "Aurum"</note> is the most perfect body, the lord of stones, and the King and head of all others. Neither does the earth corrupt it, nor do burning things consume it, nor is it diminished in the fire; rather, it is improved by the flame, because within the fire it is moistened by a certain internal humidity, and it is not altered by water. Its **complexion** <term>complexion: "complexio," the specific balance of the four qualities—heat, cold, moisture, and dryness—that determines a substance's nature</term> is tempered, and its nature is perfectly balanced in heat, cold, moisture, and dryness; nothing superfluous nor any deficiency is found within it. For it is created from the most subtle and most brilliant substance of **quicksilver** <note>original: "argenti vivi"</note>, and from a small amount of the substance of pure, clean **sulfur** of a fixed redness, which clearly tints that very substance of the quicksilver.

**Gold** is held to be the body and the **ferment** <term>ferment: "fermentum," a substance like yeast that triggers a transformation in a larger mass; in alchemy, gold "leavens" the base metals into more gold</term> of the white and red **Elixir** <note>original: "Elixiris," the transformative agent or Philosopher's Stone</note>. It is neither improved, nor perfected, nor completed except with this elixir and no other—just as dough cannot be leavened by anything other than its own **yeast** <note>original: "fermento"</note>. **Gold** is a body that endures, remaining through ages of ages. And for this reason, the philosophers have preferred and magnified it; they have even said that gold relates to other bodies in such a way...

Because its parts are concentrated so deeply at its center, gold is heavy—more so than could be explained by its **quicksilver** <note>original: "argentum vivum"</note> content alone.

For a most vehement fire consumes all things existing beneath the **lunar sphere** <note>In medieval cosmology, the "sublunary" world—everything below the Moon—was considered subject to decay, whereas the heavens were eternal. Silver is a perfect body, though less so than gold, and it is of less weight than gold. It belongs to the **parts of the Moon** <note>In alchemy, silver is almost always associated with the Moon (Luna), while gold is associated with the Sun (Sol).</note>. In a damp place it is corrupted <note>i.e., it tarnishes or oxidizes.</note>, and its taste is acid; it is diminished in fire and is burned by sulfurs.

This occurs because nature always works in a simple manner, and the perfection within these metals is simple and inseparable—unless it were perhaps driven into "flight" along with a **volatile** substance <term>volatile: a substance that easily evaporates or escapes when heated, as opposed to a "fixed" substance that resists fire</term>, for the quantity of the volatile can overcome the quantity of the fixed body.

# AVICENNA

Also note that penetration, submersion, connection, conjunction, combination, composition, and mixing signify the same thing in this art <note>the alchemical art</note>. For nothing is submerged, joined, or connected without also being mixed. For mixing is the union of mixable things by their smallest parts—that is, through indivisible units joined to one another. Know also for certain that the entire strength of this mastery <note>original: "magisterij," referring to the completion of the Great Work</note> lies in nothing but **putrefaction** <term>putrefaction: a process of slow fermentation or "rotting" under gentle heat, intended to break down the form of a substance so it can be reborn</term>. For if it has not been putrefied, it can neither be dissolved nor melted; and if it has not been dissolved, it will come to nothing.

Also know that in every work there are three dimensions, namely: width, height, and depth <note>these "dimensions" refer to the qualitative states or "layers" of a substance rather than spatial measurements</note>. This is clearly apparent in a body that is subject to our sight. For example: **Our Stone** <term>Our Stone: the Philosopher's Stone in its developmental stages</term> in its first creation is **white**, and it appears so on its surface <note>original: "in facie," literally "in its face"</note>. Because of this, we call it "cold and moist," for so it is. Hence we should study why our stone is "aquatic," for because it is cold and moist, its natural disposition is called a manifest or white body.

Furthermore, "width" is that middle disposition through which one travels toward the "deep" disposition. But that which is the middle between depth and height—as if between the contents or the opposites—makes passage through them impossible unless one quality is destroyed. Since its "high" disposition <note>its external or primary state</note> is cold and moist, one quality must therefore be destroyed—namely, the moisture—through putrefaction; then it thickens—

### On the extraction of water from the earth.
### Chapter 4.

After the matter has been **putrefied** <note>original: "putrefacta"; the process of breaking down the initial substance</note> in order to create the body and the spirit—which is impossible to achieve except in the air, that is, through **sublimation** <term>sublimation: in alchemy, this refers to the process of a substance being heated into a vapor and rising, separating the "spirit" from the heavy "body" or dregs</term>.

Know, therefore, that **our stone** is divided into two main parts: namely, the upper part which ascends, and the lower part which remains fixed at the bottom. And yet, these two parts are in harmony regarding their power <note>original: "virtute," referring to their medicinal or transformative strength</note>.

And for this reason, the philosopher <note>referring to Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary father of alchemy</note> says: "That which is below is like that which is above." This division is necessary to perform the miracles of the "One Thing"—that is, the stone. The lower part is the **earth**, which is called the **nurse** and the **ferment**; the upper part is the **soul**, which gives life to the whole stone and causes it to live again.

Thus, after the celebrated separation is performed, many miracles are accomplished through the conjunction <note>The "conjunction" is the chemical marriage or recombination of the separated elements.</note> of the stone. It must be noted that, although among some authors our stone is not divided into four parts—namely the four elements—in the first operation as was said above, it does have four principal parts: namely, one which ascends to the top and is **not fixed** <note>original: "non fixa"; meaning volatile or easily evaporated</note>; another which remains below and is called **fixed**; and the **earth** or **ferment**, which nourishes and ferments the whole stone, as has been said. 

Indeed, regarding that non-fixed part, it is necessary to have it in good quantity and give it to the stone, which is most pure and entirely without filth, until it raises the whole stone by the power of the non-fixed spirit above by **sublimating** it. And this is what the Philosopher <note>Referencing Hermes Trismegistus in the famous Emerald Tablet.</note> says:

> It ascends from the earth into heaven. <note>original: "Ascendit de terra in cælum."</note>

Afterward, it is necessary to process the stone, thus exalted, again upon a marble surface with the element extracted from the stone itself in the first operation. That element is called the <term>water of the stone</term>. And it must be worked <note>original: "affari"; likely referring to the labor of grinding or heating.</note> so many times until, through its refined state, the stone again descends into the earth; thus it receives the **superior power** by sublimating and the **inferior power** by descending. In this way, the **bodily** <note>solid matter</note> becomes **spiritual** <note>vaporous or refined</note> by sublimating, and when it is spiritual, it again becomes bodily by descending. 

And thus you possess the glory of the clarity of this world, and all darkness, poverty, and sickness flee from you: because the stone, thus composed, cures every illness. And this is the stone of all strength, <note>The text cuts off here; the catchword "nis" completes the Latin word "fortitudinis," meaning "of strength."</note>

Know, however, that when you have mixed the **body** <note>The solid, physical matter in the alchemical vessel.</note> with moisture, and the heat of the fire reaches it, the moisture turns upon the body and dissolves it. But the ancient philosophers gave our **stone** many names, such as **amalgam**, **vitriol**, and **blood** (on account of its red color), and infinite other names. ...middle state, in which there is] completed **digestion** <term>digestion</term> <note>The process of "cooking" or heating a substance over a long period to bring it to maturity.</note>. **Blackness** <term>Nigredo</term> <note>original: "Nigredo"; the first major stage of the alchemical work, representing putrefaction and the stripping away of old forms.</note> is nothing other than washing. Therefore, in **quicksilver** <term>Mercury</term> there is white sulphur, just as in gold there is red sulphur. And there is absolutely no such sulphur to be found upon the earth, neither white nor red, except that which exists within these metallic bodies. For this reason, the bodies must be prepared with great subtlety, so that we may obtain their sulphur and their quicksilver from them—the very materials from which gold and silver were originally fashioned beneath the earth.

Indeed, if I did not see gold and silver with my own eyes, I would say without a doubt that **Alchemy** <note>original: "Alchimiam"</note> was not true. For these metals are themselves the shining bodies in which the **dyeing rays** <note>The "tincture" or power to transform other metals, envisioned as a form of concentrated light or color.</note> reside; they dye other bodies into whiteness or redness, depending on how they have been prepared. 

The **alembic** <term>alembic</term> <note>The top part of a still, used for distillation.</note> and the **cucurbit** <term>cucurbit</term> <note>The lower, gourd-shaped vessel of a still that holds the liquid to be heated.</note> must be joined together so tightly that the **Mercury** <note>original: "Mercurius"</note> cannot escape, because it cannot be sublimated except by the power of the air. # 458 #

...with the philosophical [spirit], to be sublimated, and with it the **stone** may be sublimated, until in the final **sublimation** <term>sublimation</term> <note>In alchemy, sublimation involves heating a substance until it vaporizes and then solidifies again, used here to purify the material.</note> it is purified.

And this is the first order, which is called the first operation, which is performed so that the purest and most subtle substance may be drawn out.

The second is **solution** <term>solution</term> <note>original: "solutio"; the process of turning a solid substance into a liquid state.</note>, so that the matter may be dissolved into water.

The third is **putrefaction** <term>putrefaction</term> <note>original: "putrefactio"; a stage of symbolic "death" and decay, often associated with the color black, necessary before a new form can emerge.</note>, for **Morienes** <note>Morienus was a legendary 7th-century hermit and alchemist known for his dialogues on the philosopher's stone.</note> says: "Nothing animated was ever brought to birth, nor anything growing, except through putrefaction and change." Thus it is necessary for putrefaction to occur, because the destruction of one thing is the generation of another.

The fourth is **ablution** <term>ablution</term> <note>original: "ablutio"; the washing or cleansing of the matter.</note>: for it is necessary that the putrefied and filthy thing be washed and cleansed from its corrupting impurity. And the philosophers have spoken well: because as long as the water remains upon the earth, the earth is washed and **waxed** <term>ceration</term> <note>original: "ceratio"; the process of softening a substance until it has the consistency of wax.</note> all the more, so that washing and waxing are the same thing.

The fifth is **coagulation** <term>coagulation</term> <note>original: "coagulatio"; the thickening of a liquid into a solid.</note>: for it is necessary that the water, by gentle cooking in **our sun** <note>A metaphor for the alchemist's controlled heat or specialized furnace.</note>, be changed into earth, and perfectly coagulated and dried, and turned into powder.

The sixth is **calcination** <term>calcination</term> <note>The reduction of a substance to a dry powder or ash through high heat.</note>. From this you may know that a calcined thing is more suitable than one not calcined, and it is simply **fixation** <term>fixation</term> <note>original: "fixio"; making a volatile substance stable so that it no longer evaporates when heated.</note>. Hence there were many philosophers who called calcination "fixation," and they spoke well: because all these modes are contained within sublimation. For certainly...

<header>TRACTATVLVS.</header>

¶ If one **sublimates** <term>sublimation</term> <note>original: "sublimat"; in alchemy, this is the process of heating a substance until it vaporizes and then solidifies again in a purified form.</note> perfectly, they accomplish the entire work.

And you should know that all of this is completed in one **furnace** <note>original: "furno"</note> and in one **vessel** <note>original: "vase"</note>. Any intelligent person can complete these seven dispositions. Therefore, do not be negligent in sublimation. For whatever the quality of the **cleansing** <note>original: "mundatio"</note> may be, such will be the quality of the final perfection.

->*Now I wish to explain to you what Sublimation is.*<-

Sublimation is the raising up of the most subtle parts away from the fixed parts. The parts that are not fixed are raised by smoke—that is, by wind. For as we have said, one must take care that they do not escape; rather, they are fixed together with the fixed parts, and they remain, and they provide a faster **fusion** <note>original: "fusionem"; the process of melting or blending substances together.</note>. Understand that true sublimation occurs when we create a separation of the parts: those which are raised above from those which remain below. Indeed, we desire that they should simultaneously come together with their own kind, because in our **stone** <note>original: "lapide nostro"; the Philosopher's Stone, the legendary substance capable of turning base metals into gold or granting longevity.</note>, after the first **purification** <note>original: "purificatio"</note> which is completed through **solution** <term>solution</term> <note>original: "solutio"; the process of dissolving a solid into a liquid state.</note>, we do not find anything diminished or superfluous.

For this reason, **Geber** <note>Geber is the Latinized name of Jabir ibn Hayyan (c. 721–813), a foundational figure in early chemistry and alchemy whose works were highly influential in Medieval Europe.</note> said: "Let the stone be sublimated with it, until it finally arrives at the purity of sublimation." For he said *with it*, meaning without any other addition or any other foreign substance...

### *On the multiplication and fixation of the stone: Chapter VII.*

There follows the coupling of the powders, so that they may bear fruit and their fruit may remain forever; and I will teach how to **fix** <term>fixation</term> <note>original: "figere"; the process of making a volatile substance stable so that it does not evaporate or "flee" when exposed to fire.</note> the sublimated powders, so that they can remain in the fire, and be united and mixed with **bodies** <note>original: "corporibus"; in this context, the base metals that the alchemist seeks to transform.</note>.

Moreover, **fixation** is the suitable adaptation of a volatile thing to the fire. Indeed, the reason for its discovery is so that every **tincture** <term>tincture</term> <note>original: "tinctura"; the concentrated "spirit" or "medicine" capable of staining or transforming a base metal into a noble one.</note> and every alteration may be prepared, and be changed into another nature. It is fixed thus: Take that which has been sublimated, and divide it into **cucurbits** <term>cucurbit</term> <note>original: "cucurbitas"; the lower, gourd-shaped part of a distilling apparatus.</note> or **urinals** <note>original: "urinalia"; glass flasks shaped like vessels for collecting urine, used for digestion or distillation.</note>, as the quantity of the material requires. And the sign of its fixation is when the matter no longer rises into the **alembic** <term>alembic</term> <note>original: "alembicum"; the "cap" or lid of a still that directs vapors into a condenser.</note>. Or you can increase the fire greatly, and then it immediately appears. Or place some of the substance upon an iron plate; if it remains fixed, do not repeat the process.

<header>A LITTLE TREATISE.</header>

## *A Summary of the Whole.*

I say, therefore, that the summary of the entire work is nothing more than this: that the **stone** <term>stone</term> <note>The "Philosopher's Stone," the legendary substance capable of turning base metals into gold.</note>, well-known from the chapters of these books, be taken and, with diligent labor, the work of the first degree of **sublimation** <term>sublimation</term> <note>The process of heating a substance until it vaporizes, then collecting the purified solid that forms as it cools.</note> be applied to it, so that it may be cleansed of all corrupting impurity. Then, once it is dissolved, let its "white" or "red" addition <note>Alchemists distinguished between the "White Work" (creating silver) and the "Red Work" (creating gold).</note> be refined until, in the final stage of sublimation, it becomes **volatile**. <term>volatile</term> <note>In alchemy, a substance that easily vaporizes or "flies" from the fire.</note>

Furthermore, let it be **fixed** <term>fixation</term> <note>The process of making a volatile substance stable so that it no longer evaporates or changes when exposed to intense heat.</note> through the methods of fixation, until the entire substance remains still even in the harshness of the fire. Then, take the fixed part and the reserved non-fixed part and, through the methods of **solution** <note>Turning a solid substance into a liquid state.</note> and sublimation, make the substance volatile; then make the volatile fixed, and the fixed dissolved. Repeat this—making the volatile fixed and the fixed volatile—until it flows <note>Referring to the "waxing" stage where the stone melts like wax without evaporating, indicating it is ready for use.</note> and transforms into a certain **sun-making** <note>original: "solifico"; the power to create gold.</note> or **moon-making** <note>original: "lunifico"; the power to create silver.</note> perfection. And in this way is prepared the most precious **secret** <term>arcanum</term> <note>original: "arcanum"; a profound secret of nature or a "great mystery."</note>, more valuable than any price in the world, the
->incomparable treasure<-
->of all the philosophers.<-

It concludes by framing this process as the ultimate "incomparable treasure" of natural philosophy.</summary>

God made their natures diverse just like their creations, because they were created from diverse elements. For if they had been created from only one element, they would possess consistent natures.

Among these creatures, He created some from a single element: these are the angels, whom He created from fire alone. ### THE TRUMPETS <note>original: "BUCCINÆ," likely referring to the alchemical work *Clangor Buccinae* or "The Sound of the Trumpet."</note>

God in His essence does not die, except perhaps on the day of judgment. For the definition of death is the separation of that which is composed <note>i.e., death is the breaking apart of a compound into its individual parts</note>. However, in that which is not composed <note>simple or unitary substances</note>, there is no separation; hence there is no death or separation of the soul from the body [among simple beings]. For every compound made of two, three, or four components must necessarily be separated, which is the nature of death. And know that no compound lacking the element of fire eats, drinks, or sleeps. 

And how is it that since angels are created from fire, they do not eat? For it is said that fire is that which consumes <note>original: "comedit," literally eats; referring to the way a flame consumes fuel</note>. The answer is that simple fire <note>pure, celestial fire</note> does not consume, but rather "thick" or dense fire <note>material fire found on earth</note> does. For angels are not made from dense fire, but from the most subtle of the most subtle fire, which is simple. Therefore, having been created from this most subtle fire, they do not sleep, nor eat, nor drink.

Note that there are four primary qualities, namely heat, dryness, cold, and moisture. They are called the "primary qualities" because from them all the <term>elements: the four classical building blocks (Earth, Water, Air, Fire)</term> are composed; all things are "elemented" <note>given physical form through elements</note>, and all things are given a <term>complexion: the specific balance of these qualities that determines a being's nature or health</term>. And the elements themselves are made of these simple qualities. Therefore, they have the power to convert and change matter from one quality into another—sometimes into dry, sometimes into moist, sometimes into hot, and sometimes into cold—according to whether the division of nature is strengthened or weakened by the complexion of its elements. And how—

...creatures established by the creator participate in four elements and four natural <term>humors: the bodily fluids (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile) believed to control health and temperament</term>, namely: *Choler, Blood, Phlegm, and Melancholy*. Common height is that which is manifest <note>The "manifest" refers to the outward, visible appearance of a substance.</note>; depth is that which is hidden <note>The "occult" or hidden inner nature of a substance, a core concept in alchemy where the interior often has opposite qualities to the exterior.</note>; and the width partakes in the middle of these. For this reason, if a body in its height <note>meaning its external/visible aspect</note> is *earthy*, then within it there is something *cold, dry, and melancholic, bitter, acidic, foul, black, and feminine*. And consequently, in its depth <note>its hidden/internal aspect</note> it is *airy, hot, moist, sanguine <note>meaning related to the humor of blood</note>, yellow, sweet, fragrant, and masculine*. And if on one side it is *watery*, it follows that it would be *cold and moist, white, tasteless, fragrant, foul <note>original: "redolens, foetidū"; the text suggests a paradoxical smell that is both strong and putrid</note>, and feminine*. And consequently, on the other side, it will be *fiery, hot, dry, and red*.

<note>original: "BVCCINAE"; the plural of the Latin *buccina*, a curved horn or trumpet used in ancient Rome. In this context, it refers to the title of the work, signaling the "proclamation" of alchemical truths.</note>

...nature. And through other perspectives, by comparing that vein according to the direction of its potentiality <note>original: "possibilitatis"; in medieval philosophy, this refers to the capacity of matter to take on a form</note>. And by others it is called "possibility": because it has no form in itself in actuality, but it is necessary that it provides form along with possibility. Just as darkness is perceived in the act of seeing <note>meaning we "see" darkness only by the absence of light</note>, in such a way should this matter be understood—by understanding nothing of the matter itself. And for this reason, the form of the world is described to you as it is. In that way, the elements are ordered in the world, from which every thing is generated in the manner in which it appears, through succeeding heat. Thus says <term>Raymond Lully: a major 13th-century Majorcan philosopher and polymath to whom many later alchemical works were attributed</term>.

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Likewise, concerning fire—that is, concerning "formal heat"—Eximidius says in the <note>original: "Turba philosophorum"; The Assembly of the Philosophers, one of the oldest and most influential Latin alchemical texts, presented as a debate among pre-Socratic sages.</note> *Assembly of the Philosophers*: The beginning of all things—that is, of created things—is a certain nature, and that nature is perpetual and first, "cooking" all things and leading them to their due form and species. Why does he say "perpetual and first"? Perhaps someone might understand this as referring to the First Essence <note>i.e., God or the act of Creation</note>, but that is not true. Rather, he says "perpetual," meaning spiritual, and "first," meaning the most worthy of all creatures existing within the elements; for otherwise, the statement would be false. It is this which digests and cooks all things, giving shape to the <term>natural heat: the innate warmth believed by ancients to drive biological growth and chemical transformation</term>, by which all things are led to their specific form and figure.

# -> THE CLANGING <-
<note>original: "CLANGOR"; likely referring to the title of the work, *Clangor Buccinae* (The Clangour of the Trumpet), symbolizing the loud proclamation of alchemical secrets.</note>

The sun does not heat the earth, nor does it imprint its power <note>original: "virtutem"; the inherent strength or essential quality of a celestial body</note> upon the earth except through the mediation of the moon, which among the other stars is more receptive to the sun's light and heat, acting as a medium between the sun and the earth. For this reason, as the philosophers say, there are two impediments that prevent one thing from imprinting its power upon another: namely, a remote distance and an intervening medium. And so it is in the case of the sun and the earth, because the sun is far distant from the earth, and because the moon stands as a mediator there.

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;In the same way, in our alchemical art, the sun does not perfect the <term>tincture: the transformative "dye" or essence capable of transmuting base metals into gold</term> on its own except through the mediation of the moon. This is because it is distantly removed, as it has not yet reached that level of subtlety required to "tinge" or transform, and also because of those intermediate factors—namely, density and coarseness. For this reason, the moon is necessarily required there, so that she may refine the sun itself, making it rare and volatile, and separate out its impurity. For she, more than others, requires its light and nature among the other <gloss>planets, that is, metals</gloss>. <note>In traditional alchemy, the seven planets were directly linked to the seven metals: the Sun is Gold, the Moon is Silver, etc.</note>

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Therefore says **Hermes** <note>referring to Hermes Trismegistus, the mythical founder of alchemy</note> and **Aristotle** in *On Plants*: "The Sun is its father, the moon is its mother." <note>This is a famous quote from the *Emerald Tablet*, the foundational text of Western alchemy. The attribution to Aristotle's *On Plants* was common in the Middle Ages, though the text is now considered pseudo-Aristotelian.</note> Thus the moon is the mother and the field in which the solar seed must be sown; and so we have no need of anything else from which our stone and our alchemy may be made, other than the sun and the moon.

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Hence, in the *Epistle of the Sun to the Moon*, regarding the solar year when the moon begins to be joined with the sun in its thinness and to be illuminated by him, the sun first says: "In my sister the moon grows the degree of your wisdom, and not with any other of the servants..."

# -> THE SOUND OF THE TRUMPET <-

...the **prime matter** <note>original: "materia prima"; the formless foundation of all physical reality.</note> of all things exists within each of them in the form of **Mercury** <term>the "Quicksilver" principle, representing the fluid, feminine, and passive potential of matter</term>. This matter is called the generative genus, a real being, and the material boundary of nature, in which nature takes up its material principles during the act of generation, for it is the primary subject in nature. 

For it is then that species are changed into a different form than they were before—yet it is not the "species" themselves <note>In medieval philosophy, a "species" is the abstract, unchanging essence or "blueprint" of a thing (like "silverness"), whereas the "individual" is the actual physical object you can touch.</note> that are changed, but rather the individuals of those species. This is because individuals are the objects of our physical senses, and they are, by their nature, subject to decay and corruption. 

Species, however, since they are universal, are not subject to physical actions; therefore, they are not corruptible in themselves. The species of silver—which is **silverness** <note>original: "argenteitas"</note>—does not change into the species of gold, which is **goldness** <note>original: "aureitas"</note>, nor the other way around. This is because true species cannot be changed; however, the individuals of a species can certainly be reduced back to their **prime matter**.

Because when the form of a thing has been corrupted and resolved into its prime matter, then a new form is necessarily introduced—for the **corruption of one is the generation of another** <note>A fundamental law of medieval science: when one thing "dies" or breaks down, its matter immediately becomes the "birth" of something else.</note>. But because matter can never be destroyed in such a way that it does not remain under some form, it follows that when one form of a metal is destroyed, another is immediately introduced. This occurs specifically through the transmutation of **Mercury** into **sulfur** <term>the "active" or "masculine" principle of heat and structure</term> for the sake of the operation we intend. Furthermore, every individual multiplies the form of its own species and not that of another, as **Aristotle** and **Raymond** <note>Raymond Lully, a major figure in alchemical tradition.</note> say. Truly, this Mercury is not the common kind, for common mercury would not coagulate so quickly. Likewise, before all else, it will be beneficial to cleanse the spirit—that is, the Mercury—of its impurities [superfluities], and to draw out from it a substance in which there is nothing superfluous...

**To dye** <term>Tingere</term> is to transform that which is dyed into its own nature through the act of dyeing, and to remain joined with it without any separation, as seen in the nature of the fixer, the dyer, and the dyed.

The **Stone** <term>Lapis</term> is a body composed of the **fifth essence of metals** <term>quinta metallorum essentia</term> <note>The "quintessence" or highest, purest state of matter extracted from the four elements.</note>. **Oil** <term>Oleum</term> is the unctuous sliminess <note>original: "limositas"; refers to a viscous, oily state of matter.</note> of all metals floating upon the **menstruum** <term>menstruum</term> <note>A solvent used in alchemy to dissolve and prepare substances.</note> after they have been dissolved. It is essential that bodies be converted into oil, because if they are not converted, they will remain solid within themselves; thus, that which we seek will not be achieved, and the loss of all the principles of this art would follow.

The **menstruum** is that by which the bodies of metals are dissolved through natural dissolution, and their spirits are led from potential into action. According to this definition, it is demonstrated that the dissolution of metals must not be performed except with the aforementioned principle; if it were done otherwise, the result would be nothing in effect.

Moreover, the **Elixir of the philosophers** <term>Elixir philosophorum</term> is composed of three things: namely, the lunar, solar, and mercurial stone.

And likewise all things born of the earth decay and are changed, and **corruption** <note>Decay or "putrefaction" was considered a necessary stage in alchemy to release the "seed" for new growth.</note> enters upon them; then they sprout and are increased just like the increments from which they had their root and principle.

And because of this, **minerals** <term>mineralia</term> are not nourished so that they depart from their root, but each one returns to that which it was, nor is it converted from this into something else. And whoever says otherwise speaks falsely. This, therefore, is the conversion and division which the wise [philosophers] intend.

Understand it thus: For the **spirit** <note>In alchemy, the "spirit" usually refers to the volatile parts of a substance that can be evaporated or distilled.</note>, that is, **Mercury**, is the dwelling place of the **soul**—that is, of the Mercurial body—and that spirit is the **philosophers' dry water** <term>aqua sicca philosophorum</term> <note>A paradoxical term used to describe a substance that flows like water but does not wet the hands; it often refers to a highly purified or "philosophical" mercury.</note>. This is specifically the "middle substance" of living Mercury, and it is this spirit that extracts this soul from the perfected bodies. The soul itself is the **tincture** <note>The "tincture" is the concentrated essence or power of transformation that can change the color and nature of a base metal into gold or silver.</note> dissolved in the spirit, which is the water of the philosophers.

For just as a common dye is carried in its own water to color cloth, and the colored water runs into the fabric, and then the water departs through drying while the dye remains in the cloth—so too do the wise bring the water in which their tincture resides over their **white, blessed, thirsty earth** <note>The "thirsty earth" refers to a dry, chemically prepared base material (often a metallic oxide or "calx") that is ready to absorb the liquid essence.</note>. The water of the philosophers runs into their earth and is physically extended within it, staining the earth. Then the spiritual water retreats, and the soul remains in the body; this soul is the tincture. It is a subtle, invisible smoke, and its effect does not appear except within a body.

For our entire **mastery** <note>original: "magisterium"; the Great Work of creating the Philosopher's Stone.</note> is accomplished with our water. All necessary things are made from it and by it. For it dissolves the bodies themselves with a true philosophical dissolution, so that they are converted into the water from which they originated, as **Socrates** <note>Medieval alchemists often attributed their texts to ancient Greek philosophers like Socrates to lend them authority, though these attributions are usually apocryphal.</note> says. The secret of every thing is its life, namely water, as **Hermes** <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary founder of alchemy and author of the *Emerald Tablet*.</note> says. The **water of the air** <term>aqua aeris</term> existing between heaven and earth is the life of each and every thing; for this water dissolves the body...

<meta>This page (524) provides the theoretical foundation for the discussion on page 525. While page 525 describes the metaphorical "dyeing" of the metallic "fabric," this page defines the two types of Mercurial spirits—the preparing and the tinting—that make such a transformation possible.</meta>

# THE BLASTS

<page-num>524</page-num>

...into spirit, and from the dead it creates the living, and it makes a marriage between the man and the woman <note>A common alchemical metaphor for the union of opposites, such as Sulfur and Mercury or the fixed and the volatile.</note>. Indeed, it performs every benefit of the art.

And note that **quicksilver** <term>argentum vivum</term> <note>Literally "living silver"; the common name for mercury, which was viewed as a "spirit" because of its fluidity and volatility.</note>, or the spirit, is twofold: namely, the **preparing** and the **tinting**.

The **preparing spirit** dissolves the body and purifies it from corrupting causes; it extracts the second spirit existing in the body, which is the **tinting spirit**. It leads the bodies back to itself through dissolution, softens their hardness, and illuminates the bodies. By separating and removing their darkness and impurity from the purest parts, it raises them up and exalts the bodies by leading them back into a sublime nature. It inspires <note>original: *inspirat*; in this context, it refers to the infusion of a spiritual or gaseous quality.</note> and refines the substance while it makes the solid spiritual. These are the benefits and effects of the spirit, or the preparing quicksilver, which prepares the body by extracting from it the tinting spirit. 

Now this spirit—that is, quicksilver—is at first coarse, impure, and **fleeing** <note>original: *fugitivus*; refers to mercury’s tendency to evaporate or "escape" when heated.</note> because of the **sulfur** which it encounters and is mixed with in the passages of the earth. But by the operation of the art, which is performed through **distillation** <note>A process of separating components by heating and cooling.</note> and **sublimation** <note>The process of heating a substance into vapor and then collecting it as it cools back into a solid, used here to purify mercury.</note>, it is renewed, cleaned, purified, cooked down, thickened, and coagulated by means of white and red sulfur.

And this preparing spirit is twofold. The first is a dry, non-viscous vapor of much **acidity** <note>original: *acedinis*; refers to a sharp, penetrating chemical quality rather than just pH.</note>, exceedingly subtle, fleeing the face of the fire easily, having a great power of penetrating, and dissolving the mineral bodies. And this spirit comes from...

<page-num>525</page-num>

Using words equivocally, it is called Mercury, but Mercury is a spirit; therefore, by the final definition of reason, it is called a **dry spirit**. It is necessary for such a spirit to be shut away in a well-sealed **flask** <term>ampulla</term> <note>A glass vessel used in alchemical distillation and storage.</note>, and this is according to the intention of **Albertus** <note>Likely referring to Albertus Magnus (c. 1200–1280), a Dominican friar and bishop whose writings were foundational to medieval alchemy.</note>. For this spirit is generated from **astringent things** <term>rebus ponticis</term> <note>original: *rebus ponticis*; historically referring to bitter, sour, or sharp substances like vitriol or alum, named for the Pontus region.</note>; and he himself calls it a **fiery dry moisture**.

The other **preparing spirit** is moist in its vapor, not oily <term>unctuosus</term>, but viscous <term>viscosus</term> <note>The distinction between "oily" (associated with metals) and "viscous" (associated with the Stone) is a key technical point in this theory.</note>, of the greatest acidity, moderately refined, easily fleeing the harshness of fire and vanishing within it, possessing the power of dissolving bodies and spirits, being water existing within itself. Albertus also holds this view, as do many others, though they speak under the guise of other things. And such a spirit is also called Mercury by an equivocal name, and this is by way of comparison and metaphorical speech. 

For Mercury, as the philosophers say, has the greatest power of altering and penetrating bodies; it does not rest on a flat surface, and it does not wait for the test of fire. Such is the nature of these two spirits, and for that reason both are called Mercury. From these points, receive the true understanding of the sayings of the Philosophers, and your comprehension will be easy here and elsewhere; you will see that the philosophers do not contradict one another, as many have thought. Thus, it must be noted that **oily** is one thing, and **viscous** is another: for the **Stone** <term>lapis</term> is generated from viscous moisture, but **metals** <term>metalla</term> are generated from oily moisture.

...to be changed suddenly: because the material will stick to the sides of the vessel, until the material and the whole becomes like a murky mud. And then the glass vessel must be sealed and placed among hot ashes for drying as above, until it becomes a dry powder. And the greatest care must be taken, lest the spirit which dries the body, and is dried by the body, becomes volatile: for if it flies away from the body, the body cannot be perfected. Therefore, it is also required that the vessel be sealed with the Seal of Hermes <term>sigillo Hermetis; an airtight seal created by melting and fusing the glass neck of a vessel, named after the legendary father of alchemy, Hermes Trismegistus</term>. For if the vessel in our art were not closed for the inclusion of the spirit, the whole power would evaporate, just as in the generation of metal. Because if the smoke <note>original: "fumus"; in alchemical theory, metals were thought to grow in the earth from the combination of "sulfurous" and "mercurial" vapors or exhalations</note> from which metal is generated in the earth were to find an open place, it would breathe out, and would generate no metal.

It is also done so that the active elements do not withdraw from the passive elements until they reach perfect decoction <term>decoctio; a process of prolonged heating or "cooking" used to refine and mature the alchemical substance</term>, as has been shown above. And the time for each imbibition <term>imbibitio; the process of saturating the dry "earth" with liquid to nourish it, similar to watering a plant</term> for drying is twenty-five or thirty natural days. So says Arnoldus <note>Arnold of Villanova (c. 1240–1311), a highly influential medieval physician and alchemist</note>, although the Rosarius <note>likely referring to the *Rosarius Philosophorum* (The Rose Garden of the Philosophers), one of the most famous illustrated alchemical treatises</note> says: If there is one pound—that is, twelve ounces—of the imperfect body of the earth, it is fixed with its imbibitions in ninety days. The philosophers add: until it is completed as has been said. Sometimes, however, it is fixed in a greater or lesser time, according to the diligence of the operator, and because of the greater or lesser quantity of the pigments <term>pigmentalium; the raw chemical materials or coloring agents used in the work</term>.

Understand these instructions for the entire duration of the saturation <note>original: "imbibitionum"; the process of soaking a dry substance with liquid until it can absorb no more</note> processes for both the white and red stages. Repeat this cycle of dissolving and congealing—or drying—the black earth four times. When the fourth instance of dissolving and drying this earth is complete, the earth will remain fixed <term>fixa; a state where a substance has become stable and no longer evaporates or changes when exposed to fire</term> and shine with a black luster when broken; and if cast upon other metals <note>original: "corpora"; literally "bodies," usually referring to the base metals being transformed</note>, it changes their color. The more times this earth is dissolved and frozen, the more penetrating and refined its nature will become.

Another author says: The order of saturating the earth, using the reserved water, joining them, drying, and calcining must be repeated four times; in this way, you have sufficiently washed the precious earth of the Stone and managed its cooking. Through these steps of grinding, saturating with water, drying, and calcining, you have thoroughly cleansed the "Crow’s Head" <note>original: "caput corvi"; a traditional alchemical term for the "nigredo" or black stage, representing the death and decomposition of the old matter</note>—that black and foul-smelling earth—and guided it toward whiteness through the power of fire and heating. This matter is now fit to receive fermentation, which is the "animation" <note>original: "animatio"; the process of giving "life" or active power to the alchemical Stone</note> of the Stone itself.

Socrates <note>In medieval alchemy, "Socrates" was often cited as a legendary authority, though these texts are not by the historical philosopher</note> says: let four cookings be done in succession, and afterward the matter must be brought to life through a ferment and cooked once more. For he says: Join the matter to its own water and cook it; this must be done until it melts and turns white. Afterward, let it be cooked again until it reaches redness and a harmonious composition. Finally, let it be cooked again with a stronger fire, and this last cooking,

This is the action in which the body is fixed and transformed into spirit. In total, there are seven cookings <term>decoctiones; prolonged heating or boiling of a substance to refine it</term>: specifically four before the "giving of life" <note>original: "vivificationem"</note>—that is, fermentation—and three afterward. These are represented by seven "roasts," as the philosopher also states. Our bronze <note>original: "aes nostrum"; likely referring to the material in its transitional state</note> has a dropsical <term>hydropicum; swollen with excess fluid, an alchemical metaphor for a substance containing too much impure moisture</term> body, much like Naaman the Syrian was leprous. For this reason, it seeks the bath of rebirth seven times in the Jordan River, so that it may be cleansed of its innate sufferings and corruptions <note>This refers to the story in 2 Kings 5 where Naaman is healed of leprosy by washing seven times in the Jordan; here, the "leprosy" represents the impurities of the base metal</note>. Only then do you possess sulfur and non-burning arsenic that alchemists can use, and with which they produce perfect silver.

Gratian says: "Whiten the Latten <term>Laton; a brass-like alloy, used here as a code for the material at the yellow or 'citrine' stage</term>, which is to say, the bronze with Mercury." This is because Latten is an imperfect, lemon-yellow body composed of both the Sun <note>gold</note> and the Moon <note>silver</note>. Once you have whitened it and, through long cooking, brought it back to its original yellow color, you will once again have a Latten that is just as malleable <term>ductibilem; capable of being hammered or shaped without breaking</term> and in whatever quantity you wish. Then you have entered through the door and possess the very beginning of the Art. At that point, you must calcine, dissolve, and wax <term>incera; to add a 'softening' agent or moisture to a dry powder until it has the consistency of wax</term>; proceed in this way through the middle stage. If you can make the "resurrected" matter penetrable <note>meaning the substance can now seep into and transform other metals</note>, then you have reached the end.

For Rhazes <note>original: "Rafis"; a 9th-century Persian physician and alchemist</note>, Morienus, and Assiduus say: because the earth, once it has been whitened and made bright, becomes stable <term>fixa; resistant to the heat of the fire</term> due to the "fixation of the moon" <note>the stabilization of the silver stage</note>, but it is not yet stabilized by the "fixation of the sun" <note>the final gold stage</note>; therefore, it transforms things into silver. Afterward, in the Work, comes the "leap of the moon"—which is the sublimation <term>sublimatio; the process of vaporizing and re-solidifying a substance to purify it</term> of the lunar moisture—and the "circle of the sun":

### *Another practical way. Some do it this way with the earth.*

When you already have the dried earth, then put it in a glass vessel, and place upon it a sixth or seventh part of Mercury so that it may be dissolved. For this reason, weigh it first, and seal the glass with the Seal of Hermes <term>sigillo Hermetis; an airtight seal created by melting the glass neck of a vessel to prevent the escape of vapors</term> lest the "flower" <note>the volatile essence or "spirit" of the substance</note> escape, and over a gentle heat in the ashes, dry and congeal it. Repeat this dissolution and coagulation four times. Once the fourth dissolution and coagulation of this earth of ours is completed, this earth will remain fixed and bright, black when broken, and when cast upon [other] bodies it alters their color, but not Mercury. And the more times this earth is dissolved and congealed, the more penetrable and subtle it will be in its nature, as was also said above, also tending more toward whiteness <note>original: "albedinem"; the second major stage of the alchemical Great Work, following the black stage</note> in these four dissolutions—

Know <note>original: "tote," likely a fragment of "scitote" (know ye)</note> that the beginning of the whole work is whitening <term>dealbatio; the purification of the matter into a white state</term>, which redness <note>original: "rubor"; the final stage of the Great Work, Rubedo</note> follows, and then the perfection of the work. And because without ferment no **tincture** <term>tinctura; the power of the stone to change the color and nature of metals</term> is made perfect, as the Philosophers say, just as good bread is not made without fermented dough <note>original: "pasta non fermentata"</note>, so it is in our stone. For the ferment is like the **soul**, which gives life to the imperfect dead body by means of the spirit, that is, **Mercury**. Because Aristotle <note>Alchemical texts were often falsely attributed to Aristotle in the Middle Ages to lend them authority</note> says: Nothing is completed except with a refined ferment, like a spirit. 

*The Verse:* For a good dough you should use water as well as ferment; in a similar way in our stone. You will find these three things similar to the sayings of the philosophers. And the ferment is nothing other than the **Sun** <note>Sol; representing Gold</note> for both the white and red Elixir, and the **Moon** <note>Luna; representing Silver</note> for the white Elixir alone; namely, the gold or silver of the philosophers, and not the gold or silver of nature <note>A common alchemical warning: their materials are "living" or "philosophical" versions of metals, not the common metals found in a marketplace</note>. Whence the ferment of gold is nothing but its own sulfur, which converts the white into silver, because that never fixes what is not naturally fixed, nor was it ever so.

Likewise, the ferment is made from the pure matter of metals, that is, from the **sulfur of nature** and the vapor of the elements <note>original: "e-mentorum"; a common contraction/typo for "elementorum"</note>. Note, the **white ferment** <term>fermentum album; the agent used to reach the silver stage of the Great Work</term> is made thus. Feed one part of the purest **Moon** <note>Luna; the alchemical name for Silver</note>, finely filed or beaten into thin leaves, with double its amount of very clean, white **Mercury** <note>Quicksilver</note>. Grind these together strongly in a stone mortar until the Mercury "drinks up" the silver filings and it becomes like butter, so that nothing of the filings can be seen. Then wash this ferment thoroughly with strong vinegar and common salt, well prepared, until the vinegar comes out clear and very pure. Then wash away the salt with fresh water, and dry the mixture by the fire. From here, add to it one part of **white sulfur**, grinding the whole together until it returns to being a single body. Then soften it <term>incera; literally "to wax," meaning to bring a dry substance to a soft, waxy consistency by adding liquid</term> with one part of water, and set it to be sublimated, etc.

In the same way, the **red ferment** <term>fermentum rubeum; the agent used to reach the final gold stage</term> is made with the purest **Sun** <note>Sol; the alchemical name for Gold</note> as described above, although Pandolphus <note>A speaker in the *Turba Philosophorum*, one of the oldest Latin alchemical texts</note> says in the *Turba* that no **tinging poison** <note>original: "venenum tigens"; in alchemy, "poison" often refers to a potent medicinal or transformative agent</note> is generated without the sun and its shadow. Many others agree with this, because no other ferment is made for both the white and the red **tinctures** <term>tinctura; the power to change the color and nature of metals</term> than the Sun.
