Likewise, the **Rosary** <note>original: "Rosarius"; likely referring to the *Rosarium Philosophorum* (The Rosary of the Philosophers), one of the most famous medieval alchemical texts</note> and **Peter of Zalento** <note>An alchemist often cited alongside Arnald of Villanova in late medieval collections</note> say: The **ferment** <term>fermentum; the agent of transformation</term>, which is the medium that joins things together, if it is placed at the beginning or in the middle, the work is finished more quickly and does not require repetition. However, they do not say this by way of denial <note>original: "per abnegationem"; meaning they are not excluding other methods, but rather highlighting an efficient one</note>. **Arnold** <note>Arnald of Villanova (c. 1240–1311), a famous physician and alchemist</note> says: When you wish to ferment the aforementioned medicine, then dissolve it in the stated distilled moisture, as was said above, until it becomes watery like **Mercury** <note>Quicksilver</note>. Then place it in a vessel over the fire in the full **regimen** <term>regimine; the systematic process of controlled heating</term> until the colors appear, as in the first regimen, until you have the **Elixir** as before, both fusible <note>easy to melt</note> and staining <note>tingentem; the ability to "color" or transform base metal into silver or gold</note>. And then the effect of that same elixir is doubled in fermentation, quantity, and **projection** <term>proiectio; the final act of throwing the alchemical catalyst onto the molten base metal to transform it</term>, etc. Since in every dissolution and fixation it acquires for itself ten times the power in multiplication, therefore the more the medicine is dissolved, fixed, stained, and melted, the better and more powerfully it works.

Likewise, note concerning the ferment: From the perfect, nothing is made, because it is already perfected, insofar as this matter or art completes it. We have an example: leavened and baked bread is perfect in its state or being, and has reached its final end, nor can you ferment it any further. So it is in gold: pure gold has been led through the trial of fire into a firm and fi[xed] <note>The text cuts off mid-word: "fi-" likely for "firmum" or "fixum"</note>...

And in the hour of the greatest **conjunction** <term>coniunctionis; the mystical union of opposites, such as male and female or spirit and body</term>, miracles appear: for then the imperfect body is colored with a firm coloration by means of the ferment. This ferment is the soul of the imperfect body, and the spirit is joined with the body by means of the soul, and is bound together with it into the color of the ferment; it is joined...

Hence the **quintessence** <term>quinta essentia; the "fifth essence" or ether, a celestial and incorruptible substance superior to the four earthly elements</term> is a body that differs on its own from all elements and element-composed things, both in matter and in form, as well as in nature and power. It contains no **contrariety** <note>the conflict between opposing qualities, like hot and cold, which alchemists believed led to decay</note> within itself, and therefore contains no cause of corruption. **Thomas** <note>likely referring to the *Compendium Alchimiae* attributed to St. Thomas Aquinas, though modern scholars consider such works "Pseudo-Aquinas"</note> states this in his compendium, where he distinguishes between an element, an element-composed thing, and the quintessence.

Nor, conversely, can there be a transition from yellow back to white, until the compound is turned into black. Nor can gold be made into indivisible silver unless it is first destroyed, and becomes black, and is corrupted; nor can the better be made from the worse except through the corruption of itself, because the **generation of one is the corruption of the other** <note>A fundamental Aristotelian and alchemical axiom: for a new form to arise, the old form must be destroyed.</note>. And this happens with the addition of the "tinting thing" <note>the Tincture or Elixir</note> which is known to nature, and thus it is perfected. And then the **ferment** <term>fermentum; a substance (often likened to yeast) added to the alchemical work to "leaven" the mass and fix its qualities</term> is applied.

The spirit dries the body, and is dried by the body—specifically when it has been perfectly purged of its **phlegm** <note>original: "flegmate"; referring to the watery, impure moisture that must be removed for the "spirit" to stabilize</note>.

Therefore, take the **first water** <note>likely referring to the initial distilled solvent or "mercurial water" used in the work</note> separated from all corruption, in which you must cook the thing named by its own name for forty days <note>forty days represents a "philosophical month," a traditional period for digestion in alchemy</note> in its own vessel. You will then find the body converted into **quicksilver** <note>original: *argentum viuum*</note>. When, through **sublimation** <term>sublimatio; the process of heating a substance until it rises as vapor and solidifies at the top of the vessel</term>, it has been stripped of its blackness, it will become a sublime nature lacking "shadow"—that is, lacking the thick filth of the earth and the traces of burning. 

For this reason, refine the body as much as you are able, and cook it with pure Mercury. When the body has drunk in and enclosed a part of the Mercury within itself, refine it quickly with fire—using the strongest heat you can—until it ascends in the likeness of a very white powder, like snow, adhering to the joints of the **aludel** <term>aludel; a series of pear-shaped pots used as receivers in the sublimation process</term>. 

The ash remaining at the bottom is the dregs and slag of the bodies, despised and to be cast away, for there is no "life" held within it. It is a very light powder that vanishes with a slight puff of breath, as it is nothing but a **wicked sulfur** <note>original: *sulphur prauum*; in alchemy, "sulfur" often represents the combustible or "hot" principle; "wicked" sulfur refers to the impure, non-essential part that causes unwanted burning or charring</note> excluded by nature. 

Then, once these dregs are cast aside, repeat the sublimation of the white powder by itself without its dregs, until it is **fixed** <term>fixed; rendered stable and no longer volatile when exposed to heat</term>, and until it leaves behind no further dregs, but ascends most pure in the manner of snow. This is our pure **fifth essence** <term>quinta essentia; the "quintessence" or highest state of matter that contains the medicinal and transformative power of the stone</term>...

### *The method of fixing.* <note>original: "Modus figendi"; "fixing" in alchemy refers to making a volatile substance stable under heat.</note>

Prepare the **ferment** <term>fermentum; a substance used to "leaven" or transform the base metal, much like yeast in bread</term>—that is, the body before fermentation—so that it is dissolved and **calcined** <term>calcinatum; reduced to a fine powder by high heat</term>. This means the body is dissolved and calcined by means of **quicksilver** <term>argentum vivum; mercury</term>, such that the quicksilver is separated and removed from it, leaving behind a **calx** <term>calx; the powdery residue left after heating a metal</term> or the most pure ash; for if you have not prepared the ferment properly, it will be worth nothing. 

And similarly, prepare the **non-burning sulfur** <term>sulphur non urens; a purified form of sulfur that does not consume or blacken the metal</term> from the calx through **sublimation** <term>sublimatio; the process of heating a substance until it turns to vapor and then collects as a solid again in the neck of the vessel</term>, so that it becomes simple and "living." For if you do not mix this into the **Elixir** <note>the "Medicine" or "Philosopher's Stone" in liquid or powder form</note>, the body upon which the **projection** <term>proiectio; the final step of throwing the Elixir onto a molten base metal to transmute it</term> of sulfur is made will not be colored. And if you do not cleanse the body that you wish to mix into the Elixir, the body will neither direct the spirit nor retain it. Furthermore, if you do not sublimate this kind of sulfur which you wish to put into the Elixir, the resulting gold and silver will be very dark.

And if you do not cleanse the spirit, it will not withstand the fire, because an impure spirit cannot be joined to the body **in its smallest parts** <note>original: "per minima"; refers to a perfect, microscopic union of substances</note>. You must also be very cautious to make the Elixir a medium between hard and soft; because unless you know how to do this, the gold and silver will not be fit for working—that is, for hammering or for casting. For the medicine ought to be of a more subtle and more liquid substance, since these are bodies of greater fixation and retention than quicksilver is in its own nature, upon which they are projected. For as **Euclid** <note>Likely referring to a pseudo-Euclidean alchemical text common in the Middle Ages, rather than the Greek mathematician</note> says:

Our final secret is to possess the **medicine** <term>medicina; the Philosopher's Stone in its healing or transformative capacity</term> that flows before the **flight of Mercury** <note>original: "ante Mercurij fugam"; meaning the substance must melt and act before the mercury component can evaporate or "flee" from the heat</note>. For the **betrothal** <note>original: "sponsalitium"; a common alchemical metaphor for the chemical union or "wedding" of two substances</note> is nothing other than the joining of the **ferment** <term>fermentum; the substance that "leavens" or triggers the transformation of the base metal</term> with its own body, from which you intend to make the Elixir. Whence the philosopher says: First **illuminate** <note>purify or clarify</note> your body, and join it with the spirit and a clean body in **equality**, which is to say, in equal weight.

### *Regarding the weights of the ferment, sulfur, and Mercury.*

Note, for it must first be understood that the total amount of the **volatile** <term>volatilis; a substance that evaporates easily when heated</term> must not exceed the total amount of its cleansed, **fixed** <term>fixi; a substance that remains solid and stable under high heat</term> body. Otherwise, the bond of the "betrothal" would be turned into the flight of the non-fixed spirit and the volatile sulfur. The volatile must not exceed the sum of the fixed material united with it. Whence **Plato** <note>referring to an alchemical work traditionally but likely falsely attributed to the Greek philosopher</note> says: If a small amount of sulfur is cast upon a great quantity of the body, so that it holds power over it, it converts the body into a powder, the color of which will be like the color of the body upon which the **spirit of gold or silver** is cast. However, because sulfurs cannot enter into bodies unless...

...by means of the water, namely of **Mercury**, he makes their **marriage** <note>original: "matrimonium"; a metaphor for the chemical union of substances</note> with water: because it is the medium for joining the **tinctures** <term>tincturas; the color-changing or transformative essences</term>, that is, the sulfur and the ferment. Therefore, in that arrangement, first place the **calx** <term>calcem; a fine powder produced by heating</term> of the body or ferment. Second, place the water, that is, the **spirit**. Third, place the air, that is, the **soul**, or the sulfur extracted from the bodies.

And to use philosophical speech and doctrine: If you first mix oil into the earth, the oil will be **mortified** <term>mortificatum; "killed" or lost its active power</term> in the earth, because the oil enters the earth and is absorbed by it. If, however, you first place water, and then oil, the oil will stand above the water; or if you first place water, and then earth, the water will be heavier than the earth. 

When, therefore, you join the elements—namely water and air—so that they are **fixed** <term>figantur; made stable so they do not evaporate under heat</term> in the earth: If it is for the **white Elixir** <note>the preparation used to transmute metals into silver</note>, there must always be more of the earth than of any other element; otherwise the earth would not fix the spirit, but rather the spirit would fly away with it. And this must be done according to reason, following the measure of **de-watering** <term>deaquationis; the specific ratio or removal of the liquid component</term>. 

For example, for the **lunar Elixir** <note>the silver-making medicine</note>: If there is one and a half parts of air, there should be two parts of water, and there should be three parts of earth; and let the ferment of the earth be three times as much as the **white sulfur**. And in this there is neither addition nor subtraction.

Let all investigators of this art know that however much the Elixir is prepared or refined, it is all for nothing unless, after its preparation, it is joined with the true **ferment**. <term>fermento; a substance—usually gold for the red work or silver for the white—that "leavens" the Elixir and gives it the quality of the desired metal</term>.

## *Note on the ferment.*

It must be noted that when the Elixir is joined with **bodies** <note>referring to the base metals to be transformed</note>, it is necessary that it be joined *per minima* <term>per minima; a Latin phrase meaning "by the smallest parts," similar to mixing at a molecular level</term>, as **Albertus** <note>Albertus Magnus (c. 1200–1280), a medieval scholar and saint often cited as an authority in alchemy</note> says. A powerful and useful combination can never be made with solid things unless they are first **dissolved into waters** <note>turned into a liquid or "philosophical" solution</note>, and then mixed with one another; and then, in warm places with natural heat (or a heat proportional to it) acting upon them, they connect themselves through vapor over a suitable period of time. For it is necessary first to dissolve the Elixir, and afterwards to prepare and dissolve the **body** just like the Elixir, and then finally to take and join the solutions: namely, **three parts** of the Elixir and **one part** of the aforementioned bodies. Afterwards, it is necessary to congeal this whole and dissolve it again, and congeal it, and thus repeat the process until the whole is made into one without any separation. This entire process is completed through the benefit of our **Mercurial water**: for with this, the Elixir is dissolved and prepared, and with this, the bodies are dissolved and prepared. For this water is the agent of cleansing, joining, dissolving, whitening, and making red.

### *On the multiplication or augmentation of the stone.*

First, note what **augmentation** <term>augmentum; the process of increasing the power or quantity of the alchemical medicine</term> is. From which we see that augmentation is the addition to a pre-existing quantity. And augmentation in quality and goodness is to **dissolve** <term>solvere; to turn a solid into a liquid state</term> and **coagulate** <term>coagulare; to turn a liquid back into a solid</term> the **tincture** <term>tinctura; the active medicinal essence capable of transforming metals</term> itself; that is, to **imbibe** <term>imbibere; to soak a solid in a liquid until it is absorbed</term> it with our Mercury and to dry it out.

Or do it this way: Take one part of the prepared tincture and dissolve it in three parts of our **Mercury** <term>Mercurius; in this context, the "Mercury of the Philosophers," a specialized solvent, not common quicksilver</term>; then place it in a vessel, and seal the vessel, and place it among hot ashes throughout the process, as expressed above, until it is dried and becomes a powder. Then open the glass, and imbibe it again, and dry it as above; and the more times you do this, the more parts you will gain, and it **tints** <note>original: "tingit"; the ability of the Stone to spread its color and quality through a base metal</note> even further, as Arnold <note>Arnold of Villanova (c. 1240–1311), a famous physician and alchemist.</note> says.

Augmentation in quantity is this: Take three parts of the **fixed matter** <note>The stable, solid substance that has already undergone fixation.</note> that tints—that is, of the prepared tincture—and one part of the Mercury of the Philosophers, and place it in a vessel, and seal the vessel, and place it among hot ashes, as above, and dry it so that it becomes a powder. Then open the glass, and imbibe it again, and dry it, etc., as above. And the water—that is, the **quicksilver** <term>argentum vivum; literally "living silver" or mercury</term> or Mercury—adds or gives no more weight to the body except for as much of the metallic moisture as remains.

### Again, the medicine is multiplied in two ways.

### By dissolution of heat, or by dissolution of rarity.

**By dissolution of heat:** this is when you take the medicine placed in a glass vessel, and bury it in our **moist fire** <note>original: "igne nostro humido"; typically refers to a water bath (bain-marie) or the gentle, steady heat of rotting horse manure</note> for seven days or more, until the medicine is dissolved into water without any cloudiness. **By dissolution of rarity** <note>original: "solutione raritatis"; likely referring to thinning the substance through the introduction of vapor</note>: as when you take the glass vessel with the medicine, and let it be suspended in a new bronze pot, the mouth of which is narrow, in which water is boiling and the mouth is closed, so that from the vapor of the boiling water, the ascending vapor may dissolve the medicine.

[...it] surrounds the glass vessel in which the **medicine** <term>medicina; the transformative substance or "Elixir" sought by alchemists to perfect metals or heal the body</term> is kept, by a space of three fingers. And if at first it falls upon a thousand, the second time it falls upon ten thousand, the third upon a hundred thousand, the fourth upon a million, and so on even unto infinity.

...the **ferment** <term>fermentum; a substance that acts like a leaven or "starter," transforming the nature of the entire mass into its own likeness</term> for the white is pure Moon <note>original: "Luna"; referring to silver</note>: and the ferment for the red is pure Sun <note>original: "Sol"; referring to gold</note>. ### *The philosopher's stone is multiplied in three ways.*

The first way is done by the repetition of the known **corruption** <note>original: "corruptio"; in alchemy, this refers to the necessary decay or breaking down of a substance before it can be reborn in a higher form</note> back to the beginning; that is, by corrupting the stone through dissolution and **putrefaction** <term>putrefactio; a stage of blackness and decomposition seen as essential for spiritual and physical purification</term>, and through the joining of the elements, and burial in air or in earth, and through the **decoctions** <term>decoctio; a process of boiling or heating to extract or concentrate properties</term> of air and common fire.

And this applies to other particular works, through the joining of the elements with the **foliated earth** <note>original: "terra foliata"; a purified, white, flaky state of the matter often compared to "leaves" or salts</note>, and decoction by common fire, in a burial in **dung** <note>original: "fimi"; horse dung was frequently used in laboratories as a source of steady, gentle, moist heat for "incubating" the alchemical vessel</note>.

Likewise, both types of multiplication happen at once if you lead the medicine, already multiplied in quantity, to the two aforementioned **wheels** <term>rotas; refers to the cyclical, repetitive stages of the alchemical process, often visualized as a rotating wheel of transformation</term>, and do as has been said.

### *The method for projecting all the things prescribed above can be tested in this way.*

Let one part of the **medicine** <term>medicina; the finished Philosopher's Stone or Elixir</term> be taken, and ten parts of crude, purified **Mercury** <note>original: "Mercurij crudi purgati"; quicksilver</note>, in such a way that the Mercury is heated by the fire until it begins to fume. From that moment, let the medicine be projected <note>projectio; the act of "throwing" the Elixir onto the molten metal to initiate transformation</note> upon it; it will immediately flow, penetrating into the smallest parts. Then, with the fire kept vigorous, let the molten Mercury be collected. Take a small portion of this, and place it upon the fire with an equal amount of its own **living Mercury** <note>original: "Mercurij viui"; liquid quicksilver</note>, and let the weight be tested. If the added Mercury has notably receded <note>meaning it evaporated or "fled" from the heat because it was not fixed or transformed</note>, then the medicine is not sufficient for further parts. If, however, the body has not been notably diminished within the body, but the matter is still brittle, or too soft or hard, then let a small portion of this be taken again, along with an equal amount of crude Mercury, and let the process proceed through all steps as has been said, until the intent is achieved.

# THE CORRECTION OF FOOLS, A SHORT TREATISE
<note>original: CORRECTIO FATVORVM, TRACTATVLVS; this title suggests a work intended to correct the errors of "sophists" or "fools" who misunderstand the true principles of alchemy.</note>

## Prologue to the same.

<image-desc>A decorative woodcut initial letter 'C' inside a square border, featuring ornate leaf and vine motifs.</image-desc>

*SINCE* the correction <note>original: emendatio; can also mean improvement or restoration to a better state</note> of all things is the increase of the thing itself: Therefore, it is written in many sayings of the **Philosophers** <term>original: Philosophonū [Philosophorum]; likely referring to Aristotle or the collective wisdom of ancient sages</term> that nature is improved through **art** <term>original: ars; in this context, "art" refers specifically to the alchemical craft or human intervention</term> beyond the movement it possessed in its first form. For no art can labor except by the mediation of nature, since nature itself labors intrinsically and secretly within the art through the administration of the craftsman. From this it follows that the imitation of nature's power is both an increase and a labor, and an augmentation of the thing itself: because nature completes its own degree, as much as it is naturally able to complete, and it cannot surpass that unless it is hindered by some contrary force. However, art does not truly transcend nature by creating a new nature through simple labor. And for this reason it is said that art imitates nature, not that it builds a new one, but that it refines the power of that nature. Because of this, art begins to perfect where nature leaves off—namely, to uncover the subtle nature enclosed within a thing, and to make it manifest. For this reason, the mineral ore generates metals, yet it cannot generate **tinctures** <term>original: tincturas; the transformative substances or "colors" capable of transmuting base metals into gold</term>, although it truly contains a full tincture hidden within itself, just as the Philosopher says:

### ON THE UTILITY OF STUDY.

**Study** removes ignorance and leads the human **intellect** back to true **knowledge** and to the **science** of any thing. Therefore, it is necessary above all to acquire knowledge through the study of this sweet work <note>original: suauis operis; likely referring to the "Great Work" of alchemy, often described in sensory or emotional terms by practitioners</note>, and to sharpen one's wit through **physical** <term>original: physica; here referring to natural philosophy or the laws of the physical world</term> sayings, since the knowledge of **truth** is found within them. For it is impossible for such a person to prepare the secrets of the philosophers to a perfect end. ## *How many parts of minerals there are.*
### Chapter II.

Mineral bodies are specifically distinguished into two parts: namely, the metallic part and the mineral part. The metallic part refers to the metals which derive their origin from **Mercury** <note>original: Mercurio; in alchemical thought, Mercury is the "mother" or the fluid, feminine principle that combines with Sulfur to form all metals</note>. The mineral part refers to those things that do not draw their origin from Mercury. Examples of metals include gold, Silver <note>original: Luna</note>, Mercury, Tin <note>original: Iupiter</note>, Iron <note>original: Mars</note>, Lead <note>original: Saturnus</note>, and electrum <note>a natural or artificial alloy of gold and silver</note>. Examples of minerals include salts, inks <note>original: atramenta; refers to various metallic sulfates used for making dyes and writing fluids</note>, alum, vitriol, arsenic, and orpiment <note>original: auripigmentum; a gold-colored arsenic sulfide mineral</note>. These are distinct from the metals that derive their origin from Mercury.

Moreover, all metals that have taken their origin from Mercury are **ductile** <term>original: ductibilia; the property of a metal that allows it to be hammered thin or shaped without breaking</term> and **meltable**. This is because their material is a watery substance mixed with an earthy substance in such a strong combination that one cannot be separated from the other. For this reason, that watery substance is solidified by cold even more so after the action of heat, and they will therefore be ductile or workable by a smith. Water alone does not solidify except when combined with an earthy dryness that alters its wateriness, since there is no oily moisture within them. Because their solidification is caused by this earthy dryness, they are not easily dissolved or melted except by the action of intense heat upon them, according to how strongly and firmly they have been bound together.

### Chapter III.

The nature and substance of all meltable things come from quicksilver <note>original: argento vivo; another name for Mercury</note>, because [the metal] is solidified by means of that same quicksilver from the vapor or heat of white or red non-burning sulfur. This is because every dry thing naturally drinks its own moisture so that it may be unified in its parts.

Therefore, the vapor of the sulfur that solidifies the quicksilver is composed of an earthy, subtle, and airy substance, **boiled** and **digested** <term>original: decocta & digesta; alchemical terms for the maturation of substances through steady heat, mimicking the Earth's natural processes</term> from the first mixture, united to itself by the action of heat, and afterwards raised, boiled, and digested until it possesses the sulfurous power of solidifying quicksilver into metallic bodies. ## *On the generation of Mercury and which metals are generated from it.*

### Chapter IV.

Quicksilver <term>original: Argentum vivum; literally "living silver," the common name for Mercury</term> in its first root is composed of a white, subtle earth, highly sulfurous, strongly mixed with clear water until it becomes a single substance. This substance does not rest on a flat surface, nor does it stick to what touches it, because of the dryness that has altered the watery nature within it. It is, however, homogeneous in its nature: for either the whole remains in the fire and is fixed, or the whole flies away in smoke, since it is non-combustible and airy. And this is a sign of perfection. Therefore, when it first flows heated through sulfurous earth, it ascends to the top. Hence its nature is such that it is refined <note>original: subtilietur; made subtle or thin</note> by heat.

Nevertheless, by continual sublimation <term>original: sublimatione; the process of vaporizing a substance and then allowing it to condense back into a solid, used here to describe nature's way of purifying minerals</term> it is greatly purified, boiled down, and thickened, and is gradually congealed by means of white and red sulfur.

Since sulfur is dissolved many times, the sublimated quicksilver is first coagulated and made waxy <note>original: inceratum; an alchemical state where a substance becomes soft and pliable like wax, a stage preceding the final hardening into metal</note> by the action of heat, until over the course of thousands of years, by the successive work of nature, it is coagulated into a perfect metal. Indeed, from this substance, nature itself works metals within "mineral vessels" <note>referring to the natural cavities and veins in the Earth's crust where ores form</note>. In these works, therefore, it is necessary to imitate nature, for whoever...

**Lead** <term>original: plumbum</term> possesses a coarse, bad quicksilver that is of an ill and foul flavor and weak power; thus, it is continually corrupted by the violence of fire. 

In this way, the metallic bodies differ from quicksilver according to whether there is "foreign" or "burning" sulfur present within them. This is considered so because of the power residing in them: a large quantity of sulfur is an imperfection, while a large quantity of quicksilver is a perfection. This is because quicksilver is non-combustible and airy, whereas sulfur burns and is burned, and in every work, it hinders perfection.

This reasoning does not hold; on the contrary, true gold and silver—which are by no means permitted to be made in nature or by art except through the reduction of bodies into the first matter <term>primam materiam; the formless, primordial substance that serves as the base of all physical reality</term>—are only produced in this way. Thus the species <note>the fundamental "kind" or essence</note> of things can be transmuted, as Aristotle previously suggests <note>The author is likely referencing the "Sciant Artifices," a famous passage from the *Meteora* (actually a later addition by Avicenna) which claimed alchemists cannot truly change metals unless they break them down to their core essence</note>. And this is not accomplished by mere melting <note>original: liquefactionem</note> alone, but through the dissolving <note>original: resolutionem</note> of congealed Mercury, so that when its own spirit is mixed in, the body is transformed into Mercury.

# *On the difference in the generation of*
# *common and simple sulfur,*
# *and of Mercury.*

## Chapter VI.

Since it has been stated that the sulfur which causes metals to form is the element of metals along with Mercury, I now set forth the difference in the generation of Mercury and of sulfur, although they both certainly cause the metal to be—namely, through essential Mercury and through sulfur on the accidental side <note>In alchemy, "essential" refers to the core nature, while "accidental" refers to external qualities like color or hardness</note>. However, that sulfur is yet of two types: namely, "living" <note>original: viuum; also known as virgin or native sulfur found in nature</note> and "burning" <note>original: vrens; combustible or common sulfur</note>. Living sulfur causes metals, although they still differ significantly from one another according to how much they exist infected by the viscosity of the earth; nevertheless, simple living sulfur, which causes gold and silver, is nothing but a hot and dry vapor, generated from the purest terrestrial dryness, in which fire predominates in all its qualities, and it is called— <meta>The catchword "tur" suggests the next page begins with "dicitur," meaning "it is called."</meta>

...is considered an element alongside the Mercury of metals. 
But the generation of common sulfur <note>original: "sulphuris vulgi," referring to ordinary, impure sulfur found in the earth</note> differs from the generation of Mercury, as was stated above: because the wateriness <term>aqueitas; the fluid, volatile principle</term> of common sulfur is mixed with a most viscous earthiness, along with a burning heat, and they have become oily. Nor does it adhere to what touches it, because of the dryness of the earth, which has altered the wateriness by reason of the powerful mixture. And therefore, because of their harmony in some way in their generation, sulfur is mixed with Mercury, and one alters the other in nature. For this reason, every metallic body is known to clearly contain sulfur within itself; when it is melted by the heat of fire, Mercury and sulfur appear there—Mercury in the substance, and sulfur in the color, and in the red skin <note>original: "cute rubea"; this refers to the dross or oxide layer that rises to the surface of molten metal</note> floating on top. Thus, it is the nature of the one that it becomes the attachment of the other, since one without the other cannot be generated into a metal. And insofar as the sulfur is more simple <note>In alchemy, "simple" means pure or refined to its essence, rather than a "compound" of impurities</note>, to that same degree it rejoices more in and clings to simple and pure Mercury.

### *Question.*

Since the Philosopher <note>likely referring to Aristotle, the standard authority in medieval science</note> generally speaks to the effect that sulfur coagulates, it must be said that it does not. This is because all common sulfur <note>original: "sulphur vulgi"</note>, according to the Philosopher, is foreign and contrary to metals. Avicenna <note>the Latinized name of Ibn Sina, a Persian physician and alchemist</note> says: "That which did not originate from it does not enter into the mastery <term>magisterium; the successful completion of the alchemical process</term>." For it always infects, blackens, and corrupts, in whatever way it might be prepared through the art. For it is itself an infected fire; therefore, it hinders fusion. If, however, it is calcined <term>calcination; heating a substance to high temperatures to remove volatile parts</term>, it returns to an earthy substance, like a dead powder.

In what way, then, can it inspire life in others? For it has a double superfluity <note>excess or impurity</note>, namely, an inflammable substance and an earthy dregs <term>feculentiam; foulness or impurities</term>. Therefore, consider by these things that common sulfur is not the sulfur of the philosophers, since the sulfur of the philosophers <term>sulphur philosophorum; the refined, spiritual principle of sulfur</term> is a simple living fire, bringing life to other dead bodies and ripening them, so that it supplies the defect of nature; for it is of an overflowing ripeness, according as it is perfect in its own nature and is more and more purified through the art. Whence Avicenna says: "Such sulfur is not found upon the earth, except insofar as it emerges in those bodies of the Sun and the Moon <note>alchemical code for Gold and Silver</note>, and in another thing, which is that which is told to no one unless it be revealed to them by God." In the Sun, however, it is more perfect: because it is more digested and cooked <term>decoctum; ripened or refined by heat</term>.

But because it was determined in the preceding chapter that it is impossible for lesser minerals to be artificially made into metals, it remains to be proven here. First, in this way: because lesser minerals were not generated from the first matter of metals, which is Mercury <term>Mercurius; in alchemy, this refers to the "sophic" or philosophical mercury, the fluid, metallic principle of all matter</term>. For things of one species, there is one first matter and seed <note>original: "sperma"</note> from which they are generated.

The first part of the premise is evident—that lesser minerals are not generated from Mercury—for this reason: because [Mercury] always remains in the first matter of metals, and not in foreign sulfurs. But because this cannot be done artificially <term>artificialiter; through the alchemist’s manual art or laboratory work</term>, metals can by no means be made from them. Thus the first part of the premise is sufficiently declared.

## *Again concerning the simple, non-burning philosophical sulfur.*
### Chapter VIII.

The philosophers have subtly imagined how they might extract those sulfurs from these more perfect bodies <note>Refers to the "perfect metals," gold and silver</note> and purify their qualities through art, so that they might possess through art—mediated by nature—that which did not appear in them before, even though they previously contained it fully and secretly. ## *How red sulfur is in the Sun, and white is in the Moon.*

### *How gold cures the infirmities of men and the sick bodies of metals. Chapter XI.*

Since, moreover, among both common people and Philosophers <note>alchemists often referred to themselves simply as "Philosophers"</note>, gold holds the form that, remaining in its primary disposition, it may cure leprosy and have many other virtues, this is because of its complete digestion <term>digestio; the process of being "cooked" or perfected by nature's internal heat over time</term>. For the excellence of the fire acting within it consumes all bad humors <note>In ancient medicine, humors were the four bodily fluids—blood, phlegm, black bile, and yellow bile—which caused disease if unbalanced</note> existing in sick bodies, whether caused by a hot or cold cause.

Yet by no means can art so separate the parts joined in generation that they are simply transmuted <term>transmutatio: the change of one substance into another</term> back into the elements they once were. Since primary nature has changed one quality into another, art is well able to separate them in such a way—as the moist from the dry, or the cold from the hot. But nonetheless, one quality still possesses the nature of another in some part from the natural mixture; and because of this, they can be joined back together by art just as they were divided. If it were not for the fact that one quality participates in the nature of another—for instance, **water** in the nature of **earth** through coldness, or **air** in the nature of **water** through moisture, and so on for the rest—then it would follow that the natural work would be totally destroyed, since the elements would be in their simplest state just as they were before. What shall I say of those bronze vessels <note>The author is referring to cannons and artillery.</note> with which thunder and lightning are summoned among mortals? If only they were used solely against the sacrilegious enemies of the Christian faith!

There is, moreover, the science of the **Stone** <note>The Philosophers' Stone.</note>, so sublime and magnificent that in it almost all of nature and the whole universe of things may be seen, as if in a clear mirror. For it conducts itself like a **microcosm** <term>original: "mundi minoris"; the "lesser world," a concept where a single substance or the human being reflects the entire universe</term>, where there are the four elements and the quintessence, which they call "heaven." Within this, another most noble essence has its seat, which certain philosophers (if I may speak with due reverence) were accustomed to compare to Almighty God and the most holy and indivisible Trinity. To this, perhaps, you might apply the opinion of Anaxagoras <note>Anaxagoras (c. 500–428 BC) was a pre-Socratic philosopher who famously posited that "in everything there is a portion of everything," suggesting a fundamental unity in the composition of the universe.</note>, who posited that everything is in everything. We do not say that God fills all things so that they might contain Him, but rather so that they themselves might be contained by Him. Nor should it be thought that God exists in all things in such a way that each thing can hold Him according to the measure of its own size—as if larger things held more of Him and smaller things held less. Rather, God fills all things in such a way that there is no place where He is not. Consequently, we understand Him to be inside all things, but not enclosed; outside all things, but not excluded. He is internal so that, by His own uncircumscribed magnitude, He may enclose all things. 

For this reason, Saint Dionysius <note>Refers to Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite, a 5th-6th century theologian. Conversely, it is truer to say that all things are denied of Him, since He is none of the things which He has established. ...reciting that God is in all things, or rather, all things are in God, just as all numbers are contained within unity, or as all the straight lines of a circle meet at its center. Since unity is the common measure, fountain, and origin of all numbers—containing every number uniquely joined within itself—it is the principle of all multiplicity. In a similar way, created things relate to their creator. ...light. Since any given thing claims for itself as much of God—so to speak—as it is capable of receiving light. And since nothing is more keen-eyed than the sun, many of the Platonists <note>Followers of the philosophy of Plato, who often used the sun as a metaphor for the "Good."</note>, imitating Orpheus <note>A legendary Greek figure associated with mystical hymns and the discovery of sacred mysteries.</note> in this regard, have called the Sun the "eye of the world." They did so because in it, as if in some most brilliant mirror, all things are seen and reveal themselves. Heraclitus <note>A pre-Socratic philosopher known for his focus on fire and change.</note> says that all things become known to this; yet if you were to remove the sun from the world, [what would remain?]

What is our little body if the soul is missing? No pulsing vein can be felt there, nor does any judgment of the senses remain within it. There is no vital breath in it, nor any respiration. For this reason, it has even seemed right to some to call the sun the "heart of heaven." Just as in the heart there exists a living fountain of blood, moistening and irrigating the other members of the human body and infusing them with vital motion, so in the sun is seen the growth and preservation of all things, both lower and higher. 

This is because the sun, in a certain way, breathes life and heat into the lower things by its light. Light, moreover, is a certain simple act <term>act: In this philosophical context, "act" (actus) refers to the active realization or "shining forth" of a thing's potential.</term>, turning all things toward itself with life-giving heat and permeating all beings, leading their qualities and virtues through all things and scattering shadows and darkness. Therefore, Phoebus <note>A poetic name for Apollo, the sun god, often used in alchemical and philosophical texts to represent the solar principle.</note> sits in the middle with his shining golden hair, like a King and Emperor of the world holding a scepter and a rudder. Not only Iamblichus <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher who specialized in "theurgy," or divine rituals.</note> asserts that all the virtues of the heavenly bodies are present in him...

### *On Nature. Chapter IX.*

We assert that nature is a certain force implanted in things, procreating like from like. For nature generates, increases, and nourishes all things. Therefore, it holds within itself the names of all things. An animal is from nature; a stone, wood, a tree, and the bodies you see are from nature and its bond. Nature is the ligament of the elements and the power of mixing, which effects the mixtures of elements in any thing of this sublunary <term>sublunary: literally "below the moon," referring to the Earthly realm where things are subject to change and decay, as opposed to the unchanging heavens.</term> world, and it has impressed the form suitable to its species: through which that thing is distinguished and separated from any other thing. 

Nor is nature of any one color, yet it is the participant and producer of all colors; it is also of no weight or quality, but finally is the fertile mother of all qualities and things. What then is nature? God is nature, and nature is God. Understand it thus: from God arises something...

### *What the Philosophers sought, and the nature of that which they desired, wherein the ethereal spirit is held to be the chariot of the soul.*

->*Chapter X.*<-

The stone which the Philosophers <note>In this context, "Philosophers" refers specifically to alchemists, often called "natural philosophers" or "philosophers by fire."</note> seek is an **invisible and impalpable spirit**. It is a **tincture** <term>tincture: in alchemy, a potent substance or "stain" capable of transmuting base metals into gold or silver</term> and a staining spirit. This is what another spirit, one both visible and palpable, has hidden away in its innermost depths. In the same way, the Philosophers have left this same spirit to us unexplained, hidden under a veil of riddles. That stone is the **fifth thing** <note>original: "quintum à quatuor segregatum". This refers to the "Quintessence," the purified fifth element that exists beyond the four classical elements of earth, air, fire, and water.</note> separated from the four. It is the ligament of the elements, the medium and the bond that made the elements of gold exist in harmony, and which bonded together **sulfur and mercury** <note>The "Sulfur-Mercury theory" was the standard medieval explanation for the composition of metals; sulfur provided the qualities of combustibility and color, while mercury provided fluidity and luster.</note> within the womb of the earth into a metallic body. And because such a bond, which exists in the earth, cannot be grasped because it is invisible, the Philosophers sought it in a more perfect body. Therefore, the Philosophers seek that generative nature which is able to create metals, so that they might purify it and make it into a tincture a hundred thousand times more powerful than it had been before in fixed nature. They were accustomed to call it by a more secret name: "living fire," or the "living fire of nature," or the "soul as a middle nature." And just as Physicians distinguish a human being into body, spirit, and soul, in the same way, the Philosophers [divide] their stone into those...

### Chapter XI.

Such a bond, however, cannot be easily obtained because of the incredibly strong compaction <note>original: "compactionem". Gold was considered the most "perfect" metal because its atoms were thought to be so tightly packed that neither fire nor age could destroy it; only alchemical "dissolution" could open it.</note> of gold itself, except through **dissolution**. This process is the very foundation and beginning of this noble science, and within it lies the secret of all nature. Dissolution is the treasure of this work; it is that which "raises the poor man from the dung" and makes him equal to kings and princes. <note>A common alchemical reference to Psalm 113:7, suggesting that the "Great Work" provides both spiritual salvation and material transformation.</note> Therefore, the Philosophers ask: why must bodies—that is, gold or silver—be dissolved? They answer that it is so the **pure may be separated from the impure**. For the body is dissolved for this purpose: so that the "earth" itself may be cleansed in its depths.

The "Great Year" or Platonic Year is the time it takes for all the planets and stars to return to their original positions, often calculated as roughly 25,000 to 36,000 years.</note>—the Philosopher attributes a greater degree to fire, so that he may emulate nature as his guide in a shorter time. Therefore, you might rightly say that he possesses a singular blessedness of genius who can show you the fire suitable to nature.

Philosophers call their natural fire a **bath** <note>original: "balneum." This refers to a water bath or *bain-marie*, used to provide gentle, indirect heat.</note>, or their **sun**, or **horse vapor** <note>original: "fumum equinum." This refers to the heat generated by fermenting horse manure, a standard alchemical method for maintaining a steady, low temperature.</note>. Others create this with wood or some other material, but we produce it with coals in a furnace especially adapted for this purpose. Furthermore, the **stone** is usually placed in a triple earthenware vessel, so that a gentler heat may be maintained—a heat, I say, most similar to that of a hen while she hatches her eggs. 

And by that heat the **dragon**—that is, the **earth of gold**—mortifies itself <note>original: "se ipsum mortificat." In alchemical terms, "mortification" is the process of breaking down a substance's form, often associated with the black stage or "death" of the metal.</note> when it gives up its elements and spirits from itself. Conversely, it brings itself back to life when it has received the spirits back into itself. Wherefore it is compared to **Jesus Christ**, who voluntarily offered himself to death for us, and afterwards restored himself to life by his own power through the glory of the resurrection, never to perish again. We also say in this place that the dragon spits out from itself every obscu- <meta>catchword: scuri- (obscurity)</meta>

To which the spirit replies:

> I shall certainly do so, but wretched me, I am forced to depart, when [I see] you [valued] above all **precious stones**...

We have received from those ancient philosophers, who worked by nature alone, that their living water <note>original: "aquam suam vivam" — a term for the mercurial solvent used to dissolve metals</note> was divided into two parts. They labored in almost all things just as they had from the beginning, but with a greater diligence of both fire and effort; and they believed this repetition to be a truer or greater augmentation <term>augmentation: the process of increasing the quantity or the transformative power (the "projection") of the finished stone</term>. 

Wherefore the first philosophers used a much longer time in completing the stone. However, those born later and their successors are accustomed to finish it in the course of a year. For this reason, they might wish to tincture the white stone—with which they operate on the moon <note>original: "luna" — the alchemical name for silver</note>—entirely with lunar seed, or by adding other spirits to it, namely white spirits, drawn from Jupiter <note>original: "Iove" — the alchemical name for tin</note> and Saturn <note>original: "Saturno" — the alchemical name for lead</note> through sublimation <term>sublimation: the process of heating a substance until it vaporizes and then becomes solid again, used to purify "volatile" spirits</term>...

We distinguish the **mineral stone** in three ways:
1. The **Stone of the Philosophers** is made from gold alone and nature alone; it is the more sublime one, which the philosophers claim can cure all illnesses. 
2. Another is the **simple stone**, produced when only the root and **sulfur of gold or silver** is augmented at the end by the spirits of inferior bodies. Here, the weights—one part to three, or two parts to seven—are discussed as set forth in the *Minor Assembly* <note>original: "Minori Turba," likely referring to the *Turba Philosophorum*, one of the oldest and most influential Latin alchemical texts</note>, requiring only sulfur, either of gold or of silver.

That **Plato** also did this is evident from the letter he wrote to **Dionysius** concerning the nature of the "first being," in which he concealed his teachings through receding similarities and mathematical figures. He wrote: "One must write," he said, "through **riddles and enigmas** <note>original: "per ambages & ænigmata"</note>, so that if by chance the book happens to be tossed about by sea or land, he who reads it may not understand." I believe this also gave the **Poets** a reason for storytelling: so that sublime matters would not reach the common, ignoble people, they hid the sweetest nourishment of philosophy within the strange outer shell of fables. We read that the **Egyptians**, in order to keep their dogmas in their sanctuaries, concealed them with mysterious letters—that is, with certain figures of animals—serving as a seal of nature. If I remember correctly, a **vulture** was depicted. A **dragon** drawn into a circle and biting its own tail <note>the Ouroboros, a symbol of eternity and the cyclical nature of the universe</note> represented the image of the passing year. Do not even the most curious seekers strive to assign a specific character to every single thing, so that the notation of that thing might be more hidden? Thus it happened that those ancient philosophers saw fit to hand down this **divine art** <term>divine art: a common term for Alchemy, viewed as a sacred science bestowed by God</term> under more obscure words. ...to you, **son of philosophy** <note>A traditional address to a student or initiate of the alchemical arts</note>, I might explain certain obscure propositions, from which you might most easily be able to resolve other objections put to you. The philosophers say that their **stone** <note>The Philosopher's Stone, the legendary substance capable of transmuting base metals into gold</note> is found everywhere, in mountains and in caverns. From that poorly understood proposition, I am persuaded that all errors have flowed down to posterity—those who have worked with sheep's blood, hair, and other vain and foreign substances. 

Understand it in this way: Just as the **celestial sun itself** <note>original: "solipse cœlestis"</note> is everywhere in this **greater world** <note>the macrocosm or universe</note> through its rays, so this **earthly sun**—that is, gold—is everywhere in the whole **glass vessel**—that is, the **lesser world** <note>the microcosm, represented here by the chemist's flask</note>. In the **mountains**, that is, the "head" or top of the glass vessel and the sky; and in the **caverns**, that is, in the bottom of the glass and the earth. They say the stone is born on two mountains: in the mountain of heaven and the earth; understand this to mean within the glass vessel. 

Furthermore, they assert that their stone is in all things—that is, in all metals, which are their "things." Likewise, the stone is in every thing—that is, **nature** is in every thing. And because nature has all names within itself, and nature is the whole world, therefore the stone has many names and is said to be in every thing, although it may be closer in one thing than in another, since the philosophers demand only the **generative nature** of metals. Whence they say: the **rich** <note>original: "diuites," referring to noble or "perfect" metals</note>—that is, perfect bodies, such as gold and silver—possess that nature just as the **poor** <note>original: "pauperes"</note>—that is, **imperfect metals**—do. Nevertheless, the nature of gold or silver is more perfect and more permanent in fire than in the other metals. Also, the philosophers [call] the fixed thing and...

# -> ON THE ART <-

...they seek an enduring thing which rules the whole world, such as the **sun** or the **moon**. Whence in ancient times they called the sun the **lord of the world** <note>original: "mundi dominum"</note>: in which is the life for healing all things, which creates the day by its motion, as well as the night, and illuminates the entire world with its brilliance. Wherefore the sun says: **I am the stone.** Or: **In me is the stone.** The philosophers also say that the **work of the stone is the work of a woman, and the play of children.** <note>These are two of the most famous alchemical paradoxes. "Work of a woman" suggests that once the process is started, it requires only the patient, gentle heat of a hearth; "play of children" suggests the work is easy for those who know the secret, or refers to the way the chemical elements "toil" and "jump" in the glass.</note>

The **woman** is sometimes the earth, and sometimes <term>Mercury</term> <note>In alchemy, Mercury is the "feminine" principle of fluidity and transformation</note>, which seems to complete the whole work. The **children play with the stone**, that is, the three elements play with the earth, or the "lower bodies" play with the **golden stone** when they have increased it at the end of the process. Likewise, the children play with the stone and throw it away; this means the ignorant and unskillful throw the "earth" itself to the bottom when they have performed <term>sublimation</term> <note>The process of heating a substance until it turns to vapor and then solidifies again, leaving impurities behind</note>. Some philosophers have compared the work of the stone to the **creation of the world**.

Similarly, they compare it to the **generation of man** and his natural development. But later philosophers have hidden this skill not only in modern words, but also in **painted images**. I myself have seen, depicted with a most beautiful brush, a **naked virgin**, in the flower of her youth, with ivory-white hair, dark eyes, and cheeks of blending white and red, whose breasts were milky and perfectly smooth and rounded. 

And this virgin was so remarkable for the brilliant whiteness of her whole body, and so beautifully adorned and shaped with all the gifts of nature, that she could be considered most worthy of a **royal bedchamber**—a woman for whom all philosophers, both the ancient ones and the moderns, were desperately in love. <note>This "virgin" is an allegory for the pure, white stage of the alchemical process, known as the *Albedo*. Her beauty represents the perfection of the material before it is transformed into the "Red King" or the final Stone.</note>

You shall turn the very white earth you have obtained into a lemon-yellow color <note>original: "citrinabis"; referring to *citrinitas*, an intermediate stage in the alchemical process between the white and red works.</note> with a strong fire; then, by the force of the fire, you shall make it red <note>original: "rubificabis"; the *rubedo* or "reddening," the final stage of the Great Work.</note>. **On another method of working.** Furthermore, it is pleasing to grasp that divine skill in brief sentences and with marvelous ingenuity. **Dissolve the body**, take the **sulfur**, purify it, **sublime the spirit**, join the spirit with the sulfur, and you will possess the **philosophical art**. In every perfect alchemical work, however small, it is necessary to have the spirit and the sulfur of gold. The **spirit** tints with a golden color. The **sulfur** provides the golden weight and also **coagulates** <term>thickens or solidifies a liquid substance into a solid mass</term>. If either were lacking, you would achieve nothing in the work. They say that the entire secret of nature lies hidden within the **Venus of philosophical gold** <note>original: "In Venere auri philosophici"; Venus is the symbol for copper, suggesting a specific refinement of copper toward the state of gold.</note>, and they speak most truly. For this reason, it is customarily called the **coagulum** <note>original: "coagulum"; literally "rennet" or "curd," referring to the agent that fixes or "curdles" the volatile Mercury into a stable metal.</note>, as when it is said: "Take the curd from the body, and you have the **mastery** <note>original: "magisterium"; the perfected substance or the peak of alchemical achievement.</note>, than which there is nothing greater in nature." Likewise, purify the curd and remove the impediments, and you shall tint. But just as an unclean cloth—not unlike sulfur—cannot be purified without water, so the nature of sulfur is not washed without water. **To wash is to dissolve; to dissolve is to purify.** The **water** is **Mercury**; it is the key itself. It alone opens the body and whitens the sulfur; once it is whitened, the Mercury recedes along with the impurity. I would say you flourish with singular learning if you are able to remove that [impurity]. It is the impediment and eternal death.
